Product Strategy — Case

What Strategy Is and Isn't: The FY27 Plan at Silai Floor Systems

Sunday, 8 November 2026 · Gill Road, Ludhiana, Punjab

1. Opening

The knitting units on Gill Road ran a second shift on Sundays in November, and Waheeda Ahluwalia could hear the flat-bed machines through the window as she read slide three for the ninth time. It said: Silai FY27 Strategy — be the compliance backbone of Indian apparel exports. ₹100 crore ARR by FY29. Below it sat nine workstreams, each with an owner, a quarter and a revenue number, assembled from what every function had asked for.

Her independent director, Ravneet Sohal, had read the deck on Friday and sent back one line: "Waheeda, this is a budget with adjectives on it. Where are the choices?"

The board met at eleven on Monday at the investor's office in Gurugram. Samarth Capital Partners had put ₹80 crore on the table at a ₹340 crore pre-money valuation, on two conditions: a board-approved FY27 operating plan, and — in the term sheet's own words — "a stated wedge: the single customer segment and problem the company will own." That sheet expired on 30 November. Waheeda had fourteen hours to decide whether the deck in front of her was a strategy or a wish list with a target stapled to the top.

2. Company history

Silai Floor Systems was founded in 2016 by Waheeda Ahluwalia, nine years a production planner and then merchandising manager at a Ludhiana hosiery exporter, and Harpreet Grewal, who had built barcode terminals for warehouses in Ambala. Their first product was mundane and useful: bundle-ticket tracking from cutting table to finishing, with piece-rate capture on a supervisor's tablet, so the Friday wage sheet stopped being a shoebox of chits. Style and sampling PLM came in 2018 — tech packs, trim bills of material, sample approval trails. Buyer social-compliance evidence followed in 2020, once export houses discovered that a SMETA audit is mostly a document-retrieval exercise under time pressure.

One decision from October 2021 still shaped everything. To win Ajooba Knitwear Exports — fourteen units across Ludhiana and Tiruppur, then the largest logo Silai could realistically reach — Waheeda agreed to two things: a flat annual licence of ₹6.2 lakh per factory irrespective of lines, headcount or output, with a five-year price lock running through FY27; and a bespoke fork of the piece-rate payroll engine, wired to the attendance hardware Ajooba had already bought, with a source-code escrow clause.

The flat per-factory licence became the standard price card, because it made the sale a ten-minute conversation. It also decoupled Silai's revenue from its customers' growth: an export house that doubled its lines paid the same. By FY26 the five largest customers were 41% of ARR and, on any honest allocation of implementation cost, the thinnest margins in the book. The fork occupied seven of thirty-four engineers on permanent maintenance.

FY26 closed at ₹41.6 crore ARR across 208 factories and 71 export houses, with 174 employees: 96 in Ludhiana, 38 implementation staff in Tiruppur, 22 product people in Bengaluru, eleven in sales at Gurugram, three in Amsterdam, two in Toronto and two in Singapore. Gross margin was 63%. Net revenue retention was 104% — respectable, and, given the price lock, almost entirely new factories added rather than existing ones paying more.

3. The industry

India's apparel export industry is a cluster business: Tiruppur knits, Ludhiana does woollens and hosiery, the NCR belt does woven ladieswear, Bengaluru volume basics. The large integrated players — Shahi Exports, Arvind, Vardhman, Trident, Raymond, Page Industries — run their own IT. Below them sit some two thousand mid-size export houses of ten to forty units, where Silai lived, and below those a long tail still on Excel, WhatsApp and a register.

The forces bearing on the product came from outside India. European buyers demanded evidence, not assurances: amfori BSCI and Sedex SMETA audit trails, Better Cotton and GOTS chain-of-custody documents, increasingly worker-level records of hours and piece-rate earnings. The European Union's corporate sustainability due-diligence regime and the coming Digital Product Passport under its ecodesign rules promised to make all of this mandatory rather than merely contractual — though the Union's 2025 simplification push had moved both scope and dates outwards, which was precisely the problem. In the United States, cotton-traceability enforcement had made buyers ask questions Indian mills found hard to answer quickly. At home, the Ministry of Textiles' PM MITRA parks and the production-linked incentive scheme were pulling capacity toward greenfield sites, while Bangladesh and Vietnam competed on landed cost.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act had become operational in 2026, and its notice-and-consent obligations landed awkwardly on shop floors where biometric attendance was standard and a buyer's auditor now wanted worker-level data extracted and shared. Data minimisation and audit evidence pulled opposite ways, and nobody in the cluster had settled it.

Competition came from three directions. Anchal Apparel Cloud, of Tiruppur, sold line balancing and production tracking at ₹2.1 lakh per factory and nothing else. Ankan Trace Systems, Noida-based and venture-funded, had skipped factories and sold traceability dashboards to brands. Above them, global PLM vendors such as Centric and PTC served the integrated players, and SAP, Oracle and Zoho appeared in every large tender as the safe horizontal answer.

4. The situation in detail

Exhibit 1 sets out the sequence. Each step was defensible when taken; several rested on beliefs that have since weakened.

In January 2025 the European due-diligence timetable firmed up and the company formed a view that hardened into doctrine: within three years every mid-size Indian export house would have to produce machine-readable social-compliance evidence, and whoever held that evidence would hold the factory. Everything since was reasoned from that premise. By mid-2026 it was shakier — the simplification package had narrowed near-term scope and moved dates, and the buyers Mathias Køhler met in Amsterdam were still writing the requirement into contracts rather than waiting for law.

In April 2025 Silai shipped the Audit Evidence Vault. Adoption was excellent — 68% of factories within a year — and incremental revenue was zero, because the flat licence bundled everything. Nobody named the contradiction until Kabir Rastogi built Exhibit 2.

In August 2025 the Amsterdam desk opened on the theory that European buyers would pay for visibility across their vendor base. Fourteen months later it had two pilots: Steenbergen Modehuis BV, a Dutch retailer, paying €48,000 — about ₹45 lakh — a year, and Aubertin Textile SAS of Lyon on a free evaluation extended twice. Both were bought by sustainability functions with small discretionary budgets; neither merchandising organisation was in the room.

In January 2026, Aparna Iyengar's usage telemetry went live and produced Exhibit 3, which did not say what anyone expected. In May, Ajooba served notice: extend the flat licence two further years at the locked price, or it would evaluate Anchal. Ajooba was 18% of ARR, and its answer was due by 15 December.

5. The people

Waheeda Ahluwalia — Founder & CEO, LudhianaMust present the FY27 plan on Monday. Believes compliance is the durable position but cannot prove a customer ever paid extra for it. Not saying: she has concluded the 2021 price card was her mistake, and fears naming it now costs her the room.
Harpreet Grewal — Co-founder & CTO, LudhianaWants the fork retired in FY27 and its seven engineers returned to the core platform; calls it "the tax we pay for a sale we made in 2021." Not saying: retiring it almost certainly breaks Ajooba's renewal, and he would privately accept that.
Sarita Varma — Director, Compliance Products, TiruppurWants Silai deeper into audit evidence and chain-of-custody, selling upward to buyers, where regulation lands. Her headcount doubles under it. Not saying: two of her three largest reference factories deploy on-premise and are invisible in the telemetry she cites.
Nilanjana Sen — VP Product, BengaluruReads Exhibit 3 as decisive: the floor modules are what supervisors actually open, so the company should own the floor. Not saying: the floor is exactly where Anchal competes on price, and she has no answer to a ₹2.1 lakh alternative.
Rohit Bhalla — VP Sales, GurugramWants the price card left alone through FY27 and the roadmap broad enough that every prospect sees itself in the demo. Carries a ₹19 crore new-ARR number. Not saying: three of his largest pipeline deals were qualified on features that do not exist.
Mathias Køhler — Head of European Accounts, AmsterdamArgues the payer should flip: retailers fund the network, factories get the software free. Not saying: the Steenbergen contract has a twelve-month out, and Aubertin has asked for a second free year.
Aparna Iyengar — Principal Data Scientist, TorontoBuilt the telemetry. Has twice told the leadership team Exhibit 3 is being over-read, and been thanked and ignored. Not saying: she has begun interviewing, and the instrumentation depends on her.
Kabir Rastogi — CFO, LudhianaCares less about direction than about the pricing metric; wants a per-line or per-worker basis so revenue grows with customers. Not saying: he has modelled a version in which Silai loses Ajooba, Saanjha and Aabroo and is healthier in FY28 — and has not shown it to the board.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 — FY26 revenue and adoption by module

Buyer compliance & audit evidence14.234%141No
Cut-to-ship & line balancing11.728%202No
Piece-rate capture & wage sheet8.320%196No

Footnote: Silai sells one bundled per-factory licence. The split is an internal allocation made by the sales team in July 2026, weighting each module by how often it was named in the deal's discovery notes. No customer has received a module-level invoice.

Exhibit 3 — Median weekly in-product minutes per factory, Q2 FY27

Supervisor tablets stay logged in through a shift; session time is not distinguished from active use. Audit windows cluster in February and August, outside this quarter.

Exhibits 2 and 3 do not agree, and that disagreement is the argument the leadership team has had all autumn. Exhibit 2 says compliance is a third of the business; Exhibit 3 says it is the least-touched thing Silai builds. Read naively, one supports Sarita and the other Nilanjana. Read carefully, neither measures what either claims: Exhibit 2 measures where salespeople think value sits, Exhibit 3 how long a screen stayed open.

Exhibit 4 — FY26 competitive win/loss, new-logo deals

Exhibit 5 — European buyer demand: stated versus paid

Exhibit 5 is the one most likely to be misread on Monday. Nine of fourteen buyers saying they would pay is striking until one notices these were nine of fourteen people who had already walked up to a compliance-software stand, that no price was mentioned, and that fourteen months of effort has produced ₹45 lakh against roughly ₹2.6 crore of annual cost for the Amsterdam desk. Exhibit 4 carries a quieter problem: the largest category of lost deals is not Anchal but the factory that keeps its register, and in four of five such cases nobody wrote down why.

Exhibit 6 is the arithmetic Ravneet Sohal had in mind. Every workstream carries an owner and a revenue claim; together they need 690 engineer-months against 408 available, and the shortfall concentrates in the two with the largest and least evidenced claims.

7. Voices

"We keep saying compliance is the moat. Show me one invoice where a customer paid a rupee more for it. I built the allocation in Exhibit 2 myself, and I can tell you what it is: what our AEs remember talking about."

Kabir Rastogi, CFO, in the 21 October planning review, Ludhiana

"Minutes are not value. A wage sheet takes forty minutes a week because it is forty minutes of typing. An audit pack takes eleven minutes because we did the hard part in advance. Optimise for minutes and we will rebuild the least valuable thing we own."

Sarita Varma, on the compliance channel, 22 October

"Sarita, respectfully — 202 of 208 factories open line balancing every day. 141 have the Vault switched on and 25 minutes a week of tablet time on it. One is a habit. The other is a feature we talk about at board meetings."

Nilanjana Sen, same thread, 22 October

"Both of you are arguing about modules. Nobody here has said who the customer is. Ajooba, a 14-unit export house on a locked price, and Steenbergen, a Dutch retailer with 47 vendors, are not the same business — and we build for both out of one backlog."

Aparna Iyengar, same thread, 23 October, Toronto

"I can hold the number if the roadmap holds. Narrow in January and my pipeline halves by March — then we explain a miss to Samarth with a smaller product. Let's not confuse focus with subtraction."

Rohit Bhalla, VP Sales, email to Waheeda, 30 October

"Steenbergen's sustainability head told me plainly: her budget for the whole vendor programme next year is under €200,000, covering audits, training and software. We are not selling to a retailer. We are selling to a small department inside one."

Mathias Køhler, Amsterdam, call notes, 3 November

"Every quarter we say the fork is temporary. Seven people, five years. That is the strategy we actually executed, whatever the deck says."

Harpreet Grewal, CTO, 5 November

"Two Singapore accounts have asked whether worker-level records can be shared with buyers' auditors at all under the new Indian data law. I have no answer for them."

Mabel Quek, Customer Success, Singapore, 4 November

8. The options as Waheeda currently sees them

Option A — The compliance backbone

Fund EU traceability, the passport work and the DPDP consent layer; position Silai as the evidence system of record for mid-size export houses. Waheeda believes it is the hardest position to copy and the one regulation may make compulsory. It is also the module with 325 minutes a week of use, no separate price, and a timetable that has slipped once.

Option B — Own the floor

Fund line balancing v3, the piece-rate engine and sampling PLM; be the system supervisors open every shift and let compliance ride along. Usage supports it and renewals depend on it. It also puts Silai in direct price competition with Anchal at ₹2.1 lakh, with a product costing three times as much to build.

Option C — Flip the payer

Build the buyer portal, sell to European and American retailers across their vendor base, and give the factory software away to grow the network. It has one paying customer, a twelve-month out and a departmental budget behind it, and asks a Ludhiana company to build an Amsterdam-led enterprise sales motion within a year.

Waheeda had written these three on a page and something about it bothered her. All three were named after modules or channels; none named a customer, and none said anything about the ₹6.2 lakh flat licence, which was identical under all three. The Ajooba fork survived in all three. The ₹100 crore FY29 number sat at the bottom of all three, unchanged — three routes to a destination fixed before any route was examined. Kabir had asked weeks earlier whether the real choice was a pricing choice rather than a product one, and she had moved the discussion along because there was no slide for it.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board sits at eleven on Monday, 9 November. Samarth's term sheet expires 30 November and requires a named wedge; its partner was explicit that a nine-workstream plan would not qualify. Cash stands at ₹28 crore against a ₹1.9 crore monthly burn — fifteen months, or twelve if FY27 hiring proceeds. Capacity is 408 engineer-months against 690 requested, and Harpreet will not sign estimates he did not produce.

Ajooba's answer is due 15 December: 18% of ARR at a locked ₹6.2 lakh per factory, a fork consuming 56 engineer-months a year, and an escrow clause that complicates migration. Saanjha Knit Exports and Aabroo Garment Exports hold near-identical terms expiring in FY28, and both have asked what Ajooba is getting. The Tiruppur team of 38 sits on fixed-fee deployment contracts assuming the current product shape. DPDP obligations apply whichever option is chosen, and the workstream addressing them carries no revenue.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. The FY27 deck states an ambition and lists nine funded workstreams. Which parts are goals, which are plans, and which — if any — are choices? What would have to be added for it to qualify as a strategy?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 point in opposite directions. What does each actually measure, and what evidence — which neither provides — would settle the question?
  3. Exhibit 5 is used internally to justify the Amsterdam desk. What would you need to know before treating "nine of fourteen would pay" as demand, and what does the Steenbergen contract tell you that the survey does not?
  4. The 2021 flat-licence decision was logged as a commercial term. In what sense was it the most consequential strategic choice Silai has made, and what does that suggest about where strategy actually gets decided?
  5. Options A, B and C are named after modules and channels. Propose a fourth framing that begins from a customer and a pricing metric. Does the choice look different — and is Kabir's unshown FY28 model an argument for it, or a distraction?
  6. It is Monday morning. What should Waheeda do, and what exactly should she say to the board — including the sentence beginning "We will not…" and what she tells Rohit, Sarita and Ajooba afterwards?

11. Sunday night

At a quarter past eleven Waheeda deleted slide three and typed a new heading: What we will not do in FY27. She sat with the empty slide a long while. Every line she began took something from somebody who would be in the room the next morning — Sarita's headcount, Mathias's desk, Rohit's pipeline, Harpreet's seven engineers, Ajooba's price. She could defend any one removal. She could not yet defend the set, and no longer knew whether that was because the analysis was incomplete or because a strategy is precisely the thing you cannot fully defend before you commit to it.

Outside, the second shift changed. She saved the file, empty slide and all, and did not close the laptop.

Product Strategy — Case

What Strategy Is and Isn't: The FY27 Memo at Kanan Estate Systems

12 October 2026 · Six Mile, Guwahati, Assam

Opening

Jonali Bordoloi read the draft on her laptop for the third time and still did not like it. The heading said "Kanan Estate Systems: FY27 Strategy." Underneath sat a single aspirational line — become the operating system for tea plantations across South Asia and East Africa by FY29 — followed by fourteen bullet points: a coffee-estate module, a rubber-estate module, an auction-price predictor, a mobile app redesign, and a customised build for a prospective client in Kenya. It read like a wish list wearing a strategy's clothes. The board met in eight days, on 20 October, and expected a memo that told them what the company would do — and, just as importantly, what it would not. Jonali had founded Kanan in 2018 after watching her own family's garden in Upper Assam drown in paper attendance registers each audit season. She now had to decide, before the deadline, whether Kanan's strategy was a real set of choices or merely a goal with a plan stapled to it.

Company Background

Kanan Estate Systems sells software to tea garden groups and the factories and auction houses around them. Its four modules cover field operations and plucking records (leaf weighment logged from handheld devices at the garden gate), labour attendance and Provident Fund and gratuity computation under the Plantations Labour Act, factory batch and grading records for orthodox and CTC tea, and an auction-catalogue module that files lot data with the Tea Board of India ahead of sale at centres such as the Guwahati Tea Auction Centre and through brokers like J. Thomas & Company. By FY26 the company served 312 gardens across Assam and the Dooars-Terai belt of West Bengal, employed 92 people split between Guwahati, Bengaluru and a small Kolkata support desk, and closed the year near ₹14 crore in annual recurring revenue. Its nearest rival, Khoj AgriTech of Kolkata, undercut Kanan on price but had never matched its compliance depth. Larger horizontal players — Zoho and SAP among them — were starting to pitch generic ERP suites to bigger corporate groups, a threat Jonali watched but had not yet felt directly.

The Situation

Two events had forced the question. First, the shift of Indian labour law toward the Code on Social Security had made PF and gratuity computation for plantation workers more intricate, not less — exactly the terrain where Kanan's compliance engine was hardest to copy. Second, a Kenyan grower group, Kilimo Highlands Tea Growers Ltd, had approached Kanan's Mombasa sales desk about a multi-year contract worth an estimated ₹6 crore, wanting factory grading and auction-catalogue tools adapted for Kenya's tea belt around Kericho. Devraj Oberoi, who ran that desk, called it the reference client Kanan needed to prove it could scale beyond India. From Bengaluru, VP Engineering Aditya Phukan saw a different opening: many existing customers also grew coffee or rubber on adjoining land, and a crop-agnostic platform would widen the market without a new sales motion. From Berlin, Head of Product Design Nora Albrecht argued the opposite — that chasing three fronts at once with a 92-person team would blur the one thing customers already paid for. CFO Ritwik Sarma simply wanted the memo to say no to something, since the current draft, fully funded, would burn through eleven months of runway.

The People

Jonali Bordoloi — Founder & CEO, GuwahatiMust sign the FY27 memo before the 20 October board meeting; wants a strategy the company can actually defend, not a longer roadmap.
Aditya Phukan — VP Engineering, BengaluruWants to build coffee and rubber estate modules on top of the existing platform to widen the market without new customer acquisition cost.
Nora Albrecht — Head of Product Design, BerlinWants Kanan to narrow, not widen: double down on labour compliance and factory grading, the features rivals cannot easily copy.
Devraj Oberoi — VP Sales, International, MombasaWants engineering time committed to closing Kilimo Highlands as proof Kanan can win outside India.
Ritwik Sarma — CFO, GuwahatiWants the memo to state explicit trade-offs against the company's eleven-month cash runway, whichever direction is chosen.

Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — Kanan's four product lines, FY26
ModuleRevenue (₹ lakh)YoY growthGross marginGardens using it
Labour attendance & compliance61234%71%298
Field ops & plucking records39819%64%276
Factory batch & grading25422%58%190
Auction catalogue & Tea Board filing13641%66%144

Note: a garden can use more than one module; totals do not sum to headcount of 312 gardens served.

Exhibit 1 shows where Kanan actually makes money. Labour compliance is the largest line, growing fastest apart from the still-small auction module, and carries the best margin — evidence that the hardest-to-copy feature is also the most valuable one, not a cost centre kept for goodwill.

Exhibit 2 — The FY27 wish list on the table
InitiativeProposed byEngineer-monthsEst. FY27 revenue
Coffee & rubber estate modulesPhukan, Bengaluru14₹40–60 lakh
Kilimo Highlands custom build (Kenya)Oberoi, Mombasa9₹6 crore, 3-year
Deeper small-grower / bought-leaf toolsAlbrecht, Berlin7₹90 lakh–1.1 crore
Auction-price prediction analyticsSales, Guwahati10Unproven

Engineering has roughly eighteen months of capacity across FY27. Exhibit 2's four items alone ask for forty. A memo that approves all of them is not a strategy; it is an unprioritised backlog with a growth slogan pinned above it, and Ritwik's cash-runway warning follows directly from this arithmetic.

Exhibit 3 makes the geometry of the choice visible. Kanan's moat is the labour-compliance engine tuned to the Plantations Labour Act and its transition to the Code on Social Security. Kilimo Highlands sits under Kenya's Employment Act and NSSF rules and sells through the Mombasa Tea Auction, not the Tea Board of India — a different compliance stack entirely, not an extension of the one Kanan already owns. Coffee and rubber estates sit outside plantation labour rules too. Both growth options, in other words, ask Kanan to compete on ground where its hardest-won advantage does not transfer.

The Options

Option A — Fund the full roadmap

Approve coffee, rubber, Kenya and analytics together, betting a broader platform reduces dependence on Indian tea acreage, which the Tea Board has flagged as flat for three years. Upside: a bigger funding-round story and three logos outside the core market. Cost: eighteen months of capacity split across forty months of work, a near-certain slip on all four fronts, and a compliance engine that stops improving in its one defensible market.

Option B — Chase the Kilimo Highlands deal

Commit the international desk's ask and delay small-grower and analytics work to win the ₹6 crore, three-year Kenyan contract, treating it as proof the model travels. Upside: geographic diversification, foreign-currency revenue, a reference story for East Africa. Cost: nine engineer-months rebuilding compliance logic for an unfamiliar regime, no guarantee of resale to another Kenyan grower, and Assam's fastest-growing line left untouched.

Option C — Refuse both fronts and go deeper

Say no to coffee, rubber and Kilimo Highlands for FY27; commit engineering fully to labour-compliance depth, factory grading, and the underserved small-grower and bought-leaf segment in Assam and the Dooars-Terai. Upside: reinforces the one advantage rivals cannot copy, fits the eighteen-month capacity, and gives Ritwik a runway story that holds. Cost: Devraj loses a marquee deal and an international growth story for at least a year.

Questions for Discussion

  1. Is the current draft — "become the operating system for tea plantations across South Asia and East Africa" — a strategy, or a goal with a plan attached? What exactly is missing from it?
  2. Look again at Exhibit 2. Which of the four initiatives are genuine strategic choices, and which are simply items on a wish list that a real strategy would have to refuse?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, where does Kanan's actual source of advantage sit, and does the Kilimo Highlands opportunity build on that advantage or dilute it?
  4. Which option should Jonali take into the 20 October board meeting, and what single sentence should the memo contain that begins "We will not…"?

A Note for the Learner

The habit this case is built to interrupt is a common one: mistaking a destination and a to-do list for a strategy. Kanan's draft states an ambition (become the operating system for tea plantations) and appends a roadmap (four initiatives, funded together). Neither, alone, is a strategy. A goal describes where you want to end up; a plan sequences activity to get there; a strategy is the set of choices — which customer, which problem, which capability to build — that make winning more likely than the alternatives, and it is only recognisable as one once it also says what will be refused. Rumelt's later framing of a strategy "kernel" — diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action — is the natural next step, and it is precisely what Kanan's draft skips: a diagnosis sits buried in Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 3, but no guiding policy has been written down, only a list of actions.

A well-reasoned answer starts from the diagnosis the exhibits already contain: Kanan's revenue, margin and growth all concentrate in labour compliance, the module built on regulatory complexity no competitor has matched. It then asks whether each proposed initiative reinforces that position or borrows against it. Coffee, rubber and the Kilimo Highlands deal all borrow against it — each asks the same 92 people to build expertise in an unrelated regime rather than deepen the one they already own.

One defensible path, then, is Option C. Jonali takes to the board a memo that commits FY27 engineering entirely to labour compliance, factory grading and the small-grower segment inside India, and states plainly that Kanan will not build a Kenyan compliance stack or a coffee-and-rubber platform this year. This is not the only responsible answer — a founder with a longer runway or a signed letter of intent from Kilimo Highlands might reasonably choose Option B — but any answer earns the name "strategy" only once it names what it refuses, in front of the people, like Devraj, who most wanted otherwise.
exp20v2-pstrat.what:
Strategy & Business · Product Strategy

What Strategy Is and Isn't

On the morning of 14 August 2026, Ananya Rao, head of product strategy at Pratibimb Metrics, a Bengaluru-based retail-analytics SaaS company, sat through a board meeting that would define her next three weeks. Pratibimb sold a dashboard-and-alerts product that told retail chains which shelves were losing money, and it had closed the previous fiscal year at ₹18 crore in annual recurring revenue. The board chair, reviewing a slide of the broader retail-tech market, said the number Ananya would carry out of the room: triple ARR to ₹54 crore by the end of FY29. The CEO, Rohit Malhotra, turned to her before the meeting had even adjourned. "Write the strategy," he said. "We present it at the September offsite."

Ananya's problem was not that ₹54 crore sounded implausible. It was that she had watched two previous "strategies" at Pratibimb amount to the same document: a target number, a hockey-stick chart, and a list of initiatives that ran to eleven items, none ranked against the others or against anything the company would deliberately not do. Everyone in the room could recite the goal. No one could say, in one sentence, what Pratibimb had chosen to bet on that a competitor with the same ambition had not. If Ananya produced a third version of the same artifact, the company would spend the next three years running in several directions at once and arrive, most likely, short of ₹54 crore with its engineering team exhausted. Getting the distinction right decided how ninety people would spend the next three years of their working lives.

Figure 1. The board fixed the two endpoints. Nobody had yet chosen the route — and a route is what a strategy is.

1. The idea: choices, not a goal, not a plan

Strategy, in the sense this page uses the word, is a coherent set of choices about where a company will compete and how it will win there, made under scarcity, at the deliberate cost of other choices it could have made instead. It is not the destination (that is vision or a goal), and it is not the calendar of tasks that follows from a decision (that is a plan). The distinction is not pedantic. A goal describes an amount and a date — Pratibimb's ₹54 crore by FY29 — without saying how the company will get there or, more importantly, what it will therefore not do. A plan lists what happens and when, but it is only ever as good as the choice it executes; a beautifully scheduled plan built on the wrong choice delivers the wrong outcome efficiently. Strategy sits between the two: the logic that says which customers, which problem, and which of several credible paths to money the company is committing scarce people and capital to — and it only earns the name when saying yes to one thing visibly means saying no to another.

The formulation has an intellectual lineage worth naming. Kenneth Andrews and the Harvard Business School group that wrote the Business Policy course in the 1960s treated strategy as the match between what a firm could do and what its environment rewarded. In the 1980s, Michael Porter sharpened this into a claim about trade-offs: a firm's position is defined as much by what activities it refuses to perform as by what it performs, because trying to be good at contradictory things — low cost and maximum variety, say — usually means being mediocre at both. Richard Rumelt, whose kernel this topic leads into, later diagnosed the disease directly: most documents companies call strategy are what he named "fluff and goals," restated ambitions dressed in the vocabulary of strategy with no actual choice inside them. The sentence Ananya needed to say in the boardroom without sounding glib was some version of this: "Our strategy is not the ₹54 crore number — it is the specific bet we are making about which customers we can serve better than anyone else with the resources we actually have, and the things we are choosing not to build so that bet gets enough attention to work."

Figure 2. Vision names where you are going; strategy names the route you chose and the routes you refused; a plan schedules the steps of the route.

2. How it actually works

Building an actual strategy, rather than a goal with a plan taped to it, runs through steps experienced practitioners often perform without narrating them, which is why newcomers miss them. The first is diagnosis: naming, specifically, the obstacle between the company and the goal — not "we need more revenue" but "our customers are small stores whose average deal size cannot mathematically reach ₹54 crore, so we do not yet know which larger or more numerous customer type we can win." The second is generating more than one credible where-to-play option, because a choice with no rejected alternative beside it is usually just the first idea someone had. The third is specifying how the company will win in the chosen arena — what capability it has, or will build, that a rival targeting the same customers cannot cheaply copy. The fourth, almost always left implicit, is naming what will not be built as a direct consequence: a real choice always has a casualty. The fifth is checking the arithmetic — does the chosen path, run through the company's actual resources, plausibly reach the number in the time given, and if not, is the honest move to change the resources, the timeline, or the number itself.

For Ananya, this meant starting with a diagnosis rather than a list of initiatives: Pratibimb's ₹18 crore came from roughly sixty mid-sized regional retailers paying ₹30 lakh a year, sold by four reps on nine-month cycles with a 71% win rate on qualified opportunities. The obstacle was not effort; it was addressable market at that deal size. Two where-to-play choices emerged from that diagnosis, and the discipline lay in costing both honestly before picking one.

3. A worked example, run twice

Option A kept Pratibimb in its existing lane and pushed upmarket: national organised-retail chains, at an average contract value of ₹40 lakh, sold by the same enterprise motion. Option B moved downmarket into neighbourhood kirana-tech aggregators, a self-serve product at ₹1.2 lakh a year with no sales rep involved at all. Net new ARR required, either way, was ₹36 crore over three years (₹54cr − ₹18cr).

Table 1. The same ₹36 crore target, priced through two different choices, at the board's original 3× ask
Option A — enterprise chainsOption B — kirana-tech self-serve
Average contract value₹40 lakh/yr₹1.2 lakh/yr
New logos required36,00,00,000 ÷ 40,00,000 = 9036,00,00,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = 3,000
Per year over 3 years30 logos/yr1,000 logos/yr

Read as arithmetic, not aspiration, Option A meant more than doubling the sales organisation inside eighteen months in a segment where Pratibimb had already won most of the easy accounts — hard and expensive, but tractable. Option B meant a go-to-market motion the company had never run: self-serve sign-up, usage-based billing, in-product activation, funded by roughly ten engineering person-months drawn from the same pool building analytics features. Neither table cell is a plan; each is what a specific choice costs, stated in numbers Ananya could defend line by line.

The second pass matters as much as the first, because the "right" answer is contingent on an input the board itself controls. Suppose a monsoon-linked slowdown in retail capital spending led the board to revise the ask from 3× to 2× — ₹36 crore ARR, ₹18 crore net new. Re-run Option A: 18,00,00,000 ÷ 40,00,000 = 45 logos over three years, or 15 a year — achievable at five reps, one hire beyond today's four, no new product motion required. The same framework, fed a different number, now recommends the opposite path from a paragraph ago. That is the point of treating strategy as an output of explicit choices rather than a fixed verdict: the goal is an input to the reasoning, not a substitute for it, and a real strategist re-runs the arithmetic when the input changes instead of defending the first answer out of loyalty.

4. Nuances a learner must sit with

Strategy is not the same as ambition

"We will be the market leader in retail analytics" is a legitimate ambition and tells a new hire nothing about what to build this quarter. Ambition sets the bar a strategy must clear; it cannot itself decide between Option A and Option B, and treating ambition-language as a decision is the single most common failure this topic exists to correct.

Strategy is not the same as a plan, even a detailed one

A Gantt chart with fifty tasks can execute a bad choice flawlessly. The tell: ask what the "strategy document" would have looked like had the company chosen the opposite option. If it reads identically either way, it was a plan wearing a strategy's clothes.

It builds on, but is not, the vision

Pratibimb's vision — to make every retail decision measurably better — does not change if the board revises the ARR target. The strategy, the route through customers and capability, is exactly what should change when the underlying facts change.

"Everything is a priority" is evidence of no strategy

When a roadmap lists eleven equally weighted initiatives, the honest reading is not that the company is ambitious but that no one has forced the trade-off a real choice requires. Diagnostic: ask which initiative would be cut first if headcount fell 20% tomorrow — a slow answer means a wish list, not a ranked strategy.

A choice needs a diagnosis behind it, not just an option

Picking Option B without first establishing that deal size, not sales effort, was the obstacle would have been a guess dressed as a decision. Diagnosis is what separates strategic choice from preference; Rumelt's kernel, which this topic leads into, formalises that step explicitly.

Strategy cannot promise the outcome, only improve the odds

Even a well-reasoned Option B could fail if a well-funded rival launches an identical self-serve product eight months earlier. Strategy narrows the field of moves that can plausibly work and commits resources behind the best; it does not purchase certainty.

A strategy stated once is not one revisited every sprint

Because the second pass showed the answer moving when the board's number moved, a reader might conclude strategy should be re-decided constantly. It should be revisited when a load-bearing fact changes — the goal, the cost structure, a rival's move — not on a fixed cadence, and not because this month's numbers dipped.

5. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and start-up versus scale

The mechanics above generalise, but what counts as a "choice" shifts by business type. At Spashta, a Pune-based consumer habit-tracking app, the where-to-play choice was a use case — sleep versus fitness versus study habits — and an acquisition channel, because consumer products compete for attention before they compete for wallets; the stated casualty was a social feed, dropped deliberately because the founders judged it would lift engagement while undermining the calmer positioning they were betting on. At Nirmal Mandi, a two-sided marketplace linking wholesale produce traders to kirana stores, the choice was which side to subsidise first to reach liquidity, because marketplace strategy is largely a sequencing question about which side's presence draws the other — a dimension neither a consumer app nor a single-sided seller like Pratibimb has to resolve. B2B strategy, Pratibimb's own case, more often turns on segment and deal economics, because the customer is an organisation with its own budget cycle, not an individual choosing among substitutes on a Tuesday evening.

Scale changes what a choice is a choice among. Pratibimb, at ninety employees and one product, chooses among customer segments for that product. Aaina Group, a diversified glass-and-mirror manufacturer three decades older with businesses in automotive glass, architectural glazing and home décor, makes a different order of choice: which business unit gets next year's capital at all — a portfolio decision a single-product start-up never faces, since it has only one bet to fund. The discipline is unchanged; what changes is the unit being chosen among.

6. Common mistakes

Mistake one — the strategy deck is a KPI dashboard with a narrative wrapped around it. Symptom: every slide restates the ₹54 crore goal in a new chart. Underlying error: mistaking measurement of progress for a theory of how progress occurs. Cheapest diagnostic: delete the numbers slide and check whether a reader can still state the choice from what remains.

Mistake two — the roadmap is the strategy. Symptom: features ranked by internal debate rather than by which customer segment they serve. Underlying error: skipping the where-to-play choice and jumping straight to a plan. Cheapest diagnostic: for any three roadmap items, ask which segment each was chosen for — inconsistent answers mean no segment choice underneath them.

Mistake three — no stated casualty. Symptom: a memo that reads as pure addition, nothing subtracted. Underlying error: treating strategy as accumulation rather than selection. Cheapest diagnostic: ask the author, in the room, what the company is now choosing not to build, and time the answer.

Mistake four — arithmetic asserted, not shown. Symptom: a slide claims a path "gets us to ₹54 crore" with no logo count, cycle time or headcount implication visible. Underlying error: confidence substituting for a checked model. Cheapest diagnostic: ask for the same two-line arithmetic worked through for Option A and Option B, on the spot.

7. What good looks like

Three weeks later, Ananya's offsite memo ran to four pages. It named the obstacle (deal size, not effort), stated the diagnosis and both options with arithmetic shown, and recommended Option B, kirana-tech self-serve, with a named casualty: the half-built enterprise rules engine would be shelved for a year, its two engineers moved to billing and onboarding. It stated the reversal condition — if self-serve logo growth fell below 60 a month by month nine, the company would revisit, not persist. Rohit's board pack that quarter held one paragraph of ambition and three pages of choice. Nobody needed the target repeated to know what Pratibimb had decided to become.

8. Closing

Ananya recommended Option B, and the board approved it with the reversal condition attached. Her reasoning, stripped to its core, was not that kirana-tech was more exciting than enterprise retail; it was that the arithmetic fit inside Pratibimb's actual resources without inventing a sales organisation it had never run, and that the casualty — a half-built enterprise feature — was one the company could afford to lose more than it could afford to lose a year rebuilding its go-to-market motion from a standing start. The next concepts worth studying build directly on this decision: Rumelt's kernel gives Ananya's diagnosis-guiding policy-coherent action a formal shape she can reuse on the next hard choice, and disruption theory explains why a self-serve, lower-priced entrant like Option B can, under the right conditions, eventually threaten the enterprise incumbents it starts out looking too small to challenge.

Two questions to sit with:

1. The next time you see a document at work called a "strategy," can you name the thing it has chosen not to do — and if you cannot, what is it actually?

2. If the number behind your own team's plan changed by half tomorrow, would your recommended path change with it, the way Ananya's did — or have you mistaken a fixed answer for a considered one?

What Strategy Is and Isn't

Strategy is a set of choices about where scarce resources go and what they are therefore taken away from. Everything that survives being called strategy without meeting that test is a goal, a plan, or a hope.

Section 1Two rooms, two weeks apart

On 9 September 2026, Devika Raghunathan, VP Product at Kutubnuma Labs in Hyderabad, presented a slide her CEO had not asked for. Kutubnuma built document intelligence for Indian lenders: it read bank statements, GST returns and ITRs and returned a structured income verdict to a non-banking financial company's loan-origination system. FY26 had closed at ₹26 crore of ARR across forty-one lenders on 4.1 crore documents. The slide showed one line falling — gross margin, 71% and sliding, as inference cost of ₹1.80 per document rose faster than price.

The slide behind it was worse. Eighteen months earlier Kutubnuma's extraction accuracy on scanned Indian bank statements had been eleven points better than a frontier general-purpose model with a careful prompt; in an internal bake-off that August the gap was 1.4 points and shrinking. What the company had been founded to do well was becoming something anyone could do adequately. Devika had two candidate board documents on her laptop. One committed Kutubnuma to depth — owning the adjudication of documents, the corpus of 2.3 crore analyst-verified decisions behind it, and pricing tied to rupees of fraud prevented. The other committed to breadth: a horizontal document-AI platform for insurance claims, KYC and freight paperwork. Both were plausible, both had a champion, and both could not be funded on 63 engineers and eleven months of runway.

Two weeks later and 900 kilometres away, Harish Bhatnagar, Chief Product Officer of Uttaradhruv Coldchain in Ahmedabad, faced a different version of the same problem. Uttaradhruv, founded in 2014, made IoT temperature loggers for vaccine and specialty-pharma distribution and sold a compliance cloud alongside them, to customers audited under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules and against WHO good-distribution-practice guidance. FY26 revenue was ₹112 crore: ₹86 crore of hardware at 22% gross margin and ₹26 crore of software subscription at 78%. The board's independent director put the question plainly: the hardware was becoming a commodity a Shenzhen contract manufacturer could ship for 40% less, so was Uttaradhruv a software company that happened to make a device, or a device company that happened to ship software?

Harish's honest answer was that for four years it had been trying to be both, and the R&D budget showed it: ₹14 crore split roughly 60:40, against internal estimates that leadership in compliance software needed ₹11 crore a year sustained and leadership in reusable logger hardware needed ₹9 crore. He could not fund both and had never said so. The word "strategy" appeared 31 times in the board pack, which contained no sentence of the form "and therefore we will stop."

Section 2The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree

A working definition, precise enough to referee an argument with: a strategy is a coherent set of commitments of scarce resources, made in response to a named diagnosis of why the desired outcome is not already happening, which forecloses alternatives the firm could otherwise have pursued. Four load-bearing words. Commitments: a preference that costs nothing is not a choice. Scarce: abundance dissolves trade-offs and with them the need for strategy. Diagnosis: a choice answering no question is a guess. Forecloses: if both options survive the meeting, nothing was decided.

The lineage explains the disagreements. Kenneth Andrews and the Harvard Business Policy group in the 1960s framed strategy as the fit between what a firm is distinctively able to do and what its environment rewards — the origin of the SWOT habit and of the assumption that strategy is a deliberate, top-level act of judgement. Michael Porter industrialised the environmental half: industry structure determines the profit available, and a firm earns above-average returns by occupying a position requiring activities inconsistent with the positions others occupy. His sharpest contribution is the negative one, trade-offs: if a rival can add your feature without giving anything up, you have a head start, not a position. The resource-based view of Wernerfelt, Barney, and Prahalad and Hamel pushed back from the inside — advantage lives in resources that are valuable, rare and hard to imitate, so the question is not "which attractive industry?" but "what do we have that others cannot cheaply build?" Mintzberg attacked both: realised strategy is a pattern in a stream of actions, discovered in hindsight. Rumelt gave the practitioner version its vocabulary — the kernel of diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent action, and the naming of bad strategy as fluff, goals mistaken for choices, and refusal to face the obstacle. Lafley and Martin turned it into a cascade of five linked choices and added the move that does most of the work: rather than ask which option is right, ask what would have to be true for each.

All five will sign one narrow claim: a statement a competitor with the same ambition could have written, implying no reallocation, is not a strategy. Where they part is instructive. Porter would tell Harish his 60:40 split is the textbook straddle and he must pick; Barney would ask which asset is actually rare — twelve years of validation dossiers are hard to imitate, a compliance dashboard is not — and derive the position from the resource; Mintzberg would note that Uttaradhruv's realised strategy is already visible in where its best engineers volunteer to work.

Section 3Mechanics: how the work is actually done

Experts run a sequence most strategy documents skip in the middle. It begins not with options but with the binding constraint: which resource is actually scarce? At Kutubnuma it was not money but 63 engineers and eleven months of runway; at Uttaradhruv, ₹14 crore of R&D and four hardware engineers with validated-device experience who could not be replaced within a year. Naming the scarce resource converts an argument about direction into one about allocation, which is the only kind that can be settled.

The second step is the diagnosis, stated as a causal claim that could be false. Devika's was: "Our advantage was extraction accuracy; general models have closed that gap to 1.4 points; our remaining defensible asset is 2.3 crore analyst-verified adjudications and the workflow that produced them." That is checkable: one could show lenders never valued accuracy, or that the corpus does not transfer. Compare the version in most decks — "the market is moving to AI-native solutions and we must move faster" — in which nothing can be false, which is why nothing follows from it.

Third, generate options that are genuinely mutually exclusive; the test is resource-path overlap, since two options that can both be pursued without either slowing are not alternatives but a to-do list. Fourth — the step that separates the practice from the vocabulary — invert the burden of proof: rather than argue which option is better, ask what would have to be true for each to be right, then price the belief.

The team put the probability that Option B's world arrives at about 50%, fixing B's expected value at 0.5 × 66 + 0.5 × 21 = ₹43.5 crore. The useful question then is not "how likely is A?" but "how likely does A have to be?" Solving 34 + (78 − 34)p ≥ 43.5 gives p ≥ 9.5 / 44 = 0.216. Devika did not need to argue that outcome-linked pricing was probable, only that it was not less than a one-in-five chance — far easier to defend and to check, since two of her forty-one lenders had already asked for a fraud-linked commercial structure unprompted.

Two second-order effects follow, both routinely missed. The first is the ruin constraint: expected value ranks A above B at any p over 0.216, but A's downside of ₹34 crore against a ₹40 crore cost base is a bridge round while B's ₹21 crore is a wind-down. A firm that cannot survive the low state compares downside states first and ranks only the survivors. The second is capability accretion: a quarter on A builds an adjudication workforce, an evaluation harness and a labelled corpus that make the next choice cheaper, while a quarter on B builds connectors that depreciate with each platform release. Choices are drawn not from a hat but from the pile the last one left behind.

The fifth step names the coherent actions and the casualties — which roadmap items die, which customers are not renewed, which roles are not hired — and the sixth sets the falsifier in advance. Without one, a strategy cannot be distinguished from an identity, and identities are not revised.

Section 4When the idea applies, and when it misleads

The claim that strategy is choice is not universally true. It holds under four conditions, each testable rather than assumed.

Table 2. Four testable conditions, applied to both protagonists
ConditionKutubnuma LabsUttaradhruv Coldchain
Scarcity binds. Pursuing one option measurably slows another. Holds. The nineteen evaluation engineers are the same people either way. Holds hard. ₹14 cr against ₹20 cr of thresholds.
Trade-offs are real. The activities the options require are mutually inconsistent. Holds. Outcome pricing needs analyst-in-the-loop review; a self-serve platform needs it gone. Holds. Own manufacture and a bought-in ODM device are incompatible cost structures.
The environment is legible enough to have a diagnosis. Marginal. Model capability a year out is unforecastable. Holds. Regulated pharma distribution changes slowly and audibly.
Commitment is costly to reverse, so the choice has teeth. Partly. A software pivot costs two quarters. Strongly. Exiting the Vatva line is irreversible for five years.

Where the conditions fail, the idea misleads. Where the binding constraint is information rather than resources — an early-stage company that does not yet know its customer — insisting on commitment converts ignorance into an expensive vow. In an abundant regime, trade-offs destroy value by declining adjacent revenue that costs nothing to serve. In a regulated business much of what looks like strategy is compliance: Uttaradhruv's validation regime is not a choice and will not differentiate it, though a newcomer might mistake it for a moat. The expert separates the constraint set from the choice set before choosing — and Devika, whose third condition is the fragile one, should say so rather than perform confidence she does not have.

Section 5Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

Four situations strain the definition. Multi-product firms face a recursion: the corporate choice is a portfolio allocation with which each product's choice must cohere. Mukhyadhara Health, a Chennai hospital-software company with five products and 210 engineers, found in 2024 that every product had a defensible strategy and the company had none — its sales force led with whichever product the prospect raised, giving it five go-to-market strategies and one sales capacity. Two-sided markets break the where-to-play question, because the choice is a sequence: which side to concentrate on first to make the other side's participation rational. Abhimukh Commerce, a marketplace linking textile mills to garment exporters, had to choose not a segment but a liquidity pocket — one fabric category in one corridor, dense enough that both sides found a counterparty within a day.

Hardware plus software forces a choice about where margin lives, and the halves run at different clock speeds: software can be revised in a quarter, tooling and validation in five years, so the hardware decision should constrain the software decision and not the reverse — Harish had been doing it backwards. AI-native products compress a choice's half-life. Kutubnuma's advantage was destroyed not by a competitor but by a model release, so the relevant choice is not where to play but which layer of the stack will not be absorbed by the layer below within eighteen months — a question about someone else's roadmap, answered on far less information than the frameworks assume.

The seams are where strategies die quietly. A choice made in a memo passes through roadmap prioritisation, sales compensation, pricing approvals and the quarterly forecast, and each hand-off lets a rational local actor undo it: a sales leader carrying a number accepts the out-of-segment deal, finance approves the discount, engineering builds the custom feature, and a year later the realised strategy is the average of the exceptions. Mature companies hold a line not through better documents but through three unglamorous mechanisms — a resource-allocation ritual in which the scarce resource is visibly re-divided rather than incremented, a few remembered "no" precedents that make the next refusal cheap, and an explicit exception budget. At Mukhyadhara that budget is 8% of engineering capacity per quarter, which forces sales to rank its own exceptions instead of escalating each one.

Section 6Nuances that separate the expert

A choice without a reallocation is a preference. The tell is a decision meeting that ends with no change to anyone's calendar or headcount. The obvious reading — the company has chosen a direction and will now execute — is wrong, because direction is free and capacity is not. An expert reads the resourcing sheet before the deck and treats divergence as evidence the deck is aspirational.

A "will not do" list is worthless unless the items had champions. Most no-lists contain things nobody wanted, and the tell is that nobody is visibly unhappy when it is read out. Consensus here looks like clarity and usually means nothing was foreclosed. Kutubnuma's honest no-list had to name the horizontal platform the CTO had advocated for a year, with him in the room.

Coherence beats local correctness. Individually sensible choices that do not reinforce one another lose to mediocre choices that do. The tell is an expert asking how each activity makes the others cheaper or more effective rather than whether each is separately justified. Uttaradhruv's device-led option is attractive not because the device is better but because validated hardware, audit dossiers and a compliance cloud are worth more together to a distributor facing an inspection.

Diagnosis is the falsifiable part; the policy is not. Arguments about guiding policy are usually proxy wars over an unexamined diagnosis, and the tell is that experienced reviewers attack the diagnosis first, then accept whatever follows from one they believe. The obvious reading — that the decision is the important part — inverts the epistemics: correcting a wrong diagnosis changes the decision automatically.

Often the real choice is which uncertainty to resolve first. Where the environment is illegible, the highest-value commitment is frequently an experiment rather than a position, chosen for how much it moves the decision rather than the revenue it produces. The tell is the question "what is the cheapest thing that would change our mind?" — and it is no licence to defer, since the expert still names the date the choice gets made regardless.

Emergence is real and is not an excuse. Much of what a firm ends up doing was discovered, not decided. The expert's response is to say which parts are held fixed for twelve months and which are deliberately open; the tell is a document that names its own open variables. One claiming everything is settled is not more rigorous, only less honest about where it is guessing.

The goal-versus-choice slogan breaks down at the top of the house. For a CEO deciding between growth and profitability, the goal is the choice, because selecting one forecloses the other and reallocates everything downstream. The tell is an expert who declines to recite "goals are not strategy" when the goal has a visible casualty. The distinction is about goals with no casualty, not goals as such.

Trade-offs are occasionally broken, and confusing that with straddling is expensive. A production-function change can genuinely move the frontier outward, which is what makes the value-innovation literature more than wishful thinking. The tell is an expert who asks what changed in the cost of doing both and accepts the claim only when the answer is mechanical. "Our team is unusually good" is not a mechanism; "foundation models removed the marginal cost of a second document type" might be.

Section 7How this differs by product type and by stage

The discipline does not change across product types; the unit of choice does. In consumer products the scarce resource is attention, so the choice is a use case plus an acquisition channel: a consumer compares substitutes in seconds and diffuse positioning is invisible. In B2B and enterprise it is a segment plus a deal-economics model, and the trade-off shows up as which customers you are willing to fail to serve. In platforms and marketplaces the choice carries a sequencing dimension — which side, which pocket, in what order — a real difference, not a rephrasing. In hardware it is partly irreversible and must be made earlier and on less information than anyone likes. In AI-native products the distinctive question is layer durability rather than customer segment.

Two claimed differences are not real. Consumer strategy is not "more creative" nor enterprise strategy "more analytical": both need a diagnosis and both are settled by allocation. And the belief that AI products need no strategy because capability moves fast is the oldest error in a new costume; faster obsolescence raises the value of choosing.

Stage changes the object of choice more than the method. A seed-stage company chooses which uncertainty to resolve, and premature commitment is its characteristic failure. A Series-B company like Kutubnuma chooses where to concentrate an already-real capability, and dilution is its failure mode. A company of Uttaradhruv's age chooses what to stop, and the thing to stop has a factory, a plant head and thirty years of pride attached. Late-stage firms rarely fail for want of a new choice; they fail because the old one was never retired.

Section 8Three worked examples

Mukhyadhara Health: concentration. In FY24 it had ₹64 crore of revenue across five products — an HIS, a radiology workflow, a booking app, a claims module and a pharmacy stock tool — and 210 engineers split evenly. Its diagnosis was blunt: every deal it lost, it lost to a specialist in the one product the hospital cared most about. It put 62% of engineering on the HIS and claims module, sold the radiology workflow for ₹9 crore and sunset the booking app, walking away from ₹7 crore of annual revenue. By FY26 revenue was ₹81 crore on two products and the competitive HIS win rate had gone from 31% to 48% — not through talent, but because a specialist's roadmap could finally be outpaced.

Abhimukh Commerce: sequencing. The marketplace had 4,200 mills, 1,900 exporters and an 11% match rate — plenty of users, almost no liquidity. Rather than grow both sides it chose one pocket, cotton shirting in the Tiruppur–Coimbatore corridor, subsidising supply with a seven-day payment guarantee costing ₹2.1 crore a year of working capital. Registered mills fell by design to 640; match rate in the pocket rose to 54% and GMV per active exporter tripled in four quarters. The important number is the one that fell.

Dishasoochak Mobility: the failure. Founded in 2019 to serve "the electrification of Indian commercial fleets," Dishasoochak raised ₹210 crore and built at once a charging network, a telematics platform, a battery-health analytics product and a driver app, under the stated strategy of becoming "the operating system for electric fleets." No diagnosis was ever written. By FY24 it had 1,100 chargers at 9% utilisation, 140 fleet customers with a median of four vehicles each, and ₹31 crore of revenue against ₹96 crore of cost. The failure was not a bad choice but the absence of one: every product was funded because each was defensible alone, and on every axis a specialist beat it.

The recovery was mostly subtraction. A new CEO in mid-2024 named the diagnosis aloud — charger utilisation, not software, determined unit economics — and chose intra-city three-wheeler logistics fleets in two cities. The telematics platform went for ₹18 crore, the driver app was shut, headcount fell 41%. Utilisation on the retained 380 chargers rose from 9% to 34% in five quarters, taking contribution per charger from negative ₹41,000 to positive ₹1.9 lakh a year. FY26 revenue was ₹44 crore — far below the FY23 plan, and for the first time on a path that closed. The recovery cost eighteen months and the option value of everything sold: the standard price of choosing two years late.

Missing diagnosisThe strategy reads identically under opposite market facts"What fact, if found next month, would make this wrong?"Correct execution of the wrong policy, seen only at renewal
Exception driftRising share of roadmap items traceable to a single deal"What percentage of last quarter's engineering went to out-of-segment commitments?"Realised strategy diverges silently, noticed two planning cycles later
Identity captureThe falsifier is never reviewed; defenders cite the founding story"What would we have to see to stop?"The Uttaradhruv risk: a plant kept because it is who we are

All five are cheap to detect and expensive to remedy, and the remedy cost rises far faster than the detection cost — the argument for running these questions on a calendar rather than on suspicion. Exception drift is the most under-policed, because each exception is defensible and only the aggregate is not; measure the aggregate, do not litigate the cases.

Section 10Where experts genuinely disagree

Deliberate commitment versus emergent discovery. The commitment camp rests on a real observation: firms that concentrate resources beat firms that spread them, and someone must decide the concentration because no local actor will. The emergent camp rests on an equally real one: what firms did diverges from what they planned, and the successful divergences came from managers close to customers. The first is falsified by evidence that concentrated firms underperform comparable diversified ones; the second by evidence that firms with explicit foreclosure outperform even when their diagnosis proves wrong. Neither is settled, and most operators hold a mixed position and disagree about the mixture.

Position versus resources as the starting point. The evidence is quantitative and awkward for both sides. Variance-decomposition studies of profitability find industry membership explains roughly a tenth to a fifth of the variation in returns, while business-unit effects explain two to four times as much. Read one way this vindicates the resource-based view: what you are matters more than where you stand. Read another, the business-unit effect is position, and the statistics cannot separate them — which is why the argument has outlasted three decades of data.

Do trade-offs bind? Porter holds that sustained advantage requires activities a rival cannot add without subtracting; the value-innovation tradition holds that a reconceived offering can raise buyer value and lower cost together. The strongest form of the second claim is not that trade-offs are imaginary but that they are properties of a production function technology periodically rewrites. It fails if firms claiming to have broken a trade-off turn out merely to have been early, converging to the frontier once imitated — which is what happened to many celebrated cases.

Commitment versus optionality in fast markets. The simple-rules school argues that where environments move quickly, the cost of being locked into the wrong position exceeds the benefit of focus, so firms should hold a few boundary rules and capture opportunities; opponents answer that this is indistinguishable from having no strategy and is used to justify exactly that. For Devika the question is not academic: if model capability is unforecastable over eighteen months, optionality says do not commit. Her counter was that with 63 engineers, optionality that cannot be funded is not optionality, it is delay.

Section 11What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this topic can explain that strategy is not a goal. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four ways. They ask what is scarce before they ask what is desirable, and they ask for the resourcing sheet rather than the deck. They attack diagnoses rather than conclusions, which makes their objections feel indirect until the conclusion collapses on its own. They state beliefs as probabilities with a breakeven attached, which is easy to disagree with precisely and hard to disagree with rhetorically. And they treat their own strategy as falsifiable, naming the observation that would make them abandon it and the date they expect to see it. The negative tell is as reliable: they never use "focus" as a synonym for effort.

Section 12The decisions

Devika recommended Option A — not because adjudication depth was obviously right, but because it needed only a 22% belief to beat the alternative, because two lenders had already asked unprompted for the structure it required, and because its downside was survivable with a bridge while Option B's was not. She named the casualty, the horizontal platform and the CTO's connector roadmap with it, and set the falsifier: if fewer than two of five target lenders had signed an outcome-linked contract by 31 March 2027, the diagnosis was wrong and the company would revisit rather than persist.

Harish went the other way from where his board expected, rejecting the software-led option on the resource-based argument that twelve years of validation dossiers and audited device qualifications were the rare asset and a compliance dashboard was not. He committed ₹9 crore to a single reusable logger with a five-year battery and discontinued three SKUs, including the ambient-logistics unit earning ₹11 crore of low-margin revenue; the compliance cloud was kept and narrowed to pharma. His casualty, in one sentence to the board, was the ambition to be a horizontal compliance platform — an ambition nobody had formally adopted and everybody had been funding.

Discussion questions

1. Devika's breakeven rests on four numbers estimated by the people who would execute the option. What would you need to see before treating p ≥ 0.216 as a decision rule rather than a rationalisation, and does a unanimous leadership team make it better or worse?

2. Harish used a resource-based argument to override a market-structure one. Under what conditions would the same evidence justify the opposite conclusion, and how would you know which world Uttaradhruv is in before committing the Vatva line?

3. If you had been on Dishasoochak's board in 2021, what observable would have told you the company had no strategy at a point when every product was still growing?

Section 13Going deeper

  1. Product vision and mission — the destination a strategy routes to; without it, foreclosure has no criterion.
  2. Rumelt's kernel — the diagnosis-first discipline as a reusable three-part structure, and the vocabulary for naming bad strategy in a room.
  3. Disruption theory — why the cheap, worse option you deliberately refuse can become the thing that beats you: the main risk in Harish's choice.
  4. The product strategy document — the artifact that makes a choice survive the seams, where diagnosis, casualty and falsifier are written down or lost.
  5. Risks and assumptions in strategy — what would have to be true, and how to test it cheaply: the machinery behind Table 1.
  6. Playing to Win — the five-choice cascade that keeps where-to-play coherent with capabilities and management systems.
  7. Product-market fit — the evidence standard for whether the chosen arena is real, and what a young firm resolves before committing.
  8. Wardley mapping — layer durability and commoditisation over time, the question AI-native strategies turn on.
  9. Focus and sequencing — how one choice becomes an order of operations, and where exception budgets live.
