Risks and Assumptions in Strategy

What must be true for this strategy to work, and what will we do if it isn't?

1. A crore a quarter, riding on a number nobody has seen

On the second Monday of March 2026, Priya Raghunathan sat in the Pune boardroom of Setugiri Mobility with a seven-slide deck and a Friday deadline. Setugiri built and sold electric two-wheelers to retail buyers; its board now wanted a growth story for the Series C conversation, and Priya's team had spent six weeks building one. Setugiri Fleet would buy scooters in bulk and lease them, by the month, to riders working for food and grocery delivery platforms — a business several Bengaluru rivals already ran. The plan asked the board to commit an eighteen-crore tranche over three years and projected six crore of EBITDA from Fleet by the end of year two.

The spreadsheet was clean. It also rested, Priya realized rereading it that Sunday night, on a single load-bearing number: that eighty-five percent of the leased fleet would be on rent at any given time, the utilization figure a competitor with three years of Bengaluru odometer data had actually achieved. Setugiri had never leased a scooter to anyone. If utilization came in at sixty-five percent instead of eighty-five, the six-crore profit became a two-crore loss, and eighteen crore of runway would be gone with nothing durable to show a Series C investor. The board wanted an answer by Friday. Priya's problem was not whether the plan looked good. It was whether anyone could say, honestly, what had to be true for it to be real — and how soon they would find out if it wasn't.

2. The idea: naming what the plan is actually betting on

A strategy is a chain of if-then commitments: if the following things turn out to be true, this sequence of moves produces this result. Every strategy, however carefully reasoned, is built on numbers that are estimates rather than facts, because reliable information about future customer behavior, cost curves, and competitor response simply does not exist yet at the moment the plan is written. Risks and assumptions in strategy is the discipline of separating which numbers in a plan are genuinely known from which are informed guesses, ranking those guesses by how much the plan's outcome depends on them and how little confidence anyone actually holds about them, and structuring the plan so the cheapest, earliest tests of the riskiest guesses come before the expensive ones.

This is the same move a capable product manager makes when surfacing the assumptions behind a single feature bet — done here at the scale of an entire company's strategy, which is why it traditionally forms the closing section of a strategy document: you cannot responsibly sign off on a plan whose unstated bets you have never named.

The framework was formalized most rigorously by Rita Gunther McGrath and Ian MacMillan in their 1995 Harvard Business Review article "Discovery-Driven Planning," written after they observed large corporations approving new ventures using conventional financial planning — a forecast built as though its revenue, cost, and timeline numbers were already known — and then being blindsided when the resulting business missed its own plan by several hundred percent. Their fix reverses the usual planning sequence: start from the profit the venture must deliver, work backward to name everything that has to be true for that profit to arrive, rank those things by importance and uncertainty, and release capital in checkpoint-sized tranches that buy evidence about the riskiest assumptions before buying more scale.

The sentence Priya could say in that boardroom without sounding glib: "Before the board wires the next crore, tell me what has to be true for this plan to work — and how soon we'll know if it isn't."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in a fixed sequence, and the step teams skip is almost always the same one.

Start from the end. Write down the profit, or other terminal outcome, the strategy is committing to deliver, and the date by which it must arrive. For Setugiri Fleet: six crore of EBITDA by month twenty-four.

Build the reverse income statement. Instead of forecasting forward from assumed volumes, work backward: required profit implies required revenue given the cost structure; required revenue implies required price multiplied by required volume; required volume implies a required operating metric — here, fleet utilization.

Label each backward step as an assumption, not a fact. This is the step most teams quietly skip. A number derived by working backward from a target still feels like an output of analysis; the discipline is to say the words "which we are assuming" out loud after every one of them, so it cannot slide into the plan disguised as a fact.

Rank every assumption on two independent axes — how important it is (how far the outcome moves if the number is wrong) and how uncertain it is (how little independent evidence exists for it). Assumptions that are both highly important and highly uncertain are the leap-of-faith assumptions: the ones capable of sinking the whole strategy, and the ones nobody currently knows.

Design the cheapest test that would falsify each leap-of-faith assumption — not confirm it — before committing more capital to a plan that depends on it holding.

Convert the spending plan itself into checkpoints tied to assumptions clearing their tests, rather than to the calendar.

Pre-write the response to failure. At each checkpoint, decide in advance whether a failed assumption means kill, pivot the operating model, or proceed at a smaller scale — so that failure is a normal planning outcome with a rehearsed next move, not a crisis discovered for the first time in a board meeting.

4. The worked example: Setugiri Fleet's reverse income statement

Priya's team reconstructed the Fleet plan backward. The board wanted six crore of EBITDA in year two from a planned fleet of four thousand leased scooters. Working backward through the assumed cost structure — ₹900 per scooter per month in maintenance across the full fleet, roughly ₹3.5 crore a year in insurance and battery-swap infrastructure, and ₹4.5 crore a year in operations staff and city overhead — required annual revenue of about ₹18.36 crore. At an assumed monthly lease price of ₹4,500 per scooter, that revenue required 3,400 scooters earning rent in an average month, out of a fleet of 4,000: eighty-five percent utilization, month in and month out.

AssumptionImportanceUncertaintyStatus
Utilization reaches 85%HighHighLeap of faith
Lease price holds at ₹4,500/monthMediumLowWell understood
Maintenance cost stays ₹900/scooter/monthMediumMediumWatch list
Riders will sign 12-month leasesHighHighLeap of faith

The second pass changes one input. Hold price, fleet size, and costs fixed, and drop utilization from the untested eighty-five percent to sixty-five percent — a figure closer to what a first city launch, with no existing rider relationships or repair network, might plausibly produce. Scooters on rent fall to 2,600; annual revenue falls to roughly ₹14.04 crore, since fixed maintenance is charged against the whole fleet regardless of how much of it is earning rent. Against costs of about ₹12.32 crore, EBITDA collapses to roughly ₹1.7 crore — not a smaller win, but a plan that has quietly missed its own purpose by more than four crore. Utilization was not one input among many; it was the hinge the entire six-crore story swung on, and nobody at Setugiri had ever generated it.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

Risk and assumption are not the same word

A risk is something that could happen — a rival could cut prices. An assumption is something the plan already requires to be true for its own arithmetic to work, such as eighty-five percent utilization. Every assumption carries risk, but plenty of real risks never get surfaced as an assumption at all; a strategy document that keeps the two separate lets its reader see which bets are already priced into a number and which sit entirely outside the model.

Importance and uncertainty are independent, and averages hide the split

A confident-looking model often blends several assumptions of different uncertainty into one number — "average revenue per rider" can bury a highly uncertain component (whether riders will prepay monthly) inside a well-understood one (headline pricing). Most of the analytical work in this discipline is simply unbundling a blended number into its separately-uncertain parts.

Leap-of-faith status belongs to the plan, not to the metric

Eighty-five percent utilization is a leap of faith for a first-time entrant like Setugiri and a routine, well-evidenced fact for a three-year Bengaluru incumbent with odometer logs. The label depends on how much independent evidence the specific team already holds, never on how sophisticated the metric sounds.

A checkpoint asks a different question than a review meeting

A review meeting asks whether the team is on track against the calendar. A checkpoint asks whether the assumption the next tranche depends on has been falsified or has held, and it falls whenever enough real evidence should exist — which may land nowhere near the fiscal quarter's end.

Surfacing an assumption is not the same as derisking it

The framework cannot tell a team which bet to choose; it only drags the bets already made into the open where a cheap test can reach them. Treating "we wrote our assumptions down" as equivalent to "we improved our odds" is a common and comfortable trap — the writing buys the option to check, nothing more.

It is routinely confused with a risk register

A conventional risk register inventories external threats and mitigation owners while treating a plan's core numbers as fixed. Discovery-driven planning instead treats the core numbers themselves as the unknowns to be discovered — which is why the reverse income statement, not a list of threats, sits at its center.

What to ask before trusting any of it

A thoughtful newcomer should ask three things before relying on a plan built this way: what is the smallest, fastest test that would actually change the scale decision; whose money funds the next checkpoint if this one fails cleanly; and is the person presenting the risky number the same person who will be judged on whether it holds — because incentives quietly decide which figures get labeled known rather than assumed.

6. How the picture changes by business model and by stage

In consumer products, leap-of-faith assumptions usually cluster around retention and engagement curves, and cohort data at modest scale can settle them within weeks. In a B2B business like Setugiri Fleet, the same assumptions cluster around a handful of large counterparties: a single lost anchor delivery platform can invalidate an entire volume assumption on its own, so checkpoints are built around named-account pilots rather than statistical samples. In a marketplace, assumptions split across two sides that must clear together — enough scooters and enough willing riders — so the honest checkpoint tests liquidity in one city before any argument about geographic scale is entertained.

Stage matters as much as business model. An early company is discovering its assumptions from close to zero proprietary data, so tranches should stay small and time-boxed on purpose. A large incumbent often already holds internal data that converts what looks like a leap-of-faith assumption into a genuinely well-understood one — its failure mode shifts from testing to correctly retrieving and trusting evidence it already owns, and to noticing when an old, once-solid assumption has quietly stopped holding as battery or fuel costs moved.

7. Common mistakes

Risk theatre. The risk section lists competition, regulation, and macro conditions in generic paragraphs that read identically every quarter. The underlying error is treating the section as compliance rather than as the plan's own logic laid bare. The cheap diagnostic: ask which single number in the model would actually move if each listed risk occurred; if nobody can answer within a minute, the risk was never connected to the plan at all.

Burying the assumption inside an average. A blended metric like "average revenue per unit" hides a wide distribution, and the true leap-of-faith bet is usually about the shape of that distribution, not its mean. The diagnostic: rebuild the plan at its twenty-fifth percentile outcome instead of its average and see whether anyone is still comfortable with the ask.

Treating validation as one gate, run once. A team runs a single pilot, calls the assumption "validated," and never revisits it as scale or context changes. The confusion is between "true once" and "true always." The diagnostic: check whether the plan schedules a re-test at the next major change in scale, or only ever tested at the very start.

Letting the owner of the target also own the estimate. The utilization or conversion assumption always comes back at exactly the number needed to hit the plan. The diagnostic is simple: ask who supplied the contested number, and whether that person's performance is judged on the plan's total.

8. What good looks like

A neighboring fleet operator, Taranmarg Logistics, had faced the identical decision eighteen months earlier when it moved from owning delivery vans to leasing them to last-mile contractors. Rather than asking its board for the full multi-year commitment on day one, Taranmarg's strategy team named utilization as its leap-of-faith assumption out loud in the board paper, asked for a single quarter's pilot tranche covering two hundred and fifty vans in one city, and wrote the kill and scale thresholds into the paper before the pilot began. The pilot came in at sixty-two percent utilization — well under its own hopeful case — and instead of abandoning the business or pretending the number would improve on its own, the team renegotiated its anchor contract to include a guaranteed minimum utilization clause with its largest logistics client, retested for one more quarter, and only then asked for the full tranche. The board's confidence in that second ask was higher, not lower, than if the pilot had simply confirmed the first guess, because everyone in the room had watched the team change its plan in response to real evidence rather than defend a spreadsheet.

9. What Priya decided

Priya rewrote the Friday deck. Instead of asking the board for the full eighteen crore against a six-crore promise, she asked for four crore to run a one-quarter pilot of two hundred and fifty scooters in Pune alone, named eighty-five percent utilization explicitly as an untested leap-of-faith assumption rather than a projection, and attached pre-written thresholds: below fifty-five percent, kill the model and return the capital; between fifty-five and seventy, renegotiate lease pricing and rerun the pilot; above seventy, release the remaining tranche on schedule. The board's questions changed in kind, not just in tone — they stopped asking whether six crore was the right target and started asking whether four crore was enough to learn the truth quickly. Setugiri's next milestone worth study is the beachhead memo: the sibling discipline, taught alongside this one in most strategy capstones, of choosing the single narrowest market where the leap-of-faith assumption can be tested fastest and cheapest, and writing down, with equal discipline, what the company will deliberately not build in order to reach that answer sooner.

Two questions to sit with:

Somewhere in your own current plan, what is the one number that, if you are honest, nobody has actually watched happen anywhere comparable?

If that number turned out to be wrong by half, would anyone find out before the money built on it was already spent?

Jagrat Fleet Systems: What Has to Be True

A teaching case on strategic bets, surfaced assumptions, and the cost of being wrong

1. Nagpur, 26 September 2026

At half past nine on a Saturday night, Foram Deshmukh sat alone in the first-floor conference room of Jagrat Fleet Systems' Civil Lines office in Nagpur, a hard copy of the Maharashtra State Transport Department's tender document open beside her laptop. The tender closed on 3 October, eight days away. It asked for a single vendor to fit, monitor and report on GPS location, panic buttons and driver-behaviour telematics for every registered school bus in the Nagpur, Pune and Nashik divisions — 4,200 vehicles — under the state's tightened enforcement of the national AIS-140 vehicle-tracking standard. Won, it would double the buses under Jagrat's watch overnight. Lost after a bid, it would cost the company a ₹1.2 crore bank guarantee it could not easily replace. Foram had also promised her board, and her Dubai client, a decision on two other paths that same week. What she owed herself, re-reading her own deck, was an honest list of what had to be true for each path to work.

2. A company built on RTOs and school gates

Jagrat Fleet Systems — "jagrat" is Hindi for vigilant — was founded in Nagpur in 2019 by Foram Deshmukh, a former operations manager at a regional logistics firm, after a relative's school bus was stopped by the Nagpur RTO for an expired fitness certificate and a missing speed governor. The product plots buses on a live map for transport in-charges, scores driver behaviour (harsh braking, speeding, route deviation) for fleet owners, and pushes arrival alerts to parents on a companion app. By FY26 it served 145 private schools and 38 independent bus operators across Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Gujarat, competing loosely with Pune-based Jatayu Suraksha Systems on price and with informal local CCTV-and-SIM-tracker setups on everything else. Its most sophisticated deployment sat outside India: Jyoti International School Group, an Indian-curriculum chain with fourteen campuses across the UAE, had adopted Jagrat two years earlier and wanted to expand the contract regionally. Growth had been steady rather than dramatic — roughly 18% a year — funded mostly from operating cash, with one modest seed round behind it.

3. The situation

Two events had converged. First, after a widely reported school-bus incident in Nashik in July 2026 in which no live tracking data existed for investigators, the state had accelerated enforcement of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways' AIS-140 tracking mandate and floated a state-wide tender rather than leaving compliance to individual schools, as the 2012 Supreme Court guidelines on school transport safety had originally intended. Jatayu Suraksha Systems was expected to bid aggressively low. Second, Jyoti International School Group's Dubai leadership had told Kavya Subramaniam, Jagrat's Singapore-based customer success lead, that it wanted a single regional telematics standard across its campuses within two quarters — and that it was also talking to Jaras Telematics FZE, a Dubai-registered rival built specifically for the UAE's Roads and Transport Authority reporting formats.

From Pune, VP of Engineering Mandar Kelkar worried that the tender's service terms — a 24x7 control room, alerts within 30 seconds, 99.5% uptime, ₹5 lakh a day in penalties for delay — would consume the same sixteen engineers rebuilding the alerting pipeline for Dubai compliance. From Toronto, data scientist Ananya Krishnan flagged that the driver-risk model, trained on Indian urban and highway routes, had never been tested against Dubai's motorway speed patterns or a fleet ten times the size of anything Jagrat had monitored at once. Both changes asked the same small team to be right about something new, on a fixed clock, with money already committed.

4. The people

Foram Deshmukh, Founder & CEO, Nagpur. Wants the state tender as proof, to her board and to herself, that Jagrat can operate at government scale, but has watched other regional vendors get strangled by receivables when a government department pays late.
Mandar Kelkar, VP Engineering, Pune. Wants one clear priority for his team; believes chasing both the tender and the Dubai rebuild at once will produce two half-finished systems by March.
Ananya Krishnan, Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Wants six more weeks and a bigger compute budget before either the tender's real-time alerting or Dubai's expansion goes live on the current risk model.
Kavya Subramaniam, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Wants a same-quarter commitment to Jyoti International School Group before Jaras Telematics FZE closes the regional deal instead, taking the reference account with it.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows why the decision is not obvious from the revenue mix alone: government work has so far been a thin-margin rounding error. Jagrat's only government exposure to date, a small pilot with Nagpur's Zilla Parishad schools, ran at a 31% gross margin against 64% in its core private-school business, mostly because of the manpower cost of a manual control room.

Exhibit 2 lays the three paths side by side against the question this case turns on: not "what could this earn?" but "what has to hold true, and what happens the day it doesn't?"

Exhibit 2 — The three options, their price of entry, and their load-bearing assumption

Exhibit 3 places the decision points on a single clock: the tender and the Dubai commitment compete for the same eight engineers in the same ten weeks, a fact the deck's revenue projections leave out.

Exhibit 3 — The decision clock: two irreversible dates fall ten working days apart, both drawing on the same engineering team.

6. The options

Option A — Bid for the Maharashtra state tender. Upside: 4,200 buses, a reference that could open other state transport departments, and a credible answer for Series B investors asking whether Jagrat can work with government. Cost: the guarantee ties up capital Jagrat would rather keep, the 30-second alert SLA is untested at this scale, and Indian government payment cycles routinely run past their stated terms — the very assumption the option depends on.

Option B — Deepen the private-school and bus-operator base. Upside: no new risk category, margins stay near 64%, and a strong Jyotirmay Shiksha Group reference could convert other Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh chains. Cost: it does not change Jagrat's investor story or block Jatayu Suraksha Systems from the same accounts, and it leaves Dubai's request for a decision unanswered.

Option C — Commit engineering and cash to the Dubai/Gulf expansion. Upside: a foothold in a higher-margin, hard-currency market with a client already asking to expand rather than being sold to cold. Cost: RTA-Dubai's reporting formats differ from AIS-140, a fourteen-campus group moves slowly as one buyer, and Jaras Telematics FZE is already in the room.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Jagrat actually know about the tender's payment behaviour, and what is it merely hoping is true?
  2. For each option in Exhibit 2, what single piece of evidence, gathered in the next eight days, would most change Foram's confidence in its load-bearing assumption?
  3. Engineering capacity is shared across all three options. If Foram commits fully to the tender, what should she tell Kavya and Jyoti International School Group about the Dubai timeline — and what should Mandar and Ananya stop doing?
  4. Given Exhibit 1's margins, is a government-scale ambition even consistent with the business Jagrat has built, or does it require becoming a different kind of company?

8. A note for the learner

Strategy documents fail less often because the reasoning inside them is wrong than because something outside the document — an assumption no one wrote down — turns out to be false. The discipline this case asks for is not choosing the option with the biggest number in the upside column; it is naming, for each option, what must be true for that upside to arrive, and deciding in advance what Jagrat will do the day it learns that it isn't. Option A's economics rest on the state paying within 45 days, a fact Foram can check with other Nagpur vendors before 3 October rather than discover after the guarantee is posted. Option C rests on Jyoti International School Group choosing Jagrat before Jaras Telematics FZE closes, a fact Kavya can likely force into the open with a direct question this week rather than treat as settled.

A well-reasoned answer need not rank all three options on return; it must show, for the one chosen, what was checked before betting and what triggers a reversal after. On that basis, the defensible path is Option B as the floor, protected without new risk, paired with a narrow, time-boxed move on Option A: bid, but only after confirming the state's actual payment history with a comparable vendor, and only for the Nagpur division rather than all three, capping exposure while the control-room model is proven. Option C is deferred, not abandoned — Kavya is authorised to get a written commitment date from Jyoti International School Group without Jagrat spending the ₹80 lakh until Mandar's team has bandwidth freed from the tender rollout. This does not maximise any single number in Foram's deck; it is defensible because each commitment is sized to what has actually been verified, with an owner and a deadline attached to everything still unverified.

Mahatol Yard Systems: The Weight of What We Assumed

Strategic bets, borrowed authority, and evidence that will not settle

1. Raipur, Sunday night, 27 September 2026

The lamps over the Urla industrial estate were still on at half past eleven, and from the third floor of the Mahatol Yard Systems office Eshita Chaubey could see the queue outside the Haldhar Ispat Udyog gate: forty-one trucks, engines off, drivers asleep across their seats, each carrying nine to sixteen tonnes of scrap whose grade nobody would agree on until a man at the gate prodded it with a rod and deducted what he deducted.

On her screen was Monday's board deck. Slide four was titled "One Bet, Stated As Assumptions." It had been "FY27-FY29 Growth Strategy" until Friday, when Anirudh Thakar of Mandaar Growth Partners wrote to say the board did not want one. It wanted "the three or four things that must be true for whatever you choose, ranked by how badly we would be hurt if they are not, and the date each becomes checkable."

Eshita had spent Saturday on it and produced instead a list of things she had believed in August 2025, when Mahatol raised ₹22 crore, and no longer believed. The pilot meant to prove the company's next act had produced numbers she could not clean. The customer that had made Mahatol credible across the furnace belt had offered to buy control of it. And a competitor she had dismissed now had nineteen thousand dealers on its app, none of whom paid it anything.

The cursor blinked in the empty bullet under "What we will do if it is not true." She could not fill that line for any of the three options, which she suspected was the actual finding.

2. The company, and a clause signed in 2020

Mahatol Yard Systems was founded in Raipur in 2017 by Eshita Chaubey, whose father had run a rolling mill three kilometres from the present office. The name comes from tol, the Hindi word for weighing; in the trade the weighbridge is simply "the kaanta," and everything that matters happens within four minutes of a truck rolling onto it. Mahatol's first product, still called Kaanta, replaced the carbon-copy slip with a tablet that captured weights, photographed the load and printed a slip no driver could alter. By 2019 it had ninety yards.

In March 2020 Mahatol won Haldhar Ispat Udyog, a Raipur group with two induction furnaces, a rolling mill and four captive yards. Girdhari Lal Bansal, its managing director, set three conditions: deployment entirely on-premise, an edge appliance per weighbridge from Harsiddhi Weighbridge Works of Rajkot, no yard data leaving the site; most-favoured-customer pricing; and no sales to another Chhattisgarh producer until 31 March 2027.

The decision was obviously right then. Haldhar's endorsement carried Mahatol across the Urla cluster, then to Durg, Bilaspur and Raigarh, and to service centres in Ludhiana and Faridabad. It carried three consequences invisible for four years. Mahatol has no corpus of load imagery or assay results, because it promised in writing there would not be one. It cannot sell into the densest concentration of induction-furnace capacity in India, ninety minutes away. And the architecture that made the promise credible is the one every option on Monday's deck would abandon.

A second decision compounded the first. In 2023, as GST tightened around metal scrap, Mahatol built its compliance module, Rawana, as a bolt-on: e-way bills against the NIC portal, reverse-charge handling, and the two per cent tax deducted at source on scrap above ₹2.5 lakh. Eleven weeks of defensive work. It is now the fastest-growing line, the only one customers call about at night, and it sits on the wrong side of the architecture.

3. The industry

India consumes 32 to 35 million tonnes of ferrous scrap a year, and the Ministry of Steel's Steel Scrap Recycling Policy has long described moving that supply into registered facilities. The pull is now stronger than the policy. Since October 2024 the GST treatment of metal scrap has required registered buyers to account for unregistered dealers' supplies under reverse charge and to deduct tax at source on large lots, pushing paperwork into a trade that ran on a slip and a phone call. The Motor Vehicles scrapping rules created facilities that must document what they dismantle. And since January 2026 the European carbon border adjustment mechanism has priced the embedded emissions of exported steel.

Mahatol sells to three kinds of business: collection and shredding yards, the largest Mahakosh Metal Recyclers with seven yards across Chhattisgarh and Odisha; induction-furnace and rolling mills, anchored by Haldhar in a market whose visible giants are SAIL's Bhilai plant, Jindal Steel and Godawari Power & Ispat; and service centres, where Hiranya Steel Service Centres of Faridabad is the showcase account.

Two competitors matter. Hutaash Mill Systems of Kolkata sells the melt-shop ERP most mid-sized mills already run, and in July 2026 began bundling a free yard module with renewals. Maatra Scrap Exchange of Ghaziabad raised ₹140 crore in June 2026 and launched a free app that issues a kaanta slip and an e-way bill in a minute, building toward financing and trade referrals on the flows it observes. Neither competes the way Eshita was taught to expect. One gives the product away as a feature of a larger system; the other because the product is not what it sells. Abroad, Mustaqbal Metals Trading LLC of Jebel Ali wants verified provenance on the cargoes it ships into Indian ports, and Meerhoven Metaalrecycling BV of Rotterdam signed a February 2026 memorandum on documentation European buyers accept.

4. What was believed, and what turned out to be wrong

In August 2025 Mahatol raised ₹22 crore from Mandaar Growth Partners at ₹110 crore post-money. The plan attached to that round had one load-bearing sentence: that Mahatol would stop selling licences per weighbridge and earn a fee per tonne instead, on the strength of an assay both sides would accept, and that per-tonne revenue would be thirty per cent of ARR by FY28. It is 1.3 per cent today.

The chain of belief ran like this. In January 2025 Mahatol launched Chhanti, pairing a handheld X-ray fluorescence reader with a camera-based contamination score built by Anwesha Ghoshal's team in Toronto, on the belief that mills would accept a third-party number in place of the gatekeeper's eye. Three Mahakosh yards took it up and the results looked extraordinary: deductions fell, disputes fell, both sides preferred it. In February 2026 Farida Qureshi signed the Meerhoven memorandum, on the belief that export documentation would pull provenance demand from the far end of the chain.

Three things have since come apart. In February 2026 Haldhar installed an imaging and radiation portal at its Urla gate for reasons unconnected to Mahatol, at almost exactly the point the pilot results improved most sharply. In June, reading the memorandum against its commercial annexe, Farida found that Meerhoven wanted provenance on cargoes leaving Europe and expected the Indian buyer to pay, while Mustaqbal wanted the same data to price against its own suppliers and would not pay either. In July Hutaash began bundling; Mahatol lost two mill accounts worth ₹64 lakh of ARR, and Hiranya froze its renewal pending "a comparison exercise."

In August, Bansal offered ₹168 crore for fifty-one per cent of Mahatol as the Haldhar group's technology arm, releasing the exclusivity at once. Mandaar holds twenty per cent with a one-times participating preference; the offer returns roughly ₹33.6 crore on a ₹22 crore cheque, three years in.

5. The people

Eshita Chaubey — Founder and CEO, Raipur. Position: the per-tonne network is the only path that does not end with Mahatol as a feature of someone else's system. Incentive: her standing in the Urla cluster matters more than her payout in any sale. Not saying: she has stopped believing the pilot numbers.
Nandita Rath — Chief Financial Officer, Raipur. Position: decide nothing before the ₹26 crore certification on 31 March 2027; missing it forfeits the second tranche. Incentive: she built the covenant model and would own the miss. Not saying: the fastest route to that number is renewing Haldhar on Haldhar's terms, which is also the fastest route to permanent dependence.
Suryakant Bhoi — VP Engineering, Raipur. Position: the rewrite is eleven months for twenty-two people and every option needs it, so the strategy debate is theatre until funded. Incentive: he has asked since 2023 and is now right. Not saying: his estimate assumes the Harsiddhi appliances can be retired, and four hundred remain under support.
Anwesha Ghoshal — Head of Data Science, Toronto. Position: the model cannot be sold as a neutral standard; it trained on three yards, all Haldhar-facing. Incentive: she is judged on model quality, and a premature launch destroys her only asset. Not saying: a larger recycling firm has approached her.
Parminder Kalra — Head of Sales, Ludhiana. Position: kill the per-tonne idea; go deeper into mills and service centres, where buyers sign contracts. Incentive: his variable pay is all licence bookings. Not saying: his team ran Exhibit 4, and he chose the sample.
Farida Qureshi — Export Accounts, Singapore. Position: the export corridor is the only place where somebody asks for provenance rather than being sold it. Incentive: the export accounts are hers. Not saying: Mustaqbal cooled in August and her updates stayed optimistic.
Rajat Vaidya — Head of Design, Berlin. Position: the dealer app is the real product; the kaanta man is the only user who ever changed his behaviour without a mill telling him to. Incentive: nine months on a prototype with no owner. Not saying: he thinks Maatra has won.
Anirudh Thakar — Partner, Mandaar Growth Partners, Gurugram; board. Position: one bet, falsifiable, with kill criteria and dates. Incentive: his fund is in its harvest window and ₹33.6 crore is below its hurdle. Not saying: whether Mandaar would consent, counsel having called a per-tonne model a possible change in principal business.

7. Voices

8. The options, as Eshita currently frames them

Path A — Mill depth. Push into the melt shop: heat balance, charge mix, yield reconciliation against Chhanti data. It defends the ₹4.3 crore mill line by being better where Hutaash is merely free, and keeps the covenant safe. It also concedes that Mahatol is a feature inside another firm's system of record, and needs Haldhar's goodwill exactly when Haldhar has reason to withhold it.

Path B — The per-tonne assay network. Rebuild in the cloud, publish an assay standard, charge per tonne on both sides, anchor on export documentation where regulation makes a buyer. The prize is a position no competitor can bundle away; the cost is cash exhaustion in April 2027, and a neutrality borrowed from Haldhar.

Path C — Down-market to the dealer. Give away the kaanta slip and the e-way bill to thirty thousand dealers, own the origination point before Maatra does, monetise later on compliance and trade. It alone aligns with Mahatol's fastest-growing line. It also asks a firm with sixty-eight per cent margins and an enterprise sales team to become a consumer-scale operation against an opponent holding ₹140 crore.

The framing has a seam nobody has named. Each path is named by the customer it serves, yet all three need the same rewrite, the same eleven months and the same release from the 2020 clause; the technical decision is made by default in every one. A fourth option is on no slide: take Bansal's offer and the exclusivity release, and become the group's technology arm with a guaranteed cluster and no covenant. And a fifth, raised twice by Nandita and folded each time into Path A: do nothing strategic, and put the engineering budget behind Rawana, which grew 107 per cent at seventy-eight per cent margin because the government created the demand.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at nine on Monday; the Haldhar offer lapses on 31 October. The exclusivity and the ₹26 crore covenant both fall on 31 March 2027, eleven weeks after Hiranya decides. Cash is ₹14.6 crore. Four hundred Harsiddhi appliances carry support obligations into 2028. Counsel will not say whether Mandaar's consent right bites. Anwesha's model has seen three yards; Parminder's survey, forty-one respondents of his choosing. And the only pilot that proved anything ran at gates owned by the company that now wants to own Mahatol.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. List the assumptions Mahatol's August 2025 plan depended on. Which were checkable then, and which have since been falsified rather than merely disappointed?
  2. Exhibits 2, 3 and 4 form a chain: the pilot justifies the fee, the fee justifies the model. Where does it first fail, and what would repair it before 31 March 2027?
  3. For each path, name the assumption whose failure would be most expensive, and the cheapest observation in the next sixty days that would test it.
  4. Whose incentives favour getting the answer right rather than a particular answer, and what would you change about how the board hears from them?
  5. Is the three-path framing right? Argue that the real decision is architectural, or that it is about the 2020 clause, or that it was made in 2020 and everything since is consequence.
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Eshita do first, what does she tell the board she will not do, and what does she say when Thakar asks what would change her mind?

11. Later that night

At a quarter to one Eshita typed a heading she had avoided all weekend: Things we have been treating as facts. Under it she wrote that mills accept a neutral assay; that formalisation is a tide and not a policy that can be amended; that Haldhar is a customer; that the pilot measured Chhanti. She looked at the four lines and added a fifth: that Mahatol is a software company.

She did not delete any of them.

Outside, the queue had grown to forty-six trucks. Near the front a driver started his engine, the gate light came on, and a man walked out with a rod to look at a load a machine in Toronto had scored at ninety-one per cent clean.

Risks and Assumptions in Strategy

What must be true for this strategy to work, how much is it worth paying to find out, and what do you do about the part you cannot find out in time?

1. Two boardrooms, two months apart

On 3 September 2026, Nandita Anantharaman, chief product officer of Kavachdhara Systems, was rereading a board memo she had not written. Kavachdhara, 140 people in Hyderabad, sold an AI-native financial-crime detection layer that sat on the rules engines Indian banks already ran. The memo proposed abandoning per-seat licensing and repricing everything as eight percent of the fraud losses the bank's own finance function certified the model had avoided. The board liked the number at the bottom: ₹96 crore of ARR by FY29, from twelve named banks.

The commitment was neither small nor casually reversible. Outcome pricing meant rebuilding billing, restructuring sales compensation, renegotiating three live contracts, and — the part nobody had costed — teaching every buyer's finance team a measurement ritual that did not yet exist. The board would decide on 30 October. The plan was not wrong, Nandita thought, so much as untethered; she could not yet say which of its numbers carried the weight.

Eleven weeks later and 500 kilometres south, Harish Dorai faced the same problem in another shape. Dhalkosh Instruments, in Coimbatore, made water-quality sensors for industrial effluent lines, hardware with a valuable analytics subscription attached. Its new continuous-monitoring probe could be tooled in house — ₹22 crore of moulds and a line at Hosur — or contract-manufactured for ₹6 crore at half the margin. Own tooling paid back handsomely if the state pollution control boards extended continuous-monitoring mandates to mid-size plants, and destroyed a third of the balance sheet if they did not. Dhalkosh had ₹34 crore of cash; its board met on 12 November.

Both decisions turn on one discipline, and it is not the enumeration of things that might go wrong. It is the allocation of a scarce resource — learning capital, the money and calendar time a firm can spend turning a belief into evidence before it must commit. Nandita can test one assumption cheaply and cannot test the other at all in nine weeks; Harish's belongs to a regulator and can never be observed before he signs. What follows is how experts triage that, and the two errors bracketing the field: assumption work as inventory, and the belief that every uncertainty is something a pilot can settle.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

Terms first, because the confusion is load-bearing. An assumption is a proposition the strategy's own arithmetic already requires: Kavachdhara's plan does not hope banks will certify prevented fraud; it cannot produce ₹96 crore unless they do. A risk is an event that would change the arithmetic — a rival cuts price, the RBI reclassifies the product. Many risks never surface as assumptions, because the model has no term for them.

The refinement that separates practitioners is narrower. A load-bearing assumption is one whose plausible range straddles the value at which the decision flips. Uncertainty alone does not qualify, and neither does importance: an assumption can be wildly uncertain and irrelevant, because every value in its range leads to the same choice, or nearly certain and decisive, because the decision sits on a knife-edge. The work is finding the straddlers, pricing what it costs to narrow them, and designing a response to those that stay wide.

The intellectual history runs on two tracks. Knight's 1921 distinction between risk (a known distribution) and uncertainty (none available) set the terms; planning in Ansoff's mould then treated strategy as forecast plus execution, which worked in stable industries and failed in new ones. Wack's scenario work at Shell abandoned the point forecast for irreducible uncertainties; Howard's decision analysis, and later Dixit and Pindyck on investment under irreversibility, formalised what information is worth before you buy it and why waiting has value. McGrath and MacMillan's Discovery-Driven Planning (1995) gave operators the procedure: work backward from the required profit, name every step as an assumption, release capital against evidence rather than the calendar. Alongside sit the critiques its admirers skip — reference-class forecasting, Klein's premortem, and Martin and Lafley's reversal of the burden of proof.

They disagree sharply enough to write down as propositions each camp would and would not sign.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Discovery-driven falsification (McGrath, Blank)No capital without a named assumption and a test built to falsify it.That some assumptions are created by commitment, never observed first.
Decision analysis (Howard, Raiffa)Rank by the value of information; spend nothing on an uncertainty that changes no choice.That a pilot is worth running because it is cheap.
Real options (Dixit, Pindyck)Irreversibility plus uncertainty gives waiting a computable value.That staging is free.

3. Mechanics: from a sentence to a variance, and from a variance to a price

Expert practice has a shape — nine steps, of which the middle four are usually left implicit.

First, write the commitment as an equation rather than a paragraph. Nandita's team reduced the ₹96 crore to its thinnest independent factors: revenue equals banks closed, times fraud exposure in the covered segment, times the recall uplift over the incumbent rules engine, times the share of prevented loss the bank's finance function certifies, times the eight percent fee. Written that way the plan can be interrogated term by term.

Second, run it forward at the medians — not at the values required to hit the target, which is where plans reverse-engineer their own inputs. Eight banks, ₹250 crore of exposure each, a twelve-point recall uplift, half the prevented loss certified, eight percent fee: ₹1.2 crore per bank and ₹9.6 crore of ARR.

Third, elicit ranges rather than points, from whoever would be embarrassed if the number were wrong, as an eighty percent interval. Most of the honest information in a planning process lives here, and templates with a cell for a number and none for a range discard it.

Fourth, decompose the variance. Because revenue is a product of five factors, log-revenue is a sum; if the factors are roughly independent, the variance of log-revenue is the sum of their log-variances, and each factor's variance share is its share of that sum. Converting an eighty percent range into a log standard deviation is arithmetic: divide the log of the high-to-low ratio by 2.56.

FactorMedian80% rangeσ of logVariance share
Recall uplift over incumbent rules engine12 pts4 – 25 pts0.7244%
Share of prevented loss the buyer certifies0.500.20 – 0.850.5728%
Banks closed by FY2984 – 140.4921%

Three results fall out that discussion had not produced. The total log standard deviation is 1.08, so the plan's own beliefs imply an eighty percent range spanning a factor of sixteen, ₹2.4 crore to ₹38 crore; ₹96 crore lies outside the distribution the team itself described. The market-size figure argued over for a fortnight carries five percent of the variance. And the certified share — an assumption about somebody else's finance department — outweighs everything except model performance, and had no owner.

One subtlety, because it is the commonest misuse: in a purely multiplicative model every factor has an elasticity of one, so ranking by variance share collapses to ranking by dispersion. Introduce fixed costs, thresholds or capacity constraints and elasticities stop being equal — a modest percentage error in a high-leverage input swamps a large error elsewhere — and the ranking must be done on elasticity times dispersion.

Fifth, find each factor's flip threshold — holding the others at their medians, at what value does the decision change? Outcome pricing beats per-seat only if the certified share exceeds about 0.34; below that Kavachdhara earns less than its current licence and has surrendered revenue predictability too. The question stops being “will certification work?” and becomes “how confident are we that it clears a third?”, which a nine-week study can answer.

Sixth, price the information before buying it. Dhalkosh's near-binary decision makes the arithmetic vivid. Harish's team put the chance of the mid-size mandate landing inside the payback window at 55 percent. Own tooling returns ₹48 crore of NPV if it lands and loses ₹19 crore if it does not; contract manufacture returns ₹21 crore and ₹2 crore. Expected value favours tooling, 17.85 against 12.45, and a less careful team would stop there.

The value of perfect information is ₹9.45 crore — the ceiling on what any regulatory intelligence could be worth. A realistic study, eighty percent accurate in each direction, is worth ₹4.58 crore. It costs ₹1.2 crore and five months of delay, priced at ₹3.8 crore of lost position with two bottling groups already specifying the product. Net: minus ₹0.42 crore. The study is genuinely informative and still not worth buying — a conclusion enthusiasm for evidence never produces on its own.

The last three steps make it operational. Seventh, classify each assumption as revealed or created, the distinction where the sharpest disagreement lives. Eighth, for the residue that cannot be resolved in time, stop testing and start structuring: bound the loss, buy a hedge, split the commitment into the part that works under both futures and the part that does not. Ninth, name the owner, the date and the response in advance.

4. When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are worth stating as checkable claims. One: the commitment is large relative to what the firm can absorb. Dhalkosh passes emphatically; Kavachdhara passes subtly, since the cash at risk is modest but reversing eighteen months of repricing is costly with the same twelve buyers the strategy needs. Two: evidence can arrive before the commitment date for less than the information is worth. Kavachdhara passes for certification, fails for recall; Dhalkosh fails outright. Three: the assumption is revealed rather than created. Both pass; a marketplace would not. Four: learning has somewhere to go — once the order is placed, a perfect study is worth zero.

The idea misleads in three situations. When a commitment's value comes precisely from irreversibility and earliness, analysis becomes a respectable form of delay; the commitments producing durable advantage are often those a stage-gate process would refuse. When the enumerated crowds out the unenumerated: no variance table has a row for “the bank's fraud operations head reads this tool as an audit of his own team.” And when precision on cheap assumptions is reported as validation of the whole.

5. Hard edge cases, and what the seams do

In multi-product firms, assumptions correlate across lines. Nine plans each risking ₹40 crore look like nine independent bets; if six assume the same regulatory change or distribution partner, exposure to that one proposition is ₹210 crore and no line owner can see it. Variance does not diversify when the drivers are shared.

In two-sided and platform businesses the central assumptions are created rather than revealed. Fill rate, liquidity and trust are functions of committed scale, so a deliberately small pilot measures a system denied the very input the assumption concerns. The right object of measurement is the cost of creating the level — rupees of supplier guarantee per point of fill rate.

In regulated markets the assumption's owner sits outside the firm and owes it no predictability. You cannot test a regulator; you can handicap, hedge, and design a product with a use under both rulings. Sophisticated firms separate regulatory timing from direction, because the two are differently uncertain.

In hardware-plus-software, testability is asymmetric: software assumptions are cheap to test, tooling assumptions are irreversible and untestable, and teams over-invest in the half that responds to effort. Dhalkosh's most valuable move was a design one — a dual-cavity mould serving both SKUs, which reduces the outcome's exposure to the variance rather than the uncertainty itself.

In AI-native products the load-bearing assumption is a conditional distribution, not a point: performance at the deployed base rate, under drift, on the customer's data rather than the benchmark's. Offline evaluation and live performance answer different questions. The second class — the price and capability trajectory of a dependency the firm does not control — has been the most volatile input in AI plans for three years and is rarely modelled at all.

At the organisational seams, assumptions go unowned: Kavachdhara's certification assumption belongs jointly to product, sales and the customer's finance team, which is to say to nobody. What mature firms actually do, rather than what their templates say, is keep a short private list of the four or five propositions the year rests on, and rely on one or two people who remember which assumptions were already falsified.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Uncertainty without decision weight is a distraction. The tell is that the risk consuming the most meeting time has the narrowest range, or no threshold inside it. The obvious reading — the scariest risk deserves the most attention — is wrong, because a risk that changes no action has an information value of zero.

Dispersion is half of weight; elasticity is the other half. Where there are fixed costs or thresholds, a ten percent error in a high-leverage input moves the outcome further than a doubling of a low-leverage one. The tell is a register sorted by the team's confidence, with no column for how far the outcome moves per unit of error.

Assumptions are revealed or created, and the class determines what a test can do. A revealed assumption exists independently of your commitment and a pilot observes it. A created one — liquidity, density, trust, category legitimacy — comes into being only above a scale of commitment the pilot withheld. The tell: the quantity measured is a function of your own committed scale. Pilots understate created assumptions and overstate revealed ones, because early customers get attention no scaled operation reproduces.

A test whose confidence interval straddles the threshold buys nothing. The tell is that nobody has said, before the pilot starts, how wide the interval it can return will be. An underpowered pilot does not return “no information”; it returns a point estimate the organisation reads as fact, which is worse than running nothing.

Information has a delivery date, and late information is worth zero. Experts ask when the answer arrives relative to when the cheque is signed before they ask what it costs. A nine-month study supporting a four-month decision is a rounding error dressed as care.

Pre-written thresholds are organisational instruments, not analytical ones. Their function is to defeat escalation of commitment by fixing the criterion before anyone's budget depends on it. The tell that they will not hold: they were written by the team whose funding dies if invoked, in comparative language — “meaningfully below” — rather than numeric.

Validated assumptions expire silently. A number verified in 2024 migrates into 2026 decks as a fact, stripped of date and method. The tell is a load-bearing input with no provenance line: what was tested was the value under conditions that have since moved.

Independence is assumed far more often than it is true. Six assumptions each rated eighty percent likely give a twenty-six percent joint probability if independent, which almost no plan acknowledges; but they usually are not independent, and the shared driver can make the conjunction far better or far worse than the naive product. The tell is a plan that states confidence per assumption and never in the conjunction.

Asymmetry dominates expectation. Two options with identical expected value are not equally choosable if one downside is absorbable and the other ends the company. The tell is a deck with base, upside and downside cases and no sentence saying which downside the firm survives — which is why Harish's ₹19 crore case deserved more scrutiny than its probability weight implied.

7. Differences by product type and stage

In consumer products the load-bearing assumptions are mostly revealed and cheap — retention, activation, willingness to pay — settled with cohorts in weeks; the characteristic error is misreading early cohorts whose superiority is a selection artefact. In B2B and enterprise, assumptions about the buyer's internal machinery — procurement, security review, attribution, who gets credit — outweigh assumptions about the product, and the small number of counterparties makes statistics useless; the substitute is a handful of named accounts, each a designed experiment. In platforms the dominant assumptions are created, so the analysis targets the cost of creation. In hardware the irreversible commitment precedes the information, pushing the discipline from testing toward hedging.

What does not differ is worth saying plainly: elasticity times dispersion, the flip threshold and the value-of-information test are identical everywhere. Only testability changes. Stage matters as much. A seed-stage company has no reference class of its own and little use for a reverse income statement; affordable loss is the operative logic. The discipline pays most between Series B and Series D, where commitments have grown fatal and there is just enough data to test something. At incumbents the problem inverts: retrieving evidence the firm already owns, noticing which settled assumptions have expired, and seeing correlated exposure across a portfolio planned line by line.

8. Three worked cases

Kavachdhara: a pilot that could not have answered the question

The obvious test was a ninety-day live pilot at one bank against the incumbent rules engine. Nandita's data science lead in Pune did the power calculation instead of the project plan. Detecting a twelve-point difference between a 62 percent baseline and a 74 percent treatment, at conventional confidence and eighty percent power, needs roughly 233 confirmed fraud events per arm. The pilot segment produces about ninety a quarter in total — 45 per arm — at which the interval around an observed twelve-point difference runs from minus seven to plus thirty-one.

That interval contains zero, the eight-point commercial threshold and the optimistic case alike. The pilot would have cost a quarter and returned a number the organisation would have treated as settled. The redesign pooled fourteen months of alert logs from three banks — 2,300 adjudicated events — for ₹40 lakh and nine weeks, narrowing the interval below four points. The caveat was recorded alongside: a backtest on adjudicated alerts measures recall on cases a prior process already surfaced, a friendlier question than live recall. Experts say both halves out loud.

Varmanpath Commerce: the discipline applied to the wrong class of assumption

Varmanpath ran a B2B ordering marketplace for small-town pharmacies. In 2022 its strategy team did everything the textbook asks: it named fill rate — the share of a pharmacy's order lines actually served — as the leap-of-faith assumption, set eighty percent as the threshold below which the model does not work, and ran a disciplined pilot in Nashik with sixty pharmacies and thirty-eight distributors. Fill rate came in at 61 percent. The team did not argue with its own threshold; the board killed the line.

A competitor committed ₹40 crore to exclusive distributor guarantees across four districts and reached 86 percent fill rate at 400 pharmacies within a year. Fill rate had never been a property of the market waiting to be observed; it was a property of committed distributor density, and the pilot had been designed to withhold exactly the input the assumption was about. Varmanpath re-entered twenty months later and paid ₹62 crore for a position it had priced at ₹18 crore. The recovery is the instructive part: created assumptions are now tested not for their level but for the elasticity of creation. The second entry measured that each point of fill rate cost about ₹1.9 crore of distributor guarantee, declining above 75 percent — one number that turned an unanswerable question into an investment decision with a slope.

Rakshakosh Payments: correlation at portfolio level

Rakshakosh, a large Mumbai payments incumbent, ran nine product lines whose FY27 plans each carried a properly written risk section. A new head of strategy did what no line plan could: she cross-tabulated every load-bearing assumption by its underlying driver. Six plans — ₹210 crore of committed spend — turned on the timing of one regulatory change, which each had independently rated “moderate risk, ₹40 crore exposure.” The response was portfolio surgery: one line hedged to work under both rulings, one accelerated, three re-planned. No individual plan had been wrong.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Test theatre
Piloting what is easy rather than what is decisive. Sign: the test plan reads like the product roadmap. Diagnostic: which number in the model will this move, and by how much? Late, it costs a quarter and manufactures confidence in a plan whose centre was never examined.
Underpowered evidence
A study that cannot distinguish the outcomes that matter. Sign: nobody has stated the interval it can return. Diagnostic: how many events will we observe, and where does the threshold sit inside that interval? Late, the firm kills a good business or scales a bad one and cannot tell which.
Threshold erosion
Sign: the result is “directionally encouraging” rather than a number. Diagnostic: read the threshold aloud from the original memo before the result is presented. Late, it costs tranches two and three.
Silent expiry
A once-tested assumption ages into a fact. Sign: a load-bearing input with no date or source. Diagnostic: require provenance on every number in the chain. Late, a plan rests on a cost structure that moved two years ago.
Correlated bets
Sign: risk sections written line by line with no cross-view. Diagnostic: tabulate assumptions by driver, not by owner. Late, several businesses miss together and the board blames execution.
Analysis as delay
Sign: each study generates a request for the next and the flip threshold keeps moving. Diagnostic: fix the decision date first, then ask what can be known by then. Late, the position is gone and the analysis is immaculate.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Stage the commitment, or make it? The discovery-driven position rests on a large body of post-mortems in which capital was released on a calendar and the core assumption never examined. Ghemawat's is that advantage is manufactured precisely by commitments rivals cannot cheaply match, and a firm making only reversible moves has chosen a strategy anyone can copy in a quarter. Both are well-evidenced because they answer different questions. The commitment school would be wrong if staged entrants routinely beat committed ones into attractive positions; the staging school would be wrong if write-offs among committed entrants were rare. Neither base rate is cleanly measured.

Does small-scale evidence generalise? The lean tradition holds that a well-designed small test is the best available forecast of the large case. The reflexivity critique — Varmanpath's lesson — holds that for a whole class of assumptions the measured quantity is a function of the commitment withheld; the reference-class school adds that your pilot is one draw from a distribution you could have looked up. Lean would be wrong if pilots mispredicted at scale in a direction set by assumption type; reflexivity would be wrong if committed entrants in network businesses failed as often as staged ones.

Should kill thresholds bind? The behavioural case is strong: escalation of commitment is among the better-replicated findings in organisational behaviour, and a number fixed before anyone's budget depends on it is the cheapest defence available. The counter-case is that a rigid threshold discards information arriving in a form it did not anticipate, and that metrics chosen to be binding are selected for measurability rather than importance, which makes them gameable. The practical middle keeps the threshold binding but requires an override in writing, by a named person.

Should strategic uncertainties carry probabilities at all? The decision-analytic answer is yes: calibration is trainable, structured estimation beats intuition, and without numbers you cannot compute what information is worth. The Knightian and scenario answer is that attaching 0.55 to a unique regulatory event launders ignorance into precision, and that the response should be a few rehearsed futures and a strategy robust across them. Dhalkosh's 0.55 is the contested object: it produced the ₹9.45 crore ceiling that stopped the team buying a study worth less, and it was a number three people made up in a room.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in observable ways. They ask for ranges before numbers, and notice when a range is suspiciously narrow. They reach for the flip threshold early — at what value does our answer change? — and often find the argument was unnecessary. They can be heard declining to test something because the answer would change no decision, the behaviour that most distinguishes them from a diligent practitioner. They price delay as a cost of information. They do not send a pilot to measure what the firm creates rather than observes. And when the residue cannot be resolved in time, they stop analysing and start structuring.

12. What Nandita and Harish decided

On 30 October, Nandita neither asked the board to approve outcome pricing nor to reject it. She presented the variance decomposition, the ₹9.6 crore median against the ₹96 crore target, and the sixteen-fold range, and proposed treating the two dominant assumptions differently because their testability differed. Certification — 28 percent of variance, cheap to test — would be settled by the nine-week attribution exercise with three banks' finance teams, the decision rule written as a number, 0.34. Recall, 44 percent of variance, could not be tested to decision precision in the window, so the pricing model would not be bet on it: a per-seat floor with capped outcome upside, sacrificing the ceiling to survive the downside.

On 12 November, Harish committed to own tooling, but not the tooling in the paper: a ₹14 crore dual-cavity mould serving both variants, the Hosur line deferred two quarters, the regulatory study declined on the arithmetic above, and ₹35 lakh spent on a ninety-day call option with a contract manufacturer. He did not reduce his uncertainty about the mandate at all. He reduced the amount of outcome that depended on it — which, when the information does not arrive before the cheque clears, is the only move available.

For discussion.

1. Kavachdhara's largest source of variance was the one it could not test in time. Did Nandita allocate her learning capital correctly, or simply buy the answer that was for sale?

2. Varmanpath honoured its own pre-written kill threshold and was destroyed by doing so. When should a team override a threshold it wrote itself, and how would you draft that escape clause without making the threshold meaningless?

3. Harish's 0.55 was invented in a room, yet it determined that a ₹1.2 crore study was not worth buying. Would a scenario process without probabilities have produced a better decision, or only a less accountable one?

13. Going deeper

  • The product strategy document — the container this work closes; an assumption list detached from the commitments it qualifies is never read twice.
  • Surfacing assumptions — the same discipline at feature scale, where the habit is built.
  • What strategy is and isn't — decides which propositions are eligible to be load-bearing.
  • Rumelt's kernel — the assumptions that matter most hide inside the diagnosis, where nobody looks.
  • Playing to Win — the source of the reverse-the-burden move and of candidate flip thresholds.
  • Product-market fit — the canonical created-versus-revealed problem.
  • Wardley mapping — gives assumptions a time axis: not “will this hold?” but “for how long?”.
  • Disruption theory — the reference class for one dangerous assumption: that incumbent response will be rational and timely.

Waseela Care Networks: Ten Days Before Diwali

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 12 October 2025, Karthik Venkataraman was at the dining table of his flat in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, with a laptop, a cold filter coffee and a document he had rewritten four times. The board of Waseela Care Networks met at nine the next morning off the Financial District road, and the only substantive item was the FY27 product strategy document that Karthik, Head of Product, had been asked to present.

The ask had come eleven days earlier from Ashwin Dasgupta, the Chief Business Officer who joined in July, in a sentence Karthik had stuck to the edge of his monitor: "Nine pages. Tell me who we are for, what we will not build, and what has to be true for the numbers to work." Karthik had produced twenty-two pages twice and nine pages once, and the nine-page version came back with a single comment on the first line: "This is a budget with adjectives."

What made the night uncomfortable was not a shortage of options. Karthik had three, each with a sponsor, a model and slides. What he could not settle was whether the three were the real choice at all — or whether the document's silence about a contract signed six years before he joined made every one of them a fiction. The board would not ask about that contract. Pranay Mukhopadhyay might.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Waseela Care Networks was founded in Hyderabad in 2017 by Dr. Sunita Ramabhadran, a paediatrician who had run a two-doctor clinic in Vijayawada for eleven years, and Aneesh Varghese, an engineer she met through a hospital IT tender. The product was unglamorous and well-loved: a clinic operating system handling appointments, queues, e-prescriptions, a lightweight medical record, GST-compliant billing and WhatsApp reminders, for the single-doctor and two-to-five-doctor clinics that deliver most of India's outpatient care on paper registers and software written in the 1990s. It ran on a ₹9,000 Android tablet without broadband, in Telugu, Tamil, Hindi, Marathi and English.

The decision that still shaped everything came in August 2019, when Waseela had 1,300 clinics and eight months of cash. Witaran Pharma Distribution, a Nagpur distributor with roughly 2,900 medical representatives calling on clinics across eleven states, offered a channel agreement: its representatives would sell and install Waseela during existing calls, Waseela would price at a channel rate, and Witaran would take 22 per cent of subscription revenue from clinics it originated. The agreement ran to March 2027, with exclusivity on any Indian pharmacy integration Waseela built and a right of first refusal on diagnostics-order routing.

The deal saved the company. It also, by FY25, accounted for 61 per cent of Waseela's paying clinics and a similar share of subscription revenue — at a lower price, under a contract Waseela could neither reprice nor escape for seventeen more months. Dr. Ramabhadran defended it whenever it came up: without it there would be no company to have a strategy for. Karthik did not disagree. He simply could not write a true paragraph on differentiation, monetisation or acquisition without mentioning it, and could find no way to mention it that did not read, to a board, like an accusation.

3. The industry

India's outpatient software market in 2025 was crowded at the top and thin in the middle. Practo had the consumer brand and the discovery traffic; HealthPlix and Eka Care had credible clinical workflow products with venture backing; Bajaj Finserv Health bundled clinic tooling with financing and insurance; Apollo 24/7 and Tata 1mg pulled patients toward integrated pharmacy and diagnostics. None had solved the economics of selling a ₹2,500-a-month subscription to a doctor in Warangal or Hubballi — precisely the ground Waseela and Witaran's field force had taken.

Two regulatory forces bore on the roadmap. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission had made ABHA-linked records and the Health Facility Registry a practical requirement for clinics in state schemes, and Waseela's 2021 ABDM integration was an acquisition advantage for eighteen months before competitors matched it. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, phasing in through 2025 and 2026, made Waseela a Data Fiduciary for several crore patient records held for clinics, and raised unresolved questions about consent architecture for any patient-facing product or data product sold to insurers. The National Medical Commission's telemedicine guidance limited what a vendor could automate inside a consultation.

Exposure outside India was small but growing fast. Since 2023 Waseela had sold to 34 UAE polyclinics, anchored by Wahaj Medical Group LLC, a nine-site Dubai group whose Group Medical Director, Dr. Faisal Rahman, was now the company's most demanding customer. Gulf clinics paid roughly fifteen times Indian ARPU, required Dubai Health Authority compliance and Arabic localisation, and had introduced Waseela to a buyer with a procurement function — a species its India product had never met.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In January 2022, on 148 per cent growth, Waseela raised a ₹210 crore Series B led by Wafaa Capital Partners at ₹1,150 crore post-money. That plan assumed the Witaran channel would keep compounding while direct inside sales grew alongside it, and that a diagnostics module would attach to 30 per cent of the base within two years.

By FY24 two of those beliefs had weakened. The diagnostics module attached to 11 per cent of clinics in its first full year, not 30. Direct inside sales worked, but at a cost per clinic roughly eight times the reported cost of the channel, which made it indefensible in a monthly business review even though its clinics paid more and stayed longer. Reading the comparison at face value, the board in April 2024 shifted two-thirds of the inside-sales budget into channel support. Direct acquisition fell from 2,100 clinics in FY24 to 1,180 in FY25, and blended ARPU declined for the first time in the company's history.

In February 2025 Dr. Malini Iyer, lead data scientist in Toronto, showed the leadership team a model predicting outpatient claim rejection at what she reported as 0.89 AUC, trained on four years of de-identified prescription, diagnosis-code and billing data. Wusat General Insurance, a mid-sized private health insurer, asked about a pilot, and the FY26 plan gained a ₹6 crore line. In August, a review by Aneesh's platform team established that 71 per cent of the training data came from 312 clinics in Tamil Nadu and Kerala using the optional structured-coding feature — a set skewed heavily toward multi-speciality clinics with in-house billing staff. The ₹6 crore line was not removed; it was moved to FY27.

In June 2025 Dr. Ramabhadran told the board she would move to an Executive Chair role within a year. Ashwin Dasgupta was hired in July with a mandate his appointment letter called "commercial focus and path to profitability". His first act was to halt the FY27 planning cycle and ask for a strategy document instead of a budget; his second was to ask Karthik, on 22 September, a question Karthik had not stopped turning over: "If Witaran walked away in March 2027, what would we still be?"

5. The people

Karthik Venkataraman, Head of Product, Hyderabad. Joined 2022 from a Chennai SaaS company; believes the defensible asset is clinical depth in Indian-language, low-bandwidth settings. Incentive: a retention-weighted bonus on the existing base. Not saying: he thinks Witaran must be renegotiated or exited, and cannot propose it without appearing to attack the founder's judgement.

Dr. Sunita Ramabhadran, Co-founder and CEO, Hyderabad. Wants Waseela to stay a clinical product company; uneasy about monetising patient data. Incentive: the integrity of what she built, and a move to Executive Chair that does not look like retreat. Not saying: a strategic acquirer approached her in August with an indicative all-cash offer she has mentioned to nobody on the management team.

Aneesh Varghese, Co-founder and CTO, Bengaluru. Argues none of the options is buildable on the current architecture without an eighteen-month re-foundation, costed at ₹14 crore. Incentive: a system he can hire against. Not saying: a third of that estimate is undoing shortcuts his own team took in 2019 to meet Witaran's installation deadlines.

Ashwin Dasgupta, Chief Business Officer, Chennai. Ran a ₹400 crore unit at a large Indian SaaS company. Wants one audience, one wedge, and a list of what Waseela will not build. Incentive: the two-year profitability mandate attached to his hiring. Not saying: he thinks the Gulf business is the only part with pricing power, and has no settled view on whether India is worth its overhead.

Zoya Farooqui, Head of Design, Berlin. Two quarters into a patient app — records, family profiles, medication reminders — with usability evidence that patients adopt it when a doctor introduces it. Incentive: to ship the first Waseela product an end user ever touches. Not saying: her research covered 240 patients in Hyderabad and Pune, all recruited through already-enthusiastic clinics, and a Berlin recruiter has been in touch.

Dr. Malini Iyer, Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Believes the claims layer is the only asset a competitor cannot replicate by writing better software. Incentive: a real payer deployment on her record. Not saying: she agrees the Tamil Nadu and Kerala skew is disqualifying nationally, and has not corrected the 0.89 figure still in three internal decks.

Gerald Fernandes, Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey. Built Wahaj into a ₹5.6 crore line; argues Gulf-first with a US follow-on. Incentive: bookings-weighted commission, no retention clawback. Not saying: two of the four largest Gulf accounts expire in Q1 FY27 and want Arabic clinical templates nobody has committed to build.

Serena Koh, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Covers the Indian channel base and the Gulf accounts; reports that Witaran clinics generate a third of the support load of direct clinics. Incentive: a support-cost-per-account target. Not saying: she reads that low load not as efficiency but as evidence that much of the base never adopted the product.

Pranay Mukhopadhyay, Partner, Wafaa Capital Partners, Mumbai; board member. Led the Series B and sits closest to the valuation question. Incentive: a mark that survives a Series C at or above the 2022 price. Not saying: his fund has flagged Waseela for a structured secondary, and he is testing whether the claims layer, not the clinic software, is the story a later-stage investor would buy.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sat on page two of every draft: growth, but slower, at a falling price, with gross margin three points down in two years.
