7. Voices

"I do not want a plan that is only credible if a distributor in Nagpur behaves well. Tell me the version where they don't."
— Ashwin Dasgupta, leadership review, 30 September

"Sixty-one per cent of our clinics came from Witaran's representatives knocking on doors in towns we have never visited. That is not a weakness in the strategy. For four years it was the strategy."
— Dr. Sunita Ramabhadran, same meeting

"Whichever of the three we pick, the first nine months are the same nine months of platform work. I would rather we said that out loud than discovered it in February."
— Aneesh Varghese, email, 2 October

"Dr. Rahman asked me again about Arabic templates. I said Q1. Karthik, please tell me it is Q1."
— Gerald Fernandes, chat, 6 October, 04:12 IST

"I can give you a number for the patient app. I cannot give you a number I believe, because everyone I tested with was already sitting in a clinic that likes us."
— Zoya Farooqui, design review, 7 October

"Support tickets from channel clinics are low. I have stopped reporting that as a good sign. Two-thirds of them have never opened the prescription module."
— Serena Koh, operations note, 9 October

"The model is real. The dataset is not national. Both sentences are true and only one of them is in the deck."
— Dr. Malini Iyer, call, 9 October

"I am less interested in which of the three you pick than in what you think we own. If the answer is a channel relationship, say so, and we should talk about a very different kind of company."
— Pranay Mukhopadhyay, email, 11 October, 22:40 IST

8. The options as Karthik currently frames them

Option A — Win the clinic completely

Deepen the clinical product: insurance workflow, ABDM-native records, structured coding, a claims module alongside the Wusat pilot. Waseela owns the encounter, and depth raises ARPU inside 9,240 clinics without new acquisition spend. But most of that base was acquired by a partner at a price the partner sets, and the best attach opportunity may sit inside an exclusivity nobody has tested.

Option B — Reach the patient

Ship Zoya's patient app, monetise a family subscription, use the clinic as distribution. Patients are the only counterparty in Indian healthcare with rising willingness to pay, and a consumer brand would free Waseela from any distributor. But Practo, Apollo 24/7 and Tata 1mg have built that habit for a decade, DPDP consent architecture is unbuilt, and the evidence is 240 favourably recruited patients.

Option C — Follow the money to the Gulf

Fund Arabic localisation, DHA compliance and a Dubai team, expand from 34 polyclinics to a regional footprint, treat India as a cash base. Fifteen-times ARPU, and a buyer with a procurement budget. But a nine-month sales cycle, two renewals at risk, a product team stretched across three roadmaps.

Karthik had written all three, and a fourth paragraph he kept deleting. The fourth was less an option than a suspicion: that the three were geographies dressed as strategies, that Ashwin's real question — who is Waseela for, and what will it refuse to build — was answered by none of them, and that the only choice with consequence was whether the document said out loud that Waseela's distribution was rented, on a lease with seventeen months to run.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 09:00 on Monday, 13 October 2025. Dr. Ramabhadran has asked for a recommendation, not a menu. Cash stands at ₹38.4 crore against ₹2.1 crore of monthly net burn — roughly eighteen months before a raise becomes urgent — and Ashwin's breakeven mandate implies no more than ₹12–14 crore of incremental FY27 investment unless growth accelerates first. Aneesh's ₹14 crore re-foundation sits in none of the option budgets. The Witaran agreement runs to March 2027, with a 180-day notice window opening in September 2026, carries Indian pharmacy exclusivity, and is silent on insurance workflow. Two Gulf contracts worth ₹2.1 crore renew in Q1 FY27 with an unfunded Arabic-template commitment. DPDP obligations for a patient product are unscoped, headcount is frozen at 214, and Zoya cannot fill three design roles.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Write the one-sentence audience statement that should open the FY27 document. Who, precisely, is the customer — and does the answer change if the payer is a clinic, a patient or an insurer?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 each contain a number the company acted on. Identify what each actually measures, and which decisions since April 2024 would have gone differently under the other reading.
  3. Exhibit 4 shows two models disagreeing nearly fivefold on Option B. What would you need to observe, over what period, before putting either number in front of a board?
  4. Waseela's differentiation is described internally both as "clinical depth in low-bandwidth, Indian-language settings" and as "the Witaran field force". Which, if either, is a right to win, and what in the exhibits supports or undermines each?
  5. The stakeholders' positions are individually rational and collectively incoherent. Choose the two whose incentives most distort the document, and say how you would change what is written — or measured — so the distortion becomes visible to the board.
  6. It is Monday morning. What goes on page one, what does Karthik name as the thing Waseela will not build, and how does he raise Witaran in front of the founder who signed it — or does he not raise it at all?

At ten to midnight Karthik opened a new document and typed a heading he had not used in any of the four drafts: What we are choosing not to be. Below it he wrote three lines, deleted two, and left the third: A company whose distribution belongs to someone else. Then he deleted that one too, because he could not tell whether it was a diagnosis or a resignation letter, and because Dr. Ramabhadran would read it at nine beside her co-founder, her new Chief Business Officer and the investor who had priced the company at ₹1,150 crore.

Somewhere across Gachibowli a first round of crackers went off, ten days early. Karthik saved the file with no recommendation in it and sat looking at the heading.

Strategy & Business · Product Strategy

The Product Strategy Document

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Rohan Bhatt, a senior product manager at Sphatik Analytics, opened an email from his VP of Product, Ananya Deshmukh, that named a date rather than a task: October 12, the day the board would review the case for Sphatik's Series C. Sphatik, a seven-year-old workforce-analytics company in Pune, sold a platform that watched agent desktops and call metadata inside business-process-outsourcing units and gave floor supervisors real-time quality scores. It carried ₹38 crore in annual recurring revenue across 46 accounts, growing 34 percent year over year — respectable, but short of the 40 percent investors had privately signalled they wanted sustained for two more quarters before committing at the valuation Sphatik's founders were asking.

Ananya's email did not ask Rohan to build anything. It asked him to choose between two things engineering could build, and to write down, in a form she could defend to sceptical board members, why one deserved the next two quarters of capacity and the other did not. Sphatik had roughly fourteen engineer-quarters free before the checkpoint — enough for one initiative, not both. Option one, Sphatik Copilot, was an AI quality-audit assistant existing customers had wanted for a year, sellable as a warm upsell into the 46 live accounts. Option two, Sphatik Shopfloor, extended the same anomaly-detection engine from call centres to factory floors — a manufacturing-analytics market a well-funded Bengaluru rival, Taamra Cloud, was already prospecting with two signed pilots and, by rumour, a ₹40 crore raise earmarked for exactly this push. Rohan had four weeks to write the document that made the case either way.

Exhibit 1 — Sphatik Analytics, September 2026 snapshot
MetricValue
Annual recurring revenue₹38 crore
Active accounts (logos)46
Average contract value₹82 lakh
Year-over-year growth34%
Board's growth checkpoint40% by Q4 FY27
Free engineering capacity~14 engineer-quarters

The argument, not the plan

A product strategy document is a written, falsifiable argument for how a specific product will win a specific customer's money against a specific set of alternatives — not a description of features, not a schedule of work. It states a diagnosis of the situation the product is in, a guiding policy for what the team will do about it, and a small set of coherent actions and evidence consistent with that policy, laid out precisely enough that a reader who disagreed could name the exact sentence they disagreed with. The structure practitioners use today — audience, problem, value proposition, differentiation, competition, acquisition, monetisation, metrics, plan, risks — descends from strategist Richard Rumelt's "kernel" of diagnosis, guiding policy, and coherent action, set out in his 2011 book Good Strategy/Bad Strategy as a corrective to the vague, ambition-only strategy documents Rumelt had spent two decades watching companies write and then quietly ignore.

Product organisations absorbed the kernel through a related lineage: Amazon's narrative six-page memos, formalised under Jeff Bezos in the mid-2000s to replace slide decks with sentences a reader could interrogate line by line, and the product-strategy writing that came out of the Silicon Valley Product Group through the 2010s, which broke the kernel into specific questions — who is this for, what problem, why us, against whom, how will they find us, how will we charge, how will we know, what happens first, what could go wrong. The document Rohan had to write was that same kernel, with Sphatik's own numbers filling every section. The sentence he could repeat in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: a strategy document exists so a sceptical reader can find the one assumption the whole plan rests on, and press on it before the company spends a rupee building anything.

Ten answers, in order, that build on each other

Writing the document is not filling in ten headings independently; each section constrains the next. Rohan opened with an audience more specific than "BPO supervisors" — pulled straight from persona work Sphatik's research team had done that spring: a Head of Quality at a 1,500–2,500 seat voice BPO, reporting to an Operations Head, judged quarterly on cost-per-contact-resolved and an audit sample covering three to five percent of calls. That persona did double duty: as the buyer for Copilot, and, restated for a plant setting, as the template Rohan had to build from nothing for Shopfloor, since no comparable research existed there yet — an uncomfortable early finding in its own right.

The problem section names the specific job the customer is failing at today; the value proposition section states the promise the product makes about that job. Here Rohan hit the rule newcomers usually miss: the value proposition statement is not a section to reinvent. Sphatik already had one, tested in every sales deck — "give supervisors an early warning on quality failures instead of a monthly audit sample" — and for Copilot it held with a single clause added. For Shopfloor it plainly did not: plant heads run yield and downtime, not quality audits, so Rohan had to draft a new value proposition from a standing start.

Differentiation and competition come next, and only once the customer's actual next-best alternative is named — the specific thing the customer would do instead, whether that is Taamra Cloud, an in-house spreadsheet, or doing nothing for another quarter. Acquisition and monetisation follow with a channel and a price the customer already trusts. Two mechanics newcomers leave implicit belong here too: stating, in one sentence, everything the option deliberately will not do this cycle, and writing the kill metric before writing the growth targets that make the option look attractive. Metrics and the ninety-day plan close the document, followed by risks, written as the counter-argument a sceptical reader would raise, answered inside the document rather than saved for the meeting.

The arithmetic that carried the argument

Rohan's document earned its five pages mostly in one exhibit: a side-by-side sizing of both options using the same four numbers each — cost to acquire a customer (CAC), average contract value (ACV), gross margin, and the resulting cash payback period, the time before the customer is worth having taken on. Sphatik Copilot, sold to the quality lead inside an existing account, carried a CAC of about ₹4 lakh, mostly customer-success time, against a 35 percent attach rate on the 46-account base in year one — sixteen logos. At an add-on ACV of ₹18 lakh and Sphatik's blended 80 percent margin, incremental year-one ARR came to ₹2.88 crore, and payback worked out to CAC ÷ (ACV × margin): ₹4 lakh ÷ (₹18 lakh × 0.80), or 0.28 year — about three months.

For Sphatik Shopfloor, Rohan built the sizing top-down and checked it bottom-up: an India total addressable market for shop-floor quality analytics of roughly ₹450 crore, a serviceable segment of mid-size manufacturers already on a modern ERP of about ₹120 crore, and a first-eighteen-month obtainable share — given one informal reference customer — of about 2 percent, or ₹2.4 crore. Reaching that meant closing ten new logos at a lower ACV of ₹24 lakh each, through an unproven motion to plant heads nobody at Sphatik had called on, with a nine-month cycle and a heavier CAC of ₹22 lakh. Payback: ₹22 lakh ÷ (₹24 lakh × 0.75), or 1.22 years — about fifteen months, five times slower than Copilot on Sphatik's own optimistic assumption.

Exhibit 3 — Payback sensitivity: one changed assumption moves the conclusion
Copilot (upsell)Shopfloor — 1st passShopfloor — 2nd pass
CAC per logo₹4 lakh₹22 lakh₹22 lakh
ACV assumption₹18 lakh₹24 lakh (hopeful)₹15 lakh (Taamra pilots)
Gross margin80%75%75%
Cash payback0.28 yr (~3 mo)1.22 yr (~15 mo)1.96 yr (~23.5 mo)

The document did not stop at the first pass, because the board's real question was not which option was bigger but which survived being wrong. Rohan reran Shopfloor with one input changed — an ACV of ₹15 lakh, drawn from the two known Taamra Cloud pilot sizes rather than Sphatik's own hopeful figure. Payback stretched to 1.96 years, past the eighteen-month cash-runway ceiling the board had set that year. One changed assumption moved Shopfloor from "slower but plausible" to "outside the constraint that mattered" — visibly, inside the document, where a reader could see exactly which number had done the moving.

What a learner must become aware of

A strategy document is not a roadmap

A roadmap lists what a team will build and when; a strategy document states why that list, rather than another, is the right bet. Skip the diagnosis and go straight to a features-and-dates table, and the result looks identical while answering a different question — schedule, not choice. Rohan's first Shopfloor draft made exactly this mistake: a tidy Gantt chart with no paragraph explaining why plant heads, rather than any other buyer, were the right beachhead.

The value proposition is ground truth, not raw material

Teams under deadline pressure often draft a fresh value proposition inside the strategy document rather than reusing, or explicitly revising, the one already tested with customers. That produces a document that displays a company's confusion about its own promise instead of hiding it. The correct move, when the existing statement genuinely does not fit a new context, is to say so openly, as Rohan did for Shopfloor.

Competition means the customer's alternative, not a features matrix

A checklist of rival capabilities answers "what do they have" when the document needs to answer "what would this customer do instead, and why pay us rather than that." The true alternative is frequently not a competitor at all but inertia — a spreadsheet, a manual process, another quarter of waiting — and a document that only benchmarks named rivals will misjudge the size of the switching decision.

It is routinely confused with the PRD and the business case

A strategy document argues why a direction is right; a product requirements document, once chosen, specifies what gets built; a business case tests whether the finance behind that direction works at the detail a CFO needs. Merging the three under deadline pressure produces one document trying to sell, spec, and justify at once, and doing all three poorly.

It cannot verify its own diagnosis

A well-written strategy document makes reasoning inspectable, not correct. A sceptical VP's job is to attack the diagnosis paragraph directly, asking what evidence would have to differ for it to be false. Ananya's read of Rohan's Shopfloor section tested precisely this: whether "plant heads care about yield more than quality" was established by evidence or merely asserted.

Choose leading metrics, not only lagging ones

Revenue and logo count are lagging; a document listing only these gives no early warning before two quarters are already spent. Rohan's metrics section for Copilot named a sixty-day leading signal — trial-to-paid conversion among the first eight upsell accounts — so the team would know by November, not April, whether the attach-rate assumption underneath the sizing exhibit was actually holding.

It earns its cost only when resources are genuinely scarce

A full ten-section document for a two-week task with no competing use of that time is over-process: the format forces a real trade-off into the open, and applying it where none exists adds ceremony without adding a decision. Sphatik's fourteen-engineer-quarter constraint made the document necessary; an optional bug-fix sprint would not have.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and company stage

The ten sections mean different things depending on who is buying. In B2B, like Sphatik's, buyer and user often differ, so the audience section must name both, acquisition is dominated by a sales cycle and a champion rather than a channel, and the board metric is logo and net revenue retention more than daily actives. In consumer products, the audience section is built from funnels and cohorts rather than a job title, differentiation is often about brand and experience rather than a discrete feature, and monetisation and acquisition are argued together through lifetime value against paid-channel cost — the discipline a wellness app like Manikya Wellness lives or dies by, since one mis-costed channel can erase a quarter's growth. Marketplaces complicate the kernel further because there are two audiences, not one: a document for a company like Kanchan Bazaar must diagnose supply and demand as separate sections with separate acquisition economics, since a guiding policy addressing only buyers ignores the chicken-and-egg problem that determines whether the marketplace exists at all.

Company stage changes the document's evidentiary weight more than its structure. An early-stage team can defend a two-page version built on ten customer interviews and a founder's pattern-matching; a mature company reviewing a document like Rohan's expects quantified sizing, an explicit trade-off against every other team competing for the same capacity, and a review cadence that revisits the document on a fixed schedule rather than only when someone gets nervous.

Common mistakes

The wish-list document. Symptom: the strategy reads "we will win on quality, speed, and price," naming every dimension the team hopes to win on. Misunderstanding: mistaking ambition for choice, when a real strategy states what it will not do. Diagnostic: ask what the document rules out; silence answers the question.

The orphaned competition section. Symptom: a table of rival features with checkmarks and no connecting argument. Misunderstanding: conflating naming competitors with explaining differentiation. Diagnostic: delete the company names and check whether the prose still explains why this customer picks this product.

Metrics theatre. Symptom: a dashboard listing ten or twelve KPIs with no threshold on any of them. Misunderstanding: treating metrics as decoration rather than a falsification device. Diagnostic: ask which single number, at what value, would make the team stop; if nobody can answer in one sentence, it is measurement, not a metric.

The document written after the decision. Symptom: unusually smooth prose, a thin alternatives section, a timeline that matches what engineering already started building. Misunderstanding: using the document to justify a decision made informally, rather than to make one. Diagnostic: compare the document's first-draft date to the date of the first line of code.

What good looks like

Two years before Rohan's assignment, a peer company, Panna Systems, a Chennai-based inventory-forecasting SaaS, faced a structurally identical fork: an AI-forecasting upsell into its thirty-odd retail accounts, or a new vertical selling the same engine into quick-commerce dark stores, a segment growing fast enough that two funds had already asked its board about it. Panna's product lead wrote both sizings side by side using the same four numbers, ran a pessimistic pass on the new-vertical ACV before anyone asked her to, and included one paragraph naming the evidence that would change her recommendation. Her board approved the safer upsell in a single meeting, with no follow-up questions, because there was nothing left to interrogate that the document had not already interrogated. Eight months later, when the upsell's attach rate came in below the leading indicator's threshold, that same kill-metric paragraph became the basis for the next quarter's pivot conversation — the document had already done that thinking too.

What Rohan decided

Rohan recommended Sphatik Copilot, and Ananya carried it to the board on October 12 largely unchanged: the sensitivity-tested payback gap was wide enough, and the manufacturing evidence thin enough, that the safer bet's downside was smaller than the aggressive bet's chance of being wrong for reasons the document had already named. Shopfloor was not abandoned — the closing paragraph set the specific evidence, a second unprompted plant-head inbound, or a public Taamra Cloud contract above ₹20 lakh ACV, that would reopen the case at the next quarterly review. What Rohan needed to learn next was less about writing strategy documents than what surrounds them: how a risks-and-assumptions section stays a live commitment rather than a one-time forecast, and how a portfolio of bets gets reviewed on a fixed cadence rather than re-argued each time a founder gets nervous. Two questions worth sitting with: what would have to be true for Shopfloor to be the right bet after all — and does a VP who has watched strategies fail read a document more harshly, or simply more usefully, than one who never has?
case20v1-pstrat.doc:
Product Strategy · Reading Case

Ishara Retail Cloud: The Strategy Document

1. Opening

On the morning of Thursday, 18 September 2025, Ananya Rao sat in a glass-walled meeting room on the fourth floor of Ishara Retail Cloud's office in Bengaluru's Koramangala, rereading an email she already knew by heart. It was from Meenal Oberoi, a Vice President at Ishaan Growth Partners, the venture fund that had led Ishara's ₹58 crore Series B eight months earlier and now held a board observer seat. Meenal had sent back Ananya's first draft of the FY26 product strategy document two days earlier with a single line: "This reads like three good ideas looking for a reason. Pick one and defend it." The board would meet on Monday, 22 September, to approve the year's product direction before Ishara opened Series C conversations. Ananya, Vice President of Product, had four working days to turn a list of options into a document a skeptical investor would sign.

2. Company background

Ishara Retail Cloud sold a billing, inventory and payments app built for India's small offline retailers — kirana stores, apparel outlets and electronics shops that had never used a computer for their accounts. Founded in 2020 by Karan Mehta after watching a relative's garment shop lose track of stock during a festive-season rush, the product let a shopkeeper generate a GST-compliant bill, accept UPI payments, and see stock levels on a phone, in Hindi, Kannada, Tamil or English. It competed directly with Vyapar and Khatabook, and indirectly with Zoho Inventory and OkCredit, in a market where switching cost was low and word of mouth won most new merchants. By FY25, Ishara had grown to 42,000 paying merchants and ₹19 crore in annual recurring revenue, profitable at the unit level but small next to the digital footprint of Reliance Retail's merchant tools or the scale Flipkart and Meesho brought to seller onboarding.

3. The situation

The immediate trigger was not a crisis but a fork. Ishara's core billing product had matured: retention was healthy, but new-merchant growth had slowed as the easiest Tier-1 city segments filled up, and the roadmap Ananya had shepherded for two years no longer answered where the next ₹10 crore of revenue would come from. Three candidate bets had surfaced over the summer, each championed by a different part of a genuinely global team. In Pune, engineering had already built a working prototype letting a merchant's catalogue be discovered by any buyer app on the Open Network for Digital Commerce, and argued this was the natural next step for a company that already held the inventory data ONDC needed. In Toronto, lead data scientist Priya Krishnan had spent four months building a risk-scoring model on eighteen months of anonymised transaction history and believed it could underwrite working-capital loans more accurately than a bank. In New Jersey, enterprise sales head Mike D'Souza was fielding calls from Ittihad Trading FZE, a Dubai-based wholesale distributor piloting Ishara's inventory module across four warehouses, keen to roll it out to retail partners across the UAE. Singapore-based customer success lead Rachel Tan added a fourth voice: support tickets showed shopkeepers cared far more about app stability during the Diwali billing rush than any new feature. Ananya's first draft had tried to honour all four views at once, describing each opportunity fairly and concluding, vaguely, that Ishara should "pursue a balanced portfolio." Meenal's rejection made clear that a document describing options was not a strategy.

4. The people

Karan Mehta, CEO and co-founder, Bengaluru. Karan wanted the board meeting to go smoothly ahead of Series C conversations he hoped to open in November, and privately favoured whichever option Ananya could defend most convincingly, more than any option in particular.

Meenal Oberoi, Vice President, Ishaan Growth Partners, Mumbai. Covering Ishara for the fund, Meenal had seen portfolio companies chase multiple bets at once and dilute all of them; she wanted one named commitment with numbers behind it, and evidence Ananya knew which capability Ishara already owned.

Priya Krishnan, Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Priya believed the lending model was Ishara's biggest latent asset, built from data no competitor had, but was candid that it had only been back-tested, never used to underwrite a real loan, and that RBI digital-lending clearance would take months.

Mike D'Souza, Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey. Mike had built the Ittihad Trading FZE relationship over a year of calls at odd hours and wanted the Gulf opportunity in the document, arguing that one large anchor client could justify expansion that diversified Ishara away from India-only regulatory risk.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows Ishara's FY25 position: a healthy but narrowing base, weighted toward the kirana segment that had always been the company's strength and its most defensible ground.

Exhibit 1. Ishara Retail Cloud, FY25 snapshot
MetricFY25FY24
Paying merchants42,00031,500
Annual recurring revenue₹19 crore₹13.4 crore
Segment mix — kirana / general stores60%64%
Segment mix — apparel & footwear25%22%
Segment mix — electronics & accessories15%14%
Net revenue retention108%104%

Source: Ishara internal finance and product analytics, compiled for the FY26 strategy document, September 2025.

Exhibit 2 lays the three candidate bets side by side on the terms Meenal had asked for: what each would cost to build, what it might return within eighteen months, and the single biggest risk attached to it.

Exhibit 2. Candidate strategic bets, eighteen-month view
OptionUpfront investmentIncremental ARR (18 mo.)PaybackPrincipal risk
A. ONDC seller integration₹1.8 crore₹3.5 crore14 monthsBuyer-app demand still thin; commissions may compress
B. Merchant lending (Ishara Credit)₹4.2 crore₹9 crore20 monthsRBI digital-lending compliance; underwriting unproven at scale
C. GCC expansion via Ittihad₹5.5 crore₹6 crore24 monthsNo local team; revenue concentrated in one anchor client

Source: Ishara FY26 planning model; figures are management estimates pending board review.

Exhibit 3 places Ishara against its nearest rivals on two dimensions Ananya used to argue for sequencing: how deep the product went for a single merchant, and how far its distribution already reached.

Exhibit 3. Ishara sits deep but narrow; ONDC would trade some depth for wide, low-cost reach; a lending product would add depth without changing reach at all.

6. The options

Option A — Lead with ONDC integration

Ishara would finish the Pune prototype and become a seller-side network participant, letting any merchant's catalogue surface to buyers on Paytm, PhonePe or Meesho's ONDC-linked apps without building its own demand side. The upside was distribution at near-zero acquisition cost and a direct line to the government's open-commerce push. The cost was modest and the technical risk low, since it extended a catalogue Ishara already maintained. The exposure was demand-side: nothing guaranteed buyers would show up in volume, and commissions could compress once bigger players joined.

Option B — Launch Ishara Credit, a merchant lending product

Ishara would use Priya's risk model to offer short-term working-capital loans, partnering with a licensed NBFC to stay within RBI's digital lending guidelines while supplying data and the borrower relationship. The upside was the largest of the three: lending economics could roughly double ARR within two years, built on data no rival held. The cost was real capability-building — compliance, collections, a risk function — under regulatory scrutiny, with an underwriting model that had never priced a real default.

Option C — Expand to the Gulf through Ittihad Trading FZE

Ishara would localise the product for UAE retailers, using the Ittihad relationship as an anchor account into the Gulf. The upside was revenue diversified outside India's regulatory perimeter, at higher price points than the kirana segment supported. The cost was a market entry with no local team, new compliance obligations, and growth resting on one client relationship that Mike, not Ananya, controlled.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, did Meenal Oberoi's rejection of the first draft say was missing — and which sections of a proper product strategy document (audience, differentiation, monetisation, risk) would have to change to answer her?
  2. What does Exhibit 1 imply about where Ishara's right to win actually sits, and how should that shape the "target audience" section of the rewritten document?
  3. Using Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 3 together, which option is most coherent with capabilities Ishara already has, and which would require it to become a different kind of company?
  4. If you were Ananya, how would you sequence these three options in the document's plan, so the near-term ask matches what a skeptical investor will fund while still showing where the bigger bet leads?

8. A note for the learner

A product strategy document earns a skeptical reader's signature only when it does what Rumelt's kernel asks of any strategy: a clear-eyed diagnosis, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and coherent actions that follow from that policy. Ananya's first draft failed not because any of the three options were bad, but because it presented them as parallel choices rather than a single diagnosis with a sequence attached. A well-reasoned rewrite states the audience precisely (the kirana and small-format retailer who has outgrown a notebook ledger, not "small businesses in India"), grounds differentiation in what Exhibit 1 already shows — a deep, sticky merchant relationship no aggregator has replicated — and only then turns to monetisation, acquisition and metrics for the chosen path, with the other two treated as named later phases rather than abandoned ideas.

On that logic, the defensible path is to lead the FY26 document with Option A. ONDC integration costs the least, uses capability Ishara already has, and converts existing distribution strength into low-risk, near-term revenue a skeptical investor can underwrite without asking Ishara to become a lender or an overseas operator overnight. Option B belongs in the same document as the named second horizon: the diagnosis should say plainly that Priya's model is Ishara's most valuable unbuilt asset, and that ONDC's first two quarters of transaction data will both fund and de-risk the NBFC partnership lending requires. Option C should appear as an opportunistic addendum tied to Ittihad specifically, not a geographic strategy, until Ishara has proven it can run one new line well. That sequencing is what lets one guiding policy govern the next eighteen months instead of three — the coherence Meenal was asking the document to show.

The Product Strategy Document

Two decisions, eleven weeks apart

On 14 September 2026, Meera Raghunathan, VP of Product at Dishantar Robotics in Coimbatore, was given a board date and a blank page. Dishantar built autonomous mobile robots that carried shelving to warehouse pickers, sold with fleet-orchestration software. FY26 revenue was ₹64 crore — ₹47 crore of hardware at roughly ₹11 lakh a robot, ₹17 crore of software — at a blended 31 percent gross margin, hardware running at 22 and software at 74. Against ₹58 crore of cash and ₹4.2 crore of monthly burn, the board would decide on 4 November where the next eighteen months went, from Meera's document.

The candidates were not variations of each other. Dishantar Cold hardened the robot for cold-chain warehouses — pharma and dairy — needing sealed drives, ₹2.4 crore of non-recurring engineering, and a tooling commitment placed five months before shipment, with ₹1.1 crore of working capital tied up per site. Dishantar Conductor abandoned new metal and licensed the orchestration software to material-handling OEMs to run other manufacturers' robots: almost no capital, 74 percent margins, and a message to Dishantar's sales force that the robots they sold were replaceable.

Eleven weeks later, Ira Bhattacharya, Head of Product at Sahayatra Money in Bengaluru, met the same problem in a different body. Sahayatra was a consumer app for gig workers offering income smoothing, savings and UPI autopay: 820,000 monthly actives, 190,000 paying ₹49 a month, ₹11.2 crore of annualised revenue growing 3 percent a month. Her 20 January 2027 board wanted a choice between an earned-wage-advance credit product with an NBFC partner under the Reserve Bank's digital-lending rules, and a much smaller insurance-distribution product sold as an IRDAI-registered corporate agent.

Both documents look, at a distance, like the familiar ten-section artefact: audience, problem, value, differentiation, competition, acquisition, monetisation, metrics, plan, risks. That reading belongs to someone who has studied the form rather than used it. Each decision turned on one number nobody in the company had observed, and the document's real work was to find it, prove it was the one, price what learning it would cost, and force the board to choose knowingly between buying that information and betting without it.

What the document is, and the problem it solved

A product strategy document is a written, dated, falsifiable argument that a named set of customers will pay a named amount for a named promise, against named alternatives, under a named constraint — set out so a reader who disagrees can point to the sentence at issue and the evidence that would settle it. Three words carry it. Dated, because a strategy is a claim about a world that moves and an undated document cannot be scored later. Falsifiable, because a strategy no observation could contradict is an ambition. Constraint, because without scarcity there is no choice, and without choice there is no strategy, only a list.

The form has three ancestral lines practitioners blend without noticing. The first is Richard Rumelt's kernel — diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action — set out in Good Strategy/Bad Strategy (2011) against plans that named aspirations and financial targets while omitting any account of the obstacle in the way. The second is A.G. Lafley and Roger Martin's Playing to Win cascade — aspiration, where to play, how to win, capabilities, management systems — which came out of portfolio work at Procter & Gamble and treats strategy as interlocking choices rather than a response to an obstacle. The third is procedural: Amazon's six-page memo and its PR/FAQ variant, which replaced the deck with prose — sentences can be interrogated, bullets cannot — inside a ritual of silent reading and line-by-line challenge.

Three further positions matter because teams hold them unnamed. The hypothesis school, from Steve Blank's customer development, treats the document as a ranked register of assumptions, each with a next test and a price. The positional school — Wardley's mapping, more loosely Christensen's disruption theory — holds that its central object is the landscape's direction of travel, not the customer's present complaint. The anti-document position, held by strong operators rather than cynics, says strategy is revealed by resource allocation, so the honest artefact is the staffing plan.

The propositions separate them. Rumelt would sign "a document with no named obstacle is not a strategy" and refuse "it should contain a three-year financial model." Lafley and Martin would sign "you cannot choose how to win before choosing where to play" and refuse to leave capabilities and management systems to a later document — the omission that makes most product strategy documents weaker than they look. The memo school signs "if you cannot write it in sentences you have not thought it through" and refuses continuous revision; the hypothesis school refuses exactly that, signing "any strategy older than its evidence is a liability." The positional school will not sign "start from the customer's stated problem"; the anti-document school signs "the real strategy is the resource allocation."

Mechanics: finding the load-bearing assumption and pricing it

Competent practitioners write the ten sections. Experts do something underneath them, in six steps, of which the middle three are usually implicit and are where the analysis lives. Step one states the decision the document exists to make, with its date and its resource: "which of two uses of ₹18 crore and eighteen months of engineering does Dishantar commit to on 4 November 2026?"

Step two names the binding constraint — the resource that runs out first — because it determines which section is load-bearing and which ceremony. Dishantar's was not engineers but working capital: ten Cold sites tie up ₹11 crore of float against ₹58 crore of cash. Sahayatra's was regulatory standing: lending required an NBFC partner and, under the Reserve Bank's default-loss-guarantee cap, a fintech may carry first loss on no more than 5 percent of the portfolio, which converts a product decision into a balance-sheet decision.

Step three writes the model connecting strategy to money in the fewest lines that still contain the disagreement; Ira's occupied four rows. A 12 percent monthly take-up of an average ₹3,200 advance among 820,000 actives gives 98,400 advances and ₹31.5 crore disbursed a month; a 2.5 percent fee per 21-day cycle yields ₹80 an advance, ₹78.7 lakh a month, ₹9.4 crore a year — nearly doubling Sahayatra's revenue. Against that sits credit loss: at 1.0 percent of disbursal the product contributes ₹47 lakh a month, at 2.1 percent ₹12.6 lakh, at 2.5 percent it loses money. Sahayatra had never lent a rupee, and the loss rate it borrowed came from lenders whose borrowers differed, on Ira's own research, precisely in income volatility.

Step four is the ranking in Figure 2, where the two levels of practitioner part. Assumptions are ordered not by felt importance but by the rupee swing between a plausible low and high, times the team's uncertainty about where in that range the truth lies. A wide swing the team is confident about is not a risk; a narrow unknown one is not worth studying. Only the assumption that is both wide and unknown is load-bearing, and there is usually exactly one.

Step five prices the resolution of that assumption, using a formal treatment that exists and is almost never used: the expected value of information. Cold rested on whether pharma and dairy logistics operators would pay a 25 percent premium for hardened units; Meera's team put the chance at 55 percent. If the premium holds, Cold is worth about ₹14 crore of three-year net present value; if not, Dishantar has spent ₹2.4 crore plus tooling and carried inventory into a segment that will not pay — ₹3.1 crore of loss. Committing blind has an expected value of (0.55 × 14) + (0.45 × −3.1) = ₹6.3 crore, positive, which is why blind commitment is tempting.

Buying evidence first changes the shape. A ₹65 lakh, ten-week paid pilot with two pharma logistics operators, priced at the premium the case assumes, resolves it before tooling is committed: (0.55 × 14) + (0.45 × 0) − 0.65 = ₹7.05 crore. The pilot is worth ₹75 lakh — 0.45 × ₹3.1 crore of avoided loss, less its cost. Two effects follow. It is worth buying only if it can return a negative signal: discount the units to place them and the test measures willingness to accept a discount. And information is worth less as conviction rises — at a 75 percent prior the pilot is worth ₹12.5 lakh, at 85 percent it is negative. Research is most valuable when a team is least sure, which is when teams most want to stop researching and build.

Step six writes the ten sections, which now take a day, because each records a conclusion the earlier steps reached. The plan section carries the point of no return — the tooling order on 9 March 2027, after which Cold cannot be unwound for less than ₹1.8 crore — and naming that cost, with the date it jumps, is the most useful line a hardware strategy document contains.

When the document earns its cost, and when it misleads

Four testable conditions. The decision is materially irreversible within the horizon: Dishantar passes on the tooling date; Sahayatra's insurance option fails, since a distribution partnership unwinds in a quarter, while its credit option passes, an NBFC arrangement and a loss guarantee being hard to reverse quietly. Real contention for a constrained resource: both pass, for different resources, which is why two documents on one template read so differently. Informed colleagues disagree: Dishantar's sales head wanted Cold, its CTO Conductor; absent that, the document degenerates into ratification. The outcome depends on testable assumptions: this is where the tool fails most often and least visibly.

It misleads in three situations. In a novel category, where customers cannot describe the product they would buy, the demand for a named audience and a named alternative pushes teams to invent a buyer and publish fiction with decimal places. In a fast race, four weeks of writing is the largest cost in the decision, and a one-page memo written in a day beats a rigorous document delivered late. And where documents are read as political instruments, rigour loses: the careful author supplies ammunition while the vague one keeps optionality.

Hard edges

Multi-product companies face a seam no single document closes. Each team writes a locally optimal strategy and the sum is incoherent, because the genuinely scarce resources — brand permission, sales attention, a shared platform roadmap — are allocated above the level at which documents are written. Dishantar meets this the day Conductor ships: Conductor's strategy is to be robot-agnostic, the hardware business's is to be the robot. Mature companies say a portfolio review resolves it; what happens is that the senior general manager wins and the losing document is rewritten.

Two-sided businesses need two diagnoses and a statement of which side is constrained, since a policy aimed at the abundant side does nothing. Regulated products invert the authorship of the exclusion list — part of Sahayatra's is written by the Reserve Bank — and the document must separate what is law from what is risk appetite, which teams conflate expensively. Hardware-plus-software adds the capital shape: reversal date, float, and the permanent fact that a 22 percent-margin business and a 74 percent-margin business inside one company disagree about what winning means — a real disagreement, not a failure of alignment.

AI-native products break the differentiation section. "Our extraction accuracy is 94 percent against a general model's 81" is a claim about a gap a foundation-model release can close in a week, so the expert response is to state which capability trend the strategy is long and which short — long on inference getting cheaper, short on models acquiring a customer's private workflow data — because an advantage that is only a capability gap borrows its right to win from a vendor's roadmap. At the organisational seam, the awkward case is a team writing a strategy while controlling neither pricing nor channel; the honest document names that dependency in the diagnosis rather than assuming away sections it cannot execute.

Eight things experts see that competent practitioners do not

1. The unit of analysis is the decision, not the product. The tell is that an expert asks "what does this decide?" before reading a page, unsatisfied by "it sets our direction for FY28." A document without a decision has no way to be wrong, and so no way to be useful. The obvious reading — that comprehensiveness is the virtue — produces the forty-page artefact that survives review because nothing in it is sharp enough to attack.

2. Rank assumptions by swing times uncertainty, and reconcile sizing bottom-up. Experts read the sensitivity table before the narrative, and build one in the margin when there is none. Everyone agrees pricing matters, so it gets three pages; but if the team is confident within ten percent those pages resolve nothing, while the paragraph about an unmeasured number deserves the most space. The same instinct governs sizing: ignore the top-down market number and go to the bottom-up reconciliation — how many accounts, closed by how many salespeople, at what win rate. A large addressable market is evidence for nothing, being consistent with every option on the table.

3. The exclusion list must cost something. Experts scan "what we will not do" for one item with a named advocate who will be unhappy. If everything on it is something nobody wanted, the list is decoration. A long list looks like discipline, but length is uncorrelated with cost: a one-item list that kills a VP's pet initiative is worth more than a page of things the company was never going to build.

4. Competition is about why a rival will not respond. The expert's question is what it would cost the strongest competitor to match this within twelve months, and why they have not; a feature table answers neither. Sometimes the answer is structural — channel conflict, a margin they would cannibalise, an installed base they cannot migrate — and that is the right to win. When the honest answer is "nothing stops them, they simply have not," the strategy should be about speed.

5. Kill criteria need a date and an owner. "We will reconsider if attach rate is below 20 percent" is unenforceable; "if fewer than 6 of the first 14 pilot sites renew by 31 August, Meera stops the programme and reports in September" is a commitment. Experts also watch the second-order effect: a published threshold becomes a target teams manage toward, so the mature version names threshold and measurement together, and puts measurement in someone else's hands.

6. The audience is a reader nine months from now. The tell is a diagnosis that reads like a dated description of the world — shares, prices, who had raised what — rather than timeless prose. Documents written for the review meeting optimise for surviving one hour; documents written to be re-read are scoreable, and teams that score their old strategies improve in a way no template discipline achieves.

7. Expect the first draft to name the wrong constraint. Almost every draft names engineering capacity, the constraint product managers feel personally. The diagnostic is to ask what changes if the team gets twice the engineers; if the answer is "not much," engineering was never the constraint. Twice the engineers would not have produced a rupee of Dishantar's working capital, and for many enterprise products the real limit is the number of qualified sales conversations in a quarter.

8. "A or B" is usually "A then B" — and narratability distorts both. Experts convert selection into sequencing: what does doing A first do to the cost of B later? Sometimes the order is nearly free; sometimes A destroys B, as Conductor first would, since OEM partners will not fund a hardware rival's expansion. Separately, a written strategy becomes a recruiting pitch and a fundraising story, so options that tell well acquire advocates better arithmetic does not: "we are becoming the operating system for Indian warehouses" recruits engineers; "harden our robot and hold gross margin" does not. The failure is not being seduced but being seduced unknowingly.

What actually changes across product types and stages

Less than most templates imply: the ten sections are the same everywhere, and what changes is which is load-bearing and which ceremony. In consumer products it is acquisition and retention economics, because the value proposition is testable in weeks and the channel is not. In B2B it is the audience section, because buyer, user and approver differ, and a document naming only the user produces a product that demos well and does not close. In marketplaces the diagnosis doubles; in hardware the plan becomes a capital document; in AI products differentiation is the fragile section.

Exhibit 1 — Which section is load-bearing, and the question that tests it
Product typeLoad-bearing sectionTest question

B2B / enterpriseAudience (buyer, user, approver)Who signs, and what are they punished for?

Hardware + softwarePlan, as a capital shapeWhat is the reversal cost, and when does it jump?

RegulatedRisks, split law vs appetiteWhich constraints are statutory?

Stage changes evidentiary weight rather than structure. A seed-stage document rests defensibly on fifteen customer conversations and a founder's judgement, earning its keep by stating what would cheaply falsify the thesis. A growth-stage company like Dishantar owes quantified sizing, a comparison against every other claim on the same capital, and a named point of no return. A large incumbent owes one thing more: why this product, inside this company, beats a startup at it — without which the document is a good argument for someone else's business.

Three documents and what they produced

Gantavya Systems, Hyderabad, 2024. Gantavya sold compliance software to mid-market NBFCs and had two options: fraud analytics for existing customers, or a regulatory-reporting module for banks — a larger market with a sales cycle three times longer. Its product lead converted the choice into a sequence and priced the interaction: fraud analytics first would produce twenty reference deployments whose data trained the reporting module and whose logos opened bank conversations, cutting later bank acquisition cost from ₹31 lakh to ₹19 lakh, while reporting first had no such effect in reverse. Eighteen months on it came in at ₹22 lakh, close enough that sequencing-as-value was judged sound.

Anuyatra Commerce, Delhi, 2023 — the failure. Anuyatra's marketplace document for small-batch regional food brands was by every formal standard excellent: crisp diagnosis, real exclusion list, sensitivity table, kill metric. It committed ₹9 crore to demand-side growth on the diagnosis that the constraint was buyer awareness, supported by a survey in which 71 percent of lapsed buyers said they "did not think of it." The constraint was in fact supply reliability: sellers stocked out on 23 percent of orders, and buyers who said they forgot had been burned by a cancellation a median of 1.4 orders before lapsing — a fact in Anuyatra's own order data, absent from its survey. Spending drove monthly orders from 41,000 to 68,000; cancellations rose in step, repeat rate fell from 34 to 26 percent, and the kill metric, written on gross orders, rose throughout. Recovery took four quarters: rewrite the diagnosis from order data, cap demand spend at ₹40 lakh a month, buy buffer inventory for the top 300 SKUs at ₹2.7 crore, restore repeat rate to 37 percent, then restart growth.

Pathik Intelligence, Bengaluru, 2025. Pathik rested its differentiation on a 12-point accuracy advantage over general models on Indian regional-language insurance claim forms; nine months later a model release closed the gap to 3 points. Unusually, the document had named this as the top risk and specified the response: below a 5-point gap, stop competing on extraction and reposition around claims adjudication, where the advantage was customer-specific data and an insurer integration taking eleven months to replicate. Because trigger and response were written in advance the pivot took seven weeks rather than two quarters, and revenue dipped 9 percent for one quarter. The document did not prevent the shock; it converted a crisis into an execution.

Failure modes and their early warnings

Exhibit 2 — Failure modes, the signal that precedes them, and what late detection costs

Two deserve a further word. The kill-metric failure is invisible while it happens — Anuyatra's number rose throughout the period in which the strategy destroyed value — so the correction is procedural: write the story of how this strategy fails before choosing the metric, then ask which number moves first. The ratification failure is dangerous because it is socially rewarded, and its cost is not one bad decision but the loss of the only mechanism a company had for changing its mind in public.

Where experts genuinely disagree

Should the document carry a financial model at all? The case against, which Rumelt made and many senior operators hold privately, is that quantification launders assumption into rigour: a model with fourteen linked tabs is harder to challenge than a sentence, and its precision suppresses the argument the document exists to provoke, on the evidence of a long record of confidently modelled entries that failed on a parameter nobody interrogated. The case for is that an unquantified strategy cannot be falsified, and that Ira's four-row model did its job by making one unmeasured number visible. A model earns its place when it is small enough to read in full and its inputs labelled observed or assumed; the sceptics would be wrong if teams challenged models as hard as prose.

Six pages or one? The memo school holds that length is the mechanism: six pages of prose force the connective reasoning bullets let you skip, and the silent-reading ritual is what makes a room engage. The one-page school answers that the marginal five pages buy ceremony, that decision quality is bounded by the diagnosis rather than the word count, and that four weeks of writing costs real time in a moving market. The evidence against is that the practice rarely transplants, suggesting the ritual and the culture, not the page count, did the work.

Commitment or living document? If a strategy can be revised at any review, its force as a coordinating device — the thing that lets forty people make consistent small decisions without asking — decays toward zero; if it cannot be revised, the company is committed to a stale diagnosis. The practical middle — a fixed document with a scheduled review and named trigger conditions — is what most mature companies claim; many in fact write a new document each quarter and never score the old one, buying the churn with none of the learning.

Should the document pre-commit to a stopping rule? Advocates hold that sunk-cost persistence is the dominant failure of product investment and that only a dated, externally measured threshold resists it. Opponents, who are not careless, answer that pre-committed kill metrics are gamed or ignored — Goodhart applies to strategy too — and that the real stopping mechanism is a culture in which changing your mind is not career-ending. The dispute is whether the binding force lives in the artefact or in the institution.

What mastery looks like

It is visible within an hour. They ask what the document decides before what it says; they read the sensitivity table first, building one in the margin when there is none, and can state without notes which single number would flip the recommendation, treating an inability to name it as the finding. They price research instead of debating whether to do it, and write the reversal date down. They name the binding constraint even when it embarrasses a colleague, and in a regulated business separate what the law forbids from what the company is merely nervous about. And they know when not to write the document at all — when the decision is small, reversible, or so contested that rigour becomes a weapon — which is the judgement studying the form never supplies.

What Meera and Ira decided

Meera recommended neither Cold nor Conductor on 4 November, but the ₹65 lakh pilot, with the tooling decision deferred to 9 March 2027 and the ₹1.8 crore reversal cost written into the board resolution. She placed Conductor in the same document as a sequenced option rather than a rival — noting, in the paragraph her CTO disliked, that shipping it first would make Cold harder to sell to OEM partners. The board approved in forty minutes, largely because the ₹75 lakh figure made the pilot a purchase rather than a delay.

Ira recommended the insurance product on 20 January, and the recommendation was not the interesting part. Insurance, at a 9 percent attach on 820,000 actives and ₹22 a policy, was worth about ₹1.95 crore a year — a fifth of the credit case — and she said so on page one. Her argument was that the credit decision rested on a loss rate Sahayatra had never observed, and that only lending small amounts of real money would produce it. So the document proposed insurance as the committed product and a ₹4 crore capped-book pilot with Prasthan Finance as the instrument for buying the missing number, with a threshold set in advance: a cycle loss rate above 1.8 percent on ₹25 crore of cumulative disbursal ends the programme. She was explicit that the pilot, not the insurance product, was the strategy.

Three questions worth sitting with. Meera's pilot is worth ₹75 lakh at a 55 percent prior and nothing at 85 — so who should be allowed to set the prior, given that the person most confident about Cold proposed it? Anuyatra's document met every formal criterion here and still destroyed ₹9 crore: what would a reviewer have had to ask to catch it? And if Ira's real strategy is a ₹4 crore experiment, is a document that commits to a small certain thing in order to fund a large uncertain one a strategy, or an evasion of one?

Going deeper

Rumelt's kernel — why a diagnosis naming no obstacle can support no policy. What strategy is and isn't — the boundary work that stops goals and plans being mistaken for strategy. Playing to Win: where to play, how to win — the choice-led alternative, and the source of the capabilities questions product documents omit. Value proposition statement — the central claim, imported from tested work rather than drafted under deadline. Building personas from research — the audience section, and the behavioural evidence that keeps a diagnosis off surveys. Risks and assumptions in strategy — the discipline behind Figure 2.

Competitive analysis and Right to win — why a rival will not respond within twelve months. Product-market fit — the standard the claims are judged against. Focus and sequencing — the machinery behind nuance eight. Strategy narrative and memo — the argument at the length your organisation engages with. Strategy reviews and refresh cadence — commitment or ritual. Product portfolio strategy — where Dishantar's Cold-versus-Conductor incoherence is resolved. B2B vs B2C strategy and What a GTM strategy is — acquisition and monetisation opened up. Wardley mapping and Disruption theory — positional tools that start somewhere other than the customer's stated problem.

Focus and Sequencing: The Order of Expansion Is the Strategy

Which segment do we win first, and in what order do we expand?

1. Two rooms, eleven days apart

On 3 February 2026, in a converted mill office in Surat, Ritwik Barua watched a slide he did not believe. Barua ran product at Wajood Cold Chain Systems, which made a battery-powered temperature and door-event logger and the compliance software reading it. The slide ranked three candidate markets by gross profit per field-engineer-day and put fresh-produce packhouses first. His objection was not that the arithmetic was wrong, but that it answered a question nobody was asking.

Wajood had fourteen field engineers, one production firmware branch and ₹9.4 crore of cash. Its chief executive, Hemal Doshi, wanted an expansion order by the March board — the order, its reason, and what Wajood would refuse to build while it held. Three markets were live: deep freezers in frozen-dessert distribution, cold rooms in vaccine handling, pre-cooling at export packhouses. Only one could be first.

Eleven days later and 1,100 kilometres south, Lavanya Iyengar faced a structurally identical question with none of the same variables. Iyengar had co-founded Ekatra Repair Exchange, a Bengaluru marketplace matching households with verified air-conditioning technicians. It had 640 of them, and a board paper proposing Hyderabad. Her problem was that the business had a shape: air-conditioning repair peaks savagely from March to June and collapses for eight months, and each year some forty per cent of her technicians drifted away. Hyderabad would duplicate a working city, and the hole in it.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define the terms, because they are routinely conflated. Focus is a refusal: the decision not to commit resources to markets you could plausibly serve, so that what you do commit is decisive somewhere. Sequencing orders what you have not refused permanently — the claim that entering segment two second is cheaper, faster or more lucrative than entering it first. Focus without sequencing wins a niche and stays in it; sequencing without focus is a roadmap with everything on it.

Three traditions converge here. The oldest is military: concentration of force, formalised in Lanchester's square law, where effectiveness scales with the square of numbers. The second is Rumelt's kernel of diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent action, whose first honest test is whether the policy excludes more than it includes; his proximate objective is a sequencing concept in focus's clothing. The third is Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm (1991), source of the beachhead and the bowling alley, in which each segment won topples the next as references and whole-product components spill sideways. They agree on concentration and little else.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Rumelt, kernel and proximate objectiveA policy that excludes nothing is not a policy.That the order be fixed at launch; a sequence immune to evidence is a plan.
Moore, beachhead and bowling alleyA beachhead is chosen for what spills into the next.That you enter the best economics now.
Christensen, disruptionEnter where incumbents are unwilling to follow.That the first segment be the most attractive; attractiveness invites retaliation.
Hamel and Prahalad, strategic intentExpansion is a ladder of challenges outrunning present resources.That the beachhead fit current capability; they attacked "fit".
Kim and Mauborgne, blue oceanSegment boundaries are inherited assumptions."Win one before the next" as a general law.

Table 1. Six positions, each one its author would defend.

The usable synthesis is narrower than any of them: a sequence is only a strategy if you can name, as a noun, the asset that winning segment one manufactures, and show that segment two requires it. Absent it, an expansion order is a scheduling preference — and identifying it is hard, because candidate assets rank segments differently.

3. Mechanics: three metrics, three different winners

Nandita Sengupta, Wajood's analyst in Kolkata, built the sizing. Devices sold at ₹7,200 against a landed bill of materials of ₹3,400, with software priced by segment. Installation effort diverged sharply: a logger in a deep freezer took half an engineer-day; a four-sensor cold room with a validation record, two and a half; a nine-sensor packhouse, four. Fourteen engineers at 220 productive days gave 3,080 engineer-days a year: the denominator that matters.
