Read the fifth column and packhouses lead — ₹13,950 against ₹11,200, a premium of twenty-five per cent on the same people. Barua attacked the denominator. No packhouse admits an engineer to its pre-cooling chamber during the mango or grape season, so commissioning happens between October and February. That caps packhouse work at 1,400 engineer-days however many engineers Wajood hires, and first-year packhouse gross profit at 350 sites and ₹1.95 crore — against ₹3.45 crore for the same team on freezers. The winning metric had assumed a day is a day.

The second-order effect decided the case. Wajood's constraint was not people or cash but proof: pharmaceutical qualification required a field-failure rate under 1.5 per cent a year across a live installed base. Wajood's was 4.2 per cent at a thousand cumulative device-years, falling along a learning curve as field-hours surfaced firmware, seal and battery faults bench testing missed. Sengupta fitted f = 4.2 × (N/1,000)−0.32, putting the gate at 25,000 device-years — and how fast N accrues depends on the first segment.

Figure 1. The first segment moves the date the second becomes enterable by forty months.

Forty months is not a nuance; at Wajood's burn it is the difference between two fundings, and it is invisible in a table measuring what each segment pays rather than what each manufactures. The expert step, routinely skipped, is to write the asset down as a noun and check which segments produce it and which merely consume it. Wajood's was field-hours in hostile conditions: freezers sit in unairconditioned godowns at forty-two degrees, opened two hundred times a day, and a logger surviving that passes a pharmaceutical cold room. Evidence flows downhill, from the harshest environment to the most regulated.

A third step is almost never performed: pricing the reverse direction. Wajood's NABL-traceable calibration facility would cost ₹1.1 crore and eleven months, conventionally charged to the pharmaceutical entry. But national traceability also satisfies the audits European importers run on APEDA-registered packhouses, lifting pricing from ₹2,400 to ₹3,600 per sensor-year — ₹2.6 crore of recurring revenue across 2,400 sites that exists only if pharma precedes packhouses, making that segment worth forty-four per cent more entered third than first.

Figure 2. If you cannot write a noun on the arrow, there is none.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

One: something durable accumulates. If winning segment one leaves no stock — no data, certification, density or installed base — segments are independent draws, and you should enter the most profitable and stay. Wajood passes: device-years and a calibration facility are stocks. Ekatra passes less comfortably, because its stock is a trained technician, and its reservoir leaks.

Two: the next segment requires that stock. Not finds it useful — requires it. A pharmaceutical buyer will not sign without the failure-rate evidence; that is a gate, not a discount. The commonest error is treating a resemblance between markets as an edge on the graph.

Three: the stock cannot be bought. If ₹1.1 crore buys the calibration lab, no sequencing argument protects it. Wajood's defensible asset was the 25,000 device-years, which money cannot compress because it is denominated in calendar time. Most plans fail this test, which is why certifications make weaker rationales than field-hours and behavioural data.

Four: waiting costs less than the option forfeited. If a rival can take segment two irreversibly during your beachhead year, the sequence is a luxury. Iyengar judged a year's delay changed her Hyderabad odds little, since the constraint there was technician supply, which nobody had locked up.

The idea actively misleads where no stock accumulates and every pocket is contestable at once — some consumer categories, and any market where distribution is winner-take-most.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Two-sided markets. The unit of sequencing is a liquidity pocket, not a vertical, and references never travel. At Wisaal Freight Exchange in Nagpur the threshold was eleven matched trucks a day on one origin–destination lane, below which fill times exceeded ninety minutes and shippers left. Nagpur–Hyderabad cleared it in week nine; Nagpur–Kochi sat at three a day for eleven months and never did. The pricing model and playbook transferred; demand did not. Bowling-alley language imported into a marketplace promises spillover local liquidity cannot deliver.

Regulated products. At Eeman Insurance Cloud in Mumbai the sequence was partly not the company's to choose: IRDAI-facing approvals arrive on the regulator's clock, and approval for one line of business does not carry to another. Procurement paperwork does. Eeman's first insurer took fourteen months to production, including a nineteen-week security review producing ninety-four artefacts; for the second, seventy-one were reusable and the cycle fell to six months. The transferable asset in regulated B2B is an evidence pack, not a reference.

Hardware plus software. Resequencing carries a switching cost denominated in components: Wajood's gateway board had a sixteen-week lead time and a minimum order of 5,000 units, so reordering after a build commitment meant writing off inventory rather than re-planning a sprint. Hardware firms rightly treat the sequence as firmer than software firms do — and are more often trapped by one that has stopped making sense.

AI-native products. The compounding asset is usually labelled data, and the assumption that it transfers is empirically weak. Wasl Vision Systems assumed fine-tuning from its knitwear model would cut labelling for automotive inspection by seventy per cent; measured, the saving was twenty-two. What transferred completely was the annotation pipeline, edge-inference profile and drift monitoring, cutting deployment per line from nine weeks to eleven days.

What mature companies actually do. Large firms announce focus and practise portfolio. The stated sequence lives in the deck; the operative one lives in the headcount and compensation plans, and where they disagree compensation wins. If a representative earns the same accelerator on a segment-three deal as a segment-one deal, there is no sequence whatever the deck says.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The asset is a noun, named before the ranking is run

Competent practitioners rank segments, then rationalise the winner; experts name the asset the sequence runs on, pick the metric measuring its production, then rank. The tell is a team fluent on every segment's ARPU that goes quiet when asked what winning it makes. Attractiveness is a property of a segment alone; a sequence is a claim about dependencies.

Sequencing is about the shape of a constraint, not the size of a prize

Seasonality, certification clocks and cash cycles each give a segment a shape. Packhouses cannot absorb more than 1,400 engineer-days a year: that is shape, not size, and hiring does not change it. The tell is a plan with no calendar in it, segments ordered but never set against the months in which work can physically occur.

Adjacency is directional; a plan that reads the same backwards is not one

Freezers unlock pharma; pharma does not unlock freezers. Pharma unlocks packhouses through calibration traceability; packhouses unlock nothing. Experts justify each arrow in a sentence, treating any that survives reversal as proof it was never a dependency. The obvious reading — related markets help each other — mistakes similarity for cause.

The next segment's price is set by the previous segment's proof

Most models hold ARPU constant across the order, assuming what segment one taught has no commercial value in segment two. Wajood's packhouse pricing rose forty-four per cent because pharma preceded it. The tell is an ARPU column identical in every scenario; correcting it often changes the order.

A beachhead can be profitable and still a poor teacher

Packhouses had the best gross profit per engineer-day and the worst evidence yield; Wasl's automotive lines paid four times knitwear and produced a rare-class defect every two and a half hours against knitwear's five. High margin with a low event rate is the classic bad beachhead wherever the constraint is learning. The tell is a segment whose attraction is stated entirely in rupees.

Refusal must be dated and conditioned, never permanent

"Not now" without a named trigger is heard internally as "not ever", and a sales team routes around it within a quarter by selling the excluded segment as an exception. Wajood's memo said no packhouse firmware before month 30, with the failure rate as trigger, not a date. The tell is an exclusion nobody can state the expiry condition for.

The cost of a wrong order is paid off the P&L

Technician attrition, firmware regressions, a dossier written twice, engineers who learned the wrong domain first — none appear as a bad quarter. They appear as a company eighteen months behind where its revenue suggests, with no line item to point at. The tell is a board arguing about growth when the problem is capability.

A channel is not a segment

Selling the same product to the same buyer by a different route is channel expansion, and sequencing channels by growth rate is the fastest way to destroy a beachhead, because channels cannibalise each other as segments do not. The tell is a segment list whose entries are places, not people.

7. Variation by product type and stage

In consumer products the unit is a cohort or city and the asset is habit density within a social graph or delivery radius. In B2B software it is a vertical, and the asset is reference credibility plus a domain-specific whole product. In enterprise software it is often one named account whose security review and procurement artefacts become the stock, as at Eeman — which is why enterprise plans naming industries rather than artefacts underdeliver. In marketplaces it is a liquidity pocket whose density does not travel; in hardware, component lead times bind; in AI products, the event rate and label cost of data.

Where the difference is not real is worth saying plainly. The four conditions above hold identically across all of them: only the identity of the asset varies, and practitioners who believe their category exempt usually cannot name theirs.

Stage changes the stakes and the reversibility, not the logic. At Wajood's stage a wrong order is near-existential: the runway to correct it may not exist. For a large company it costs growth rather than survival, but resequencing is politically harder, since territories, quotas and champions have been built around the current order, and unwinding them is a harder negotiation than admitting the error.

8. Three worked examples

Wasl Vision Systems: sequencing on event rate. Aravind Sekar faced knitwear, automotive-component and pharmaceutical-packaging inspection at ₹1.8 lakh, ₹7.5 lakh and ₹22 lakh of annual revenue per line. Revenue said pharma. Sekar went to knitwear, because the binding constraint was 4,000 labelled instances of the rarest defect class, and Tiruppur offered six lines within twenty-five kilometres running twenty hours a day at a 3.1 per cent defect rate; the rarest class reached 4,000 in seven days. In automotive, at 0.28 per cent and two lines obtainable in year one, the threshold would have taken ten months.

Ekatra Repair Exchange: protecting an asset you already own. Technicians earned ₹470 a completed job: at 5.8 jobs a day in the March–June peak, ₹2,726; at 2.1 through the eight-month trough, ₹987 — against a local benchmark near ₹1,200 for salaried service work. Below that line monthly attrition ran at 6 per cent, so 640 technicians in June became about 390 by March, when peak demand of 3,710 jobs a day required at least 530.

Figure 3. The trough is a March supply problem, solved eight months before March.

Only one option addressed that. Hyderabad meant ₹1.56 crore of demand-side spend before the first pincode cluster reached density, and reproduced the seasonal hole in a second city. Plumbing was counter-seasonal but needed a separate supply pool and did nothing for March readiness. Society maintenance contracts reused both sides at once: 180 societies at 414 units each generated 74,520 preventive visits Ekatra could schedule inside the trough. Concentrated on 150 high-rated technicians rather than spread across 640, it gave each 2.8 block-days a week at ₹1,980, lifting blended trough earnings to ₹1,444 and cutting their attrition from 6 per cent monthly to 2.4 — rescuing 32 technicians into March, worth ₹38 lakh of peak work against ₹3.06 crore of contract contribution.

Wafaa Nutrition Brands: the failure. Kartikeya Rathore's Jaipur direct-to-consumer nutrition brand sequenced channels and called it segment strategy. On its own website, an average order of ₹2,150 at 45 per cent gross margin left ₹841 after fulfilment against a ₹1,480 acquisition cost, viable only at 1.76 orders per customer. Actual repeat was 1.4, so every customer lost ₹303. Rather than fix repeat, Wafaa entered quick commerce in month fourteen because it was growing fastest. A 32 per cent platform margin and ₹310 a unit of visibility spend left minus ₹64 a unit — ₹13.4 lakh a month on 21,000 units — while the same customers migrated to ten-minute delivery, dropping repeat to 1.1 and deepening the loss to ₹555 a customer. Each channel made the other worse.

The recovery took eighteen months and was almost entirely subtraction. Rathore cut from thirty-four SKUs to six, exited quick commerce in seven of nine cities, and rebuilt around one subscription: a kilogram of whey at ₹1,899, 68 per cent month-three retention, 4.6 orders a customer, ₹3,422 of lifetime contribution against the same ₹1,480 acquisition cost. Revenue fell from ₹41 crore to ₹23 crore; monthly burn from ₹1.9 crore to ₹28 lakh. His summary is exact: he had sequenced, on schedule, a list of places to sell rather than assets to build.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Portfolio creep dressed as focus. Sign: an exclusion list exists but the backlog holds work for every excluded segment. Diagnostic: pull two quarters of engineering hours by segment tag; if the spread tracks headcount, there is no focus. Late cost: mediocrity in three markets, defensibility in none.

The beachhead is the founder's address book. Sign: the rationale rests on a friendly pilot. Diagnostic: why would a funded competitor entering cold lose here? If the answer is a relationship, that is a customer. Late cost: learning in year three that the advantage never transferred.

Expansion on the calendar, not the gate. Sign: segment two opens in the quarter the plan named. Diagnostic: does the decision cite any number generated after segment one launched? Late cost: a year of failed qualifications.

The stock is assumed, not measured. Sign: the transfer benefit is a percentage nobody tested — Wasl assumed 70 and measured 22. Diagnostic: what experiment would falsify it, and has it run? Late cost: the rationale collapses after the roadmap rests on it.

The comfortable beachhead. Sign: segment one is won, growth has flattened, the sequence has stopped. Diagnostic: is there a dated commitment to segment two, owned by someone senior? Late cost: a permanent niche that calls itself a platform.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Deep commitment versus cheap parallel probes. The beachhead school holds that concentration is the only route to decisive advantage anywhere, and that parallel probes are dilution with a research budget attached. The options school replies that under genuine uncertainty the information value of three cheap probes exceeds the execution value of one deep commitment, citing how often category winners found their segment in a side experiment. The disagreement resolves on one quantity: minimum credible entry cost. Where a probe is cheap and informative, parallelism wins; where entry is expensive — hardware, regulated software, anything requiring field evidence — probes are too shallow to inform anything.

Learn-first versus margin-first ordering. Wajood's choice to start with the cheapest segment is contested by a serious tradition holding that firms are imprinted by their first customers: a company that learns to sell at ₹5,600 a site acquires cost structures, hiring profiles and instincts that make ₹33,200 sites hard to win later. That evidence is organisational rather than financial, and it is real. Learn-first is wrong if firms that start cheap fail to move up; margin-first is wrong if the gate is time-denominated, since no margin buys calendar time.

Whether the sequence should be published. One camp holds that a written, dated refusal is the only form of focus that survives contact with a sales organisation. The other holds that publishing the order tells competitors where to pre-empt and segment-two prospects to wait, and that the option value of silence exceeds the discipline value of publication. Both are right about their own risk; which failure a firm is prone to is a fact about the company, not about strategy.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this produces an ordered list with a rationale attached. Someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. They name the asset before opening the spreadsheet. They ask what a segment manufactures, not only what it pays, and will accept a worse first-year number to buy an earlier second-year gate. They write refusals with expiry conditions rather than dates, so the organisation knows what evidence reopens the question. And they check the commission plan against the strategy document, knowing which the company is executing.

12. What Barua and Iyengar decided

Barua took to the March board a sequence, an unlock for each arrow, and a refusal. Freezers first, consuming all 3,080 engineer-days of year one for ₹3.45 crore of gross profit and 6,160 devices under continuous hostile duty. The calibration programme funded from month three out of that profit. Pharmaceutical entry gated not on a date but on the failure rate crossing 1.5 per cent, forecast at month 34. Packhouses third, as an October-to-February overlay in year three at post-calibration pricing. The refusal memo named what Wajood would not build before month 30: mesh-gateway firmware, multi-sensor provisioning, export-audit templates. Doshi's one amendment was that the failure-rate curve be re-fitted quarterly, since the sequence rested on a single exponent.

Iyengar chose society maintenance contracts first, plumbing second, Hyderabad third — reversing her board's instinct that geography is the natural next step. Her unlock was deliberately unglamorous: the maintenance contract is not a new business but a supply-retention instrument sold as a product. Her Hyderabad lead, Farhan Qureshi, dissented on record, arguing that a different buyer, motion and contract length make it diversification wearing focus's clothing. Iyengar recorded the dissent and set one reversal trigger: if protected-cohort attrition had not fallen below 3 per cent monthly by December, the programme stops and Hyderabad moves up.

Discussion questions

  1. If Wajood's learning-curve slope were −0.20 rather than −0.32, pushing the pharmaceutical gate past month 60, which of Barua's decisions should change, and which should not?
  2. Under what definition of focus is Qureshi right, and under what definition is Iyengar? Can both be operationalised in one company?
  3. On Wafaa's board in month fourteen, what one number would you have demanded before approving quick commerce, and at what threshold?

13. Going deeper

Zanjeer Cold Chain Systems: The Order of the Queue

Pune, Sunday 15 November 2026

1. The Night Before

The Diwali lights were still up on the building opposite, a week after anyone had bothered to switch them on. Vikram Sathe sat at his dining table in Baner with a cold cup of filter coffee and a slide he had rewritten eleven times. It was titled FY28 Focus and carried one line of text. Every version of that line had felt, within a day, like a sentence he would defend for three years.

The pre-read was due at nine the next morning; the board met on Thursday in Mumbai. Vikram, co-founder and Chief Product Officer of Zanjeer Cold Chain Systems, had written eleven such documents since 2019 and never found one hard in this way. The numbers were not missing; there were too many, pointing in different directions depending on who had assembled them.

Zamurrad Growth Partners, which had led the Series A, had put a Series B term sheet on the table in October: ₹140 crore, conditional on what Farida Contractor, the Zamurrad partner on the board, kept calling “a category-leadership story” — one segment in which Zanjeer was demonstrably the default choice, the rest sequenced behind it. The term sheet expired on 31 January 2027. The pre-read had to name the segment.

Zanjeer served five. By revenue, dairy was largest and oldest; by gross margin, pharmaceutical distribution; by deal velocity, quick-commerce dark stores; by pipeline, pharma, at four times everything else combined. By retention the picture depended on a cut of the data Arnav Chatterjee had produced in April and that nobody, Vikram included, had absorbed. Underneath all five sat a hardware problem indifferent to segment: the logger carrying most of the installed base ran on a 2G module the telcos had begun to retire. He typed a line, read it, and deleted it again.

2. Company History

Zanjeer was founded in Pune in March 2019 by Vikram and Sunaina Kaul. Sunaina had spent nine years running distribution for a frozen-foods company, arguing with transporters about temperature excursions nobody could prove; Vikram had built telematics firmware while AIS-140 compliance was turning GPS boxes into a commodity. Their first product, the ZanjeerTag, was a temperature and door-event logger paired with a console that turned an excursion into a ticket with a named owner and a clock on it. The pitch was never the sensor; it was the accountability trail.

The vaccine programme of 2021 created a brief demand for validated cold-chain monitoring, which Zanjeer served badly — its devices were on no prequalification list — and then it went away. What stayed was food: chilled milk, curd, ice cream, frozen paratha, QSR patties. Unglamorous and, as Sunaina liked to say, spoiling every day whether anyone was watching or not.

The decision that shaped everything afterwards was taken in August 2022. Zaffran Dairy Foods, a ₹4,100-crore private dairy with plants across Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka, offered a five-year master services agreement covering 11,400 nodes — tankers, chilling centres, distributor freezers — worth about ₹18 crore of committed revenue. Zanjeer was eleven months from running out of money. It signed. Three clauses came with the cheque: most-favoured-nation pricing, so Zaffran could not be charged more per node than any other food customer, which set a ceiling on the whole foods category; two guaranteed roadmap seats a quarter, engineering commitments of Zaffran’s choosing; and a co-developed firmware variant for milk tankers, the ZT-D line, with joint IP.

Four years on, the ZT-D fork had diverged by some forty thousand lines, and the roadmap seats had gone on a procurement module, a yield report and, this quarter, an SAP integration. The ₹96 crore Series A had been raised on the Zaffran logo. So had the company’s reputation in dairy. So had its price ceiling.

3. The Industry

India’s cold chain is large, fragmented and improving unevenly. Refrigerated road transport is dominated by owner-operators running two or three reefer trucks against contracts renegotiated every season. Organised players — Snowman Logistics, Coldman, the temperature-controlled arms of Delhivery, the 3PLs serving Amul, Mother Dairy and Hatsun — set the standards everyone else copies.

Regulation bears from four directions at once. FSSAI governs temperature discipline in food logistics and is tightening documentation expectations. CDSCO and the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, with the WHO Good Distribution Practice norms exporters adopt for overseas buyers, govern pharmaceutical distribution — demanding calibration traceable to NABL-accredited laboratories, qualification packs and audit trails that survive inspection. BIS certification and WPC type approval govern the radios inside Zanjeer’s devices. The DPDP Act governs driver location data; one customer’s legal team held up a rollout seven weeks over consent artefacts.

Demand had changed shape. Quick commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart and the dark-store networks their suppliers run — had created thousands of small, dense, fast-turning cold points, each worth far less than a dairy plant but installable in an afternoon. Exports pulled the other way: buyers in Dubai and Singapore demanded shipment-level temperature evidence, and APEDA-registered exporters of grapes, seafood and processed dairy treated that evidence as a condition of the order, not a service to buy. Fifteen per cent of revenue came from outside India, mostly through Zahra Foods Trading LLC in Dubai.

Competition was not one thing. Zohal Telematics, a Hyderabad rival, undercut Zanjeer in foods and had never invested in compliance; truck OEMs shipped factory-fitted telematics covering location adequately and temperature poorly; global pharma specialists sold prequalified devices at four times the price and ignored anyone small. Nobody held all three positions, and Vikram had never been sure whether the middle was open or empty for a reason.

4. How the Year Unfolded

Exhibit 1 sets out the sequence; it cannot show how each step felt.

Exhibit 1 — Decisions and their consequences, 2019–2026

From board minutes, 9 November 2026. The 2022 node count is contracted, not deployed.

In January, revenue operations revised the CRM stage definitions. “Qualified” had meant budget confirmed by a named approver; it now meant budget indicated, and earlier opportunities were re-staged in bulk. Nobody flagged it to the board; it was presented as hygiene. The pharma pipeline, ₹31 crore in December, was ₹96 crore by March.

In February, Harsh Doshi announced a pharma breakthrough: a national distributor reaching into the Cipla and Dr. Reddy’s channel networks had signed. It emerged in May that the signature covered a paid pilot of 400 nodes, with rollout contingent on a validation pack Zanjeer had not built. The logo went up anyway, and ₹9.4 crore of ARR leans on that relationship.

In April, Arnav Chatterjee published a retention model built on 24 months of node-level telemetry and billing. Segment, he found, was a weak predictor of whether a customer was still there two years later. The strong predictor was whether the customer owned its reefer assets or rented them: owners renewed, users of contracted capacity churned when the contract moved. The memo drew nineteen emoji reactions and changed nothing, because no plan was organised along that axis.

In June, the dark-store business arrived almost by accident: one quick-commerce supplier ordered 2,200 nodes on a two-week window, then 1,600 more in August. The fastest revenue Zanjeer had booked, on ninety-day terms set by a procurement team that did this for a living.

In August, Zaffran’s supply chain head asked for fifth-year pricing and, in the same breath, said his team was “evaluating whether the tanker piece should sit in-house.”

In September, Tejaswini Naik’s group confirmed what everyone had deferred: the 2G modules in some 21,000 nodes needed replacing, the successor needed fresh BIS and WPC approvals, and the programme would cost ₹6.4 crore and take three quarters — four in her own estimate, given verbally and never written down.

5. The People

Argues pharma is winnable, but only as a three-quarter, ₹4.1 crore validated-device programme. Her budget triples if pharma wins. Has not told the board that two of her four quality engineers have offers elsewhere.

Champions pharma, citing the pipeline. His variable pay is weighted to bookings, not collections. Does not volunteer that the two largest pharma opportunities are one group, counted twice.

7. Voices

Farida Contractor, board call, 28 October

“₹59 crore in one segment is a category leader; ₹59 crore across five is a services company with sensors. I am not saying which to pick. I am saying the deck must pick.”

Harsh Doshi, pipeline review, 3 November

“₹140 crore of pharma. I don’t need a strategy debate, I need two quality engineers and the validation pack. Every quarter we wait, that pipeline ages out.”

Dr. Padmini Rau, reply to all, 3 November

“Harsh, nine per cent. We win one pharma deal in eleven. Either the pipeline is not real or our product is not ready, and I would like the board to be told which one we believe before they are told the number.”

Tejaswini Naik, hardware review, Coimbatore, 9 November

“Everyone is arguing about which door to walk through. Twenty-one thousand nodes are on a radio that will stop working. Pick any segment you like — you still spend three quarters and ₹6.4 crore before a new logo sees a device that is alive in 2029.”

Arnav Chatterjee, Slack, #strategy, 11 November, 06:12 IST

“Reposting April’s finding since it keeps not landing. Ownership beats segment by a mile. Win pharma distributors and we win the profile that churns. That may still be right — but we should say out loud that we choose it in spite of the retention data, not because of it.”

Siew-Ling Tan, customer call notes, Zahra Foods Trading LLC, Dubai, 12 November

“One contract covering India, UAE and Oman, same evidence pack for chilled dairy and for seafood. Commodity is irrelevant to them. If we had it I could sign three more this year. We do not, and nobody’s roadmap contains it.”

8. The Options as Vikram Sees Them

A. Win dairy and liquid foods outright

Renew Zaffran, live with the MFN ceiling, and convert the reference into the private dairies and cooperative unions that follow where Zaffran goes. Largest installed base, shortest deployments, best-understood support. Against it: the ceiling is contractual, the segment grew 13% in a year, and the roadmap seats hand the largest customer part of the engineering calendar. Winning a category may not help if it cannot be repriced.

B. Sequence into pharmaceutical distribution

Fund Dr. Rau’s ₹4.1 crore validated-device programme, bid the vaccine tender with a prequalified partner, open the North American door. Best gross margin, best ARR per node, a moat made of paperwork. Against it: a 288-day cycle, a 9% win rate, a pipeline restated in January, four customers of whom one is most of the revenue, and a profile Exhibit 6 suggests does not stay.

C. Take the dark-store volume

Ride quick commerce, where deployments take a fortnight and win rates are the highest in the book; node growth would look spectacular in a Series B deck. Against it: 47% margin, four times the support load per node, 78% concentration, ninety-day terms, and buyers who re-tender annually on price against Zohal Telematics.

D. Platform first, segment later

Spend FY28 replacing the 2G estate and shipping one segment-agnostic node, deferring the choice a year. Honest about the constraint, defensible to engineering. Against it: it does not choose, it consumes exactly the quarters the other three need, and Farida has heard it once already.

Vikram had written these four out on Saturday and been uneasy since. Every one is a segment answer, and three of the people closest to the problem do not think segment is the question. Arnav’s axis is asset ownership; Siew-Ling’s is geography; Tejaswini’s is the device platform. A fifth option, unwritten, would organise the company around one of those — and Vikram cannot tell whether that is the insight of the year or the most elegant way yet found to avoid naming a beachhead.

9. The Deadline and the Hard Constraints

  • Cash. ₹38 crore at 31 October against net burn of ₹2.6 crore a month: fourteen months.
  • The term sheet. ₹140 crore from Zamurrad, expiring 31 January 2027, with an ARR milestone of ₹85 crore by 30 June 2027. Current plans reach ₹76 crore.
  • The Zaffran MSA. Runs to 31 March 2027; renewal notice due 31 December 2026. MFN pricing and two roadmap seats per quarter continue in any renewed term. Zaffran is 26% of total ARR.
  • Hardware. 21,000 nodes on a retiring 2G radio. Replacement plus BIS and WPC approvals: ₹6.4 crore, three quarters on paper, four in Tejaswini’s judgement.
  • Regulated entry. A pharma validated-device programme — NABL-traceable calibration, qualification packs, audit trails — is ₹4.1 crore and three quarters, and cannot run alongside the radio replacement on one hardware team.
  • A tender. A state health department’s vaccine cold-chain contract, ₹58 crore over five years, closes 11 December. Zanjeer cannot bid alone: the specification requires prequalified devices it does not have.
  • People. Headcount frozen at 241, of whom 42 engineers, until Series B closes.

10. Questions for Discussion

  1. Which of Zanjeer’s five segments, if any, has it won? What evidence would settle it, and which exhibit comes closest to providing that evidence?
  2. Exhibits 3, 4 and 5 point to different priorities. For each, name the accounting or sampling choice that shapes the conclusion, and what you would recompute.
  3. The 2022 Zaffran agreement bought survival at the cost of a price ceiling, two roadmap seats and a firmware fork. Was it a good trade, what does it now rule out, and how should a four-year-old constraint weigh on today’s choice?
  4. Arnav’s ownership axis, Siew-Ling’s geographic axis and Tejaswini’s platform axis each imply a different definition of “segment.” What would the FY28 plan look like under each, and what would Zanjeer stop doing in each case?
  5. Farida wants one segment named. Is that useful discipline or a distortion introduced by the financing calendar, and how should a product leader respond when the sequencing question is asked by the clock rather than the market?
  6. It is Monday morning. What single line does Vikram put on the FY28 Focus slide, what does he commit to stopping, and what does he tell the board on Thursday about what that line leaves unanswered?

11. Baner, 11:40 p.m.

Vikram opened Arnav’s April memo again, then Tejaswini’s slide with the twenty-one thousand nodes on it, then the Zaffran renewal clause, then the tender specification with its list of prequalified devices that did not include his. Somewhere in there was a sequence: one market won properly, then the next. He could see arguments for four first moves and none that ruled any of them out.

Downstairs a neighbour was taking down the Diwali lights, one string at a time. Vikram put the cursor back at the head of the empty line and left it there.

Qadam Ledger: Which Shop Do We Win Next?

Bengaluru, 8 October 2026

1. The Deadline

Ritika Chandran read the board deck once more, though she had already memorised every number in it. It was a Thursday evening in HSR Layout, and through the glass wall of the Qadam Ledger conference room she could see the Bengaluru traffic beginning its nightly crawl on Sarjapur Road. In twelve days, on 20 October, her board would meet to approve the FY27 go-to-market plan, and with it the next tranche of a Series B her lead investor had all but promised. The one line item the board wanted resolved first was which retailer segment Qadam would open next, and in what order. Ritika had until Monday to send a recommendation to the four people whose views she trusted most, so the board paper would carry something sharper than "we will figure it out as we grow."

2. Company Background

Qadam Ledger was a digital bahi-khata: an app that let small shopkeepers record credit given to customers, track daily cash and stock, and, since early 2025, apply for short-term working-capital loans from partner NBFCs. It competed directly with OkCredit and Khatabook on the ledger, and increasingly with Vyapar and the lending arms of Bijnis and IndiaMART on credit. Founded in 2019 by Ritika and two co-founders from IIT Madras, Qadam had raised a ₹42 crore Series A in 2023 and now employed 96 people. Its product, sales and support motion had been built around one segment: kirana, the neighbourhood grocery store. By October 2026, Qadam had onboarded just over 3.1 lakh kirana retailers across Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Telangana, of whom about 74,000 used the app daily and roughly 19,000 had taken a lending product. Kirana was not small to have won — India has an estimated 12 to 13 million such stores — but Qadam had never operated outside it, and every workflow, from expiry reminders to loan underwriting, was tuned to a grocer's rhythms.

3. The Situation

The push to look beyond kirana started with a slide, not a strategy. In August, Devika Rao, head of growth analytics, working out of Toronto on a schedule overlapping Bengaluru only in the Indian evening, ran a cohort study across every retailer type that had ever piloted the app informally — a few hundred hardware, electrical and medical stores that had signed up unsolicited, after hearing about Qadam from a kirana neighbour. Her numbers, later formalised as Exhibit 1, showed hardware and electrical retailers carrying baskets nearly two and a half times larger than kirana and churning more slowly, while pharmacies showed the strongest revenue per store of all three but needed features — batch and expiry tracking by drug schedule, compliant billing for scheduled drugs — Qadam had never built. Meenal Kulkarni, VP of Sales in Pune, heard something different from the field: kirana customers wanted bigger loans and supplier-payment tools, not sales reps knocking on a hardware shop's door. Lena Hoffmann, head of product design in Berlin, had spent two weeks mapping a pharmacy-ready version of the app and concluded it was closer to a second product than a feature add. The debate had reached Faisal Rehman, the board member representing Qadam's lead investor from Dubai, who wanted capital spent on depth, not breadth, ahead of the raise.

Exhibit 1 — Segment economics, Qadam's July–September 2026 pilot data

Exhibit 1 was the number Devika kept returning to: pharmacies paid back CAC fastest and churned least, but her own footnote was a caution Ritika could not ignore — the sample was small and self-selected, so early adopters were likely more tech-forward than the market as a whole. Exhibit 2 showed the other half of the picture: how much of the kirana opportunity remained unclaimed inside Qadam's three existing states, let alone in states it had not entered at all.

Even in Karnataka, its oldest state, Qadam had reached fewer than one in five kirana stores. Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, not yet entered, held more kirana stores between them than Qadam's three live states combined. Exhibit 3 places the three candidate segments side by side, to make a point Ritika kept repeating: kirana was not a market Qadam had exhausted; it was a market Qadam had barely started.

4. The People

Devika Rao — Head of Growth Analytics, TorontoWants hardware & electrical opened now, while the data advantage is fresh and before OkCredit or Khatabook notice the same cohort.
Meenal Kulkarni — VP of Sales, PuneWants Qadam to go deeper in kirana first — her 40-person field team is already stretched onboarding Telangana, and existing customers are asking for bigger loans, not a new shop type to sell to.
Lena Hoffmann — Head of Product Design, BerlinWants whatever is chosen scoped honestly — her audit found pharmacy compliance features (Schedule H drug tracking, batch expiry) would take at least two quarters, not one.
Faisal Rehman — Board Member, DubaiWants capital discipline ahead of the raise — "kirana, done properly" is easier to underwrite than "three segments, all half-built."

5. The Options

Option A — Deepen kirana: two new states, no new segment

Pitch the board "own kirana in five states." Enter Uttar Pradesh and Bihar in FY27, while adding the bigger working-capital loans customers want. Upside: the largest addressable market, penetration still under 20% everywhere Qadam operates, a pitch that is simple and provable. Cost: it defers the diversification investors will eventually want, and cedes the early-mover opportunity Devika's data points to.

Option B — Open hardware & electrical in the existing three states

Launch a hardware-and-electrical version of Qadam in the same three states, reusing the existing city footprint and sales team, before entering any new state. Upside: larger baskets, lower churn, a natural adjacency for a rep already walking a market street. Cost: still a second segment built on a thin pilot, and Meenal's team selling two products in territories not yet saturated with one.

Option C — Build the pharmacy vertical as a distinct product

Fund a separate, compliance-heavy pharmacy product, led by Lena's team, targeting the segment with the best unit economics in Exhibit 1. Upside: highest revenue per store and stickiest customer once compliance features exist, a moat competitors would find hard to copy. Cost: the longest build, the smallest and least-validated pilot, and a distraction from the kirana engine that funds everything else.

6. Questions for Discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 say about how much of the kirana opportunity Qadam has captured, and why does that matter before any new segment is discussed?
  2. How reliable is the cohort data behind Exhibit 1, given how those customers arrived at Qadam? What would you test before trusting its CAC and churn numbers?
  3. Each stakeholder reasons from a different part of the business — data, field sales, build cost, capital discipline. Whose constraint should bind the decision, and why?
  4. If Qadam picks a second segment now, what does "winning" it before opening a third actually require, in people, months and rupees?

7. A Note for the Learner

This case is about sequencing, not selection. It is tempting to read it as "which segment is best," and Exhibit 1 all but invites that — pharmacy wins on revenue per store, hardware wins on churn. But the topic here is that the order of expansion is itself the strategy, not a detail worked out after a segment is chosen. Rumelt's test for a good strategy begins with a guiding policy focused enough to concentrate resources against; a company opening three segments at 15% depth has not diversified risk, it has diluted focus three ways at once. The discipline this topic demands is treating each new segment as a beachhead that must be won — real penetration, a repeatable sales motion, no constant exception-handling — before the next opens, since every open segment draws attention and capacity from the ones still being won.

A well-reasoned answer weighs three things: how much of the current beachhead is secured (Exhibit 2 shows kirana far from saturated in every state Qadam serves); how trustworthy the evidence for the next beachhead is (Exhibit 1 comes from a self-selected sample, which should discount but not dismiss Devika's case); and how much capacity a new segment consumes before it pays back (Lena's estimate makes Option C a two-quarter product team, not a sprint).

The defensible path is Option A, with a dated trigger toward Option B. Kirana penetration is under 20% in Qadam's best state and zero in two large ones; that is unfinished business, and a new segment must clear a high bar against it. The qualification is not to shelve Devika's finding but to test it properly: run a funded, 90-day hardware & electrical pilot inside the existing states, sized for trustworthy numbers, with a decision gate at day 90. Pharmacy, with the heaviest build cost and thinnest evidence, waits until kirana growth frees engineering capacity, or the pilot proves the thesis first. That sequence — finish winning kirana, test hardware honestly, hold pharmacy in reserve — gives the board one clear priority, a stronger Series B narrative than three unfinished fronts.

Focus and Sequencing: Win One Segment Before the Next

1. A board slide with three good answers

In April 2025, Ananya Deshmukh stood in front of Hausla Retail Cloud's board with a slide she had rewritten four times. Hausla sold a single product — a ledger, inventory and digital-payments reconciliation app built for small retail outlets — and after eighteen months of open-ended piloting, it had paying customers in three quite different worlds: kirana stores, standalone pharmacies, and auto-parts retailers. The pilots had all worked well enough to be renewed. The company had ₹4.1 crore left from its Series A and a six-person field sales team it could not meaningfully grow before the next round. The question was not which segment was good — all three were — but which one Hausla should commit its scarce selling capacity to first, which one second, and which one it would deliberately not chase this year.

Rohit Sagar, Hausla's co-founder and chief executive, put it plainly afterward: "Everyone agrees we can't do all three well at once. Nobody agrees on the order. Bring me the order, and the reasoning, by the next board." Ananya had eleven weeks. Get the order wrong, and Hausla would spend a runway proving a point the market had no intention of rewarding — a mistake that would not show up as a bad quarter so much as a company that quietly ran out of road while its dashboards still looked busy.

2. The idea

Focus, in strategy, means choosing where not to compete so the resources you do commit are concentrated enough to actually win somewhere — an idea Richard Rumelt places at the centre of what he calls the kernel of good strategy: a diagnosis of the real problem, a guiding policy for tackling it, and a set of coherent actions, whose first honest test is whether the guiding policy says no to more things than it says yes to. Sequencing is the less-discussed second half of the same discipline: once you have chosen to focus, in what order do you expand out of that first position into the next one, and the one after that. The two travel together because a company rarely wins a market in one motion — it wins a narrow slice first, then uses what that slice gave it to take the next slice more cheaply than a new entrant could. The sentence Ananya could say in a board meeting without sounding glib was this: for a company with limited capital and one sales team, the order of entry is not a scheduling detail downstream of strategy — it is the strategy, because each segment either inherits an advantage from the one before it or starts from zero.

3. How it actually works

Practitioners usually skip three steps that make this more than a gut call. The first is defining the beachhead narrowly enough to name exactly who you will lose deals to and why you expect to win instead — not "small retailers," which describes twelve million businesses, but "GST-registered kirana stores in tier-2 towns with a smartphone-literate owner." The second, skipped most often, is naming the unlock: what does winning segment one hand you that segment two specifically needs — product hardened by real use, a distributor relationship, a reference logo, regulatory comfort, or trust that travels through a local network of people who talk to each other. If you cannot state the unlock in one sentence, you have a list of markets you like, not a sequence. The third is treating the sequence as a hypothesis with a revisit date, not a plan fixed at launch — the win rates and referral patterns observed after entering segment one are better information than anything available when the roadmap was first drawn, and a sequence that cannot be revised by that evidence is a calendar, not a strategy.

Ananya's team ran this as three questions per candidate segment: how big is the reachable slice given the sales capacity actually on hand; what does winning it teach the product and team; and what, specifically, does it hand the next segment in line. The first question is arithmetic; the second and third are judgement, but judgement checkable against evidence within a couple of quarters — which is what made the exercise plannable rather than a debate that could run forever.

4. A worked example

Hausla's data lead, Meera Pillai, working from Pune, sized the three segments against the six-person field team, which could sustain roughly eight kirana deals, six pharmacy deals, or four auto-parts deals per rep per year — fewer as the buyer gets more complex, since a longer sales cycle lets a rep run fewer deals in parallel.

SegmentAddressable outletsARPU / yearSales cycleDeals / rep / yrYear-1 ARR (6 reps)
Kirana stores90,000₹21,60045 days8₹10.37 lakh
Standalone pharmacies40,000₹42,00060 days6₹15.12 lakh
Auto-parts retailers15,000₹72,00090 days4₹17.28 lakh

Table 1. Segment sizing treated as three independent bets — the analysis Ananya's first draft slide made.

Read this table the way a first-pass planner reads it, and auto-parts wins: 24 deals a year at ₹72,000 ARPU produces ₹17.28 lakh in new annual recurring revenue, more than either other segment, for the same six reps. This is what "focus" naively produces when the only question asked is "which segment is biggest today, on its own" — exactly the trap Rumelt's kernel warns against, since it optimises the guiding policy for the largest number on one slide rather than for the sequence of advantages it buys.

The second pass changes one input: whether pharmacy inherits anything from kirana having already been won in the same towns. It does, structurally, because the same wholesale distributors typically supply both kirana stores and standalone pharmacies, and pharmacy owners sit on the same town-level trade associations as kirana owners — a rep already trusted by the kirana owners on a street walks into the pharmacy next door already vouched for. That fact cuts the pharmacy sales cycle from 60 to roughly 45 days and lifts a rep's realistic pharmacy capacity from six deals a year to eight — the same six reps now close 48 pharmacy deals instead of 36, at the same ₹42,000 ARPU, for ₹20.16 lakh instead of ₹15.12 lakh: a ₹5.04 lakh gain, about 33 percent, with no new hire and no price change, purely from order of entry. Auto-parts retailers buy through a separate spares-dealer association with almost no overlap with either network, so no such discount exists whichever segment precedes it — it stays a 90-day, four-deal segment regardless of order, telling Ananya that auto-parts belongs last, entered deliberately with capital and an enterprise motion the earlier two segments pay for.

Figure 1. Same product, same ARPU, same six reps — order of entry alone is worth ₹5.04 lakh in year-two pharmacy ARR.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Focus and sequencing are not the same word

Focus is a refusal — what you will not chase right now. Sequencing is about order across time. Teams that collapse the two believe focus means "forever," when a sequencing plan actually says "not yet, and here is what has to be true before we do."

A beachhead is chosen for what it compounds into, not its size today

Ranking segments by this year's addressable revenue, as Hausla's first draft did, treats each as if it existed alone. A beachhead earns its place by what it hands the next segment — density, trust, a hardened product, references — a different quantity than its own size, and sometimes running the opposite direction.

Sequencing needs a nameable unlock, not a hopeful adjacency

"These markets feel related" is not an unlock. An unlock is a specific asset — a shared distributor, regulator, trade body, or capability segment two cannot function without — that a competitor entering segment two cold would not have.

The sequence is a hypothesis, not a launch-day commitment

The order picked before any customer is won rests on the least reliable information the company will ever have. A plan never revisited once real win rates and referral patterns exist is not discipline — it is a refusal to look at new evidence.

It will not tell you when to abandon a beachhead

Focus and sequencing describe an order of attack, not exit criteria. A team can sequence with total discipline into a first segment that was simply wrong, and mistake its own consistency for proof the strategy is working.

Adjacency between segments is often one-directional

Kirana unlocked pharmacy because trust travelled through a shared distributor and trade-body network — pharmacy would not have unlocked kirana in reverse, since pharmacy owners are not who kirana owners look to for vouching. Order matters causally, not merely by which markets look adjacent on a map.

6. How this looks different by product type and company stage

In consumer products, the unit of sequencing is usually a city or cohort rather than a named vertical — a food-delivery platform expands metro by metro because the asset it is building in each city is rider and restaurant density, which does not transfer to the next city the way a trade-association referral transfers between verticals in the same town. In B2B, as at Hausla, sequencing runs vertical by vertical, because trust travels through the distributors, regulators and associations a buyer belongs to, and a reference logo in pharmacy does little for a conversation in auto-parts. In a marketplace, the question is two-sided at once — which side to seed first, in which city or category — because a marketplace segment is really a small supply-demand pocket that must reach local liquidity before it is worth anything, and spreading thin across many pockets starves all of them rather than winning one.

Company stage changes the stakes, not the logic. For an early-stage company like Hausla, a wrong beachhead is close to existential — the runway to discover and correct it may not exist. For a large, profitable company, a wrong order slows growth rather than threatening survival, but such companies often find it harder to resequence even once the evidence is clear, because an existing sales organisation has territory assignments and internal champions built around the current order, and undoing that is a harder negotiation than admitting the error itself.

7. Common mistakes

The roadmap quietly serves everyone. Symptom: a backlog with committed features for three or four segments at once, none fully solved. Error: treating focus as language in a strategy document rather than a resourcing decision, so every regional sales lead still gets their preferred segment funded. Diagnostic: pull the last two quarters of engineering time by segment tag — if it tracks headcount rather than concentrating sharply, there is no real focus regardless of the deck.

The beachhead is really just whoever the founder already knew. Symptom: a first segment chosen for a friendly pilot customer or a founder's old employer, with no structural reason a cold competitor couldn't win it too. Diagnostic: ask whether a well-capitalised competitor entering cold would have reason to lose — if the only answer is "we know someone there," it is a relationship, not a beachhead.

Segment two arrives on schedule, not on evidence. Symptom: expansion happens exactly per the original slide, regardless of how segment one performed. Error: mistaking the sequence for a fixed plan instead of a hypothesis. Diagnostic: check whether entering segment two cites any number generated after segment one launched — if every number predates the beachhead, the sequence was never revised.

8. What good looks like

By the time Ananya returned to the board, the plan named the unlock in one sentence per transition: kirana buys the distributor and trade-body trust pharmacy specifically needs in the same towns; pharmacy and kirana together buy the cash flow and reference base that justify the longer, capital-heavier auto-parts motion later. Each transition carried a named trigger — a referral coefficient and win-rate threshold observed in the field, not a date on a slide — and a companion memo declined to build any auto-parts-specific features that year, so the wait was visible and revisitable, not merely implied. A nameable unlock, an evidence trigger, and a written refusal separate a sequencing plan from a wish list with a timeline attached.

9. What Ananya decided

She recommended kirana first, pharmacy second inside the same towns to inherit the trust asset built there, and auto-parts third, funded by the cash and sales muscle the first two would generate — reversing the naive, highest-Year-1-ARR reading of her own first table. The board approved it, with a standing quarterly review of actual referral and win-rate numbers as the trigger for the next segment, rather than the calendar. The natural next idea to study is how this logic scales into market-entry strategy once a company chooses not just which segment but which geography to enter next, carrying a beachhead's assets across a boundary larger than one town's distributor network. Two questions worth sitting with: what exactly does winning your first segment hand your second, in one sentence — and if a competitor read your plan today, which segment would they attack first, and would your order still make sense?

case20v1-pstrat.kernel:
Mashaal Skilling Systems: The Kernel Before the Board

A teaching case on strategy, diagnosis and the discipline of choosing — ISB Product Management

1. A Monday in Sitapura

On the morning of 12 October 2026, Devika Choudhary sat in the glass-walled corner office above the training floor of Mashaal Skilling Systems' flagship centre in Sitapura Industrial Area, Jaipur, with two documents open on her laptop. One was a term sheet from Falcon Crest Hospitality Group, a five-star hotel operator in Dubai, offering ₹6 crore in upfront funding for a new 500-seat hospitality-and-caregiving training centre in Kochi — in exchange for three years of exclusive supply. The offer lapsed on 31 October. The other was a seventeen-slide deck from her VP of Training Operations, Farhan Sheikh, titled "Mashaal 2030: 40 Centres, 20 Trades, 200,000 Learners a Year," which he wanted the board to bless at its meeting on 22 October, ten days away. That meeting would also decide the strategy Mashaal carried into the Series C round its investors expected to close by December. Devika had one board cycle to decide what Mashaal was actually betting on, and she did not yet have an answer that would survive being asked twice.

2. From One Trade to Eight

Devika founded Mashaal in 2018 after seven years between TeamLease and NSDC, convinced that India's vocational-training problem was less a shortage of curricula than a shortage of trust: employers doubted trainees were job-ready, and trainees doubted courses led anywhere. Mashaal's answer was placement-linked training — a trainee joined free or near-free, and Mashaal collected its fee from the employer, or a government scheme, only after the trainee was placed and retained for ninety days. The model started with one trade, retail sales associates for Reliance Retail's Rajasthan stores, from a single centre. By FY26 it ran fourteen centres across Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana and Delhi-NCR, plus a pilot in Kochi, training eight trades for employers including Voltas, Blue Star, Urban Company and Amazon India, and drawing per-trainee subsidy from the PMKVY 4.0 scheme administered through NSDC's Sector Skill Councils. Revenue had grown from ₹9 crore in FY24 to ₹42 crore in FY26. Its nearest comparators, TeamLease Skills University and Quess Corp's skilling arm, competed on scale and government-scheme volume; Mashaal had positioned itself on retention — a trainee who stayed placed was worth more, per NSDC's own audit standards, than one merely enrolled.

3. What the Growth Was Hiding

Farhan's deck made a plausible case: NSDC's PMKVY 4.0 targets rewarded volume, investors liked a growth story ahead of Series C, and every quarter Mashaal delayed opening centres was a quarter TeamLease or a fresh NSDC-empanelled entrant could claim the same district. But Leena Fernandes, Mashaal's Toronto-based Head of Data & Placement Analytics, had spent September pulling apart the retention numbers behind that revenue growth, and what she found worried her more than it excited her. Retail associate training — still the largest single trade by volume — had a ninety-day retention rate of just 41%; trainees placed with Amazon India warehouses or Reliance Retail stores were quitting within weeks for gig delivery work with Zomato or Swiggy, which paid similarly but felt more flexible. Each early exit triggered a fee clawback from the employer and, worse, an NSDC compliance query, since subsidy already booked as revenue depended on the ninety-day mark being real. Meanwhile the AC/HVAC technician trade, run for Voltas and Blue Star, held 78% retention: the job was local, no migration required, and summer heat plus rising room-AC penetration in Tier-2 Rajasthan and Gujarat towns had made it a career, not a stopgap. A new EV two-wheeler technician trade, feeding Ola Electric and Ather's expanding service network, showed early retention above 70% on small volumes; a rooftop-solar-installer trade launched this year on PM Surya Ghar demand was too new to read. Exhibit 1 laid out the dispersion; Exhibit 2 showed how it had been masked by aggregate growth; Exhibit 3 pictured it.

4. The People in the Room

Devika Choudhary — Founder & CEO, Jaipur. Wants a strategy she can defend to the board and to Series C investors without either starving growth or repeating the retail-associate problem at larger scale.
Farhan Sheikh — VP, Training Operations, Pune. Believes NSDC's expanding PMKVY targets and rival empanelment mean Mashaal must claim centres and districts now or lose them to TeamLease or Quess; his plan is built for scale, not for trade selection.
Leena Fernandes — Head of Data & Placement Analytics, Toronto. Owns the retention numbers and is uneasy that aggregate revenue growth has been quietly financed by trades that generate NSDC audit risk and fee clawbacks.
Nikunj Bhatia — Head of Employer Partnerships, Singapore. Negotiated the Falcon Crest offer and wants it signed before the window closes; a marquee Gulf anchor client, he argues, is exactly the story a Series C deck needs, even if the exclusivity clause forecloses talks he has quietly begun with a competing hotel group in Abu Dhabi.

5. The Options Before the Board

Option A — Sign the Falcon Crest exclusivity. Mashaal takes the ₹6 crore upfront, builds the Kochi centre, and commits its healthcare-aide and hospitality trade to one Dubai employer for three years. Upside: the highest-retention, highest-fee trade gets guaranteed volume and a clean growth story for investors. Cost: exclusivity forecloses the Abu Dhabi conversation and any future Gulf employer, concentrating Mashaal's best-performing vertical inside one counterparty and one geography's labour rules.

Option B — Approve Farhan's 2030 plan. Mashaal opens toward forty centres and twenty trades, chasing NSDC volume targets and the scale story the board wants before Series C. Upside: visible growth, first-mover claims on new districts, larger placement counts. Cost: the plan does not distinguish AC technician from retail associate; it scales the 41%-retention trade as fast as the 78%-retention one, multiplying the audit and clawback exposure Leena has just quantified.

Option C — Concentrate on structurally durable local trades. Devika defines a portfolio policy: expand centres and capital specifically into trades where employer demand is structurally rising and retention is high because the job does not require migration — AC/HVAC service, EV two-wheeler technician, and, once proven, rooftop solar installation. Renegotiate Falcon Crest for a large non-exclusive multi-year contract rather than exclusivity. Cap or restructure the retail-associate trade rather than scale it. Upside: a coherent, defensible growth story tied to real unit economics. Cost: a smaller FY28 headline number than Farhan's deck, and a harder conversation with NSDC and investors about why Mashaal is deliberately not chasing every available trade.

6. Questions for Discussion

1. What do Exhibits 1–3 reveal about which of Mashaal's trades are actually working, and why retention differs so sharply between them?

2. Is Farhan's "40 centres, 20 trades" plan a strategy, in Richard Rumelt's sense, or an aspiration wearing a strategy's clothes? What would it need to become one?

3. What does Mashaal give up, and what does it gain, by accepting Falcon Crest's exclusivity clause? Does that trade follow from any diagnosis, or from deal momentum?

4. Using the kernel — diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action — what should Devika bring to the 22 October board meeting, and what does that kernel rule in and rule out?

7. A Note for the Learner

Rumelt's kernel asks one question of anything called a strategy: does it contain a diagnosis of the specific challenge, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and a set of coherent actions that follow from that policy — or is it a restated goal? Farhan's plan names a destination (40 centres, 20 trades, 200,000 learners) but no diagnosis of why some trades at Mashaal work and others don't; without that, "coherent action" collapses into "do more of everything," which is aspiration, not strategy. Leena's data supplies the missing diagnosis: Mashaal's placement-linked model only works economically where the trade leads to a job the trainee has no reason to leave within ninety days — overwhelmingly, trades that are local, skilled, and riding structurally rising employer demand, such as AC service in a warming, more air-conditioned India, or EV servicing as electric two-wheelers scale. Trades that compete with flexible gig work, like retail associate roles, or trades still unproven at scale, like rooftop solar, do not yet meet that bar.

The defensible path is Option C. It converts the diagnosis directly into a guiding policy — concentrate expansion capital in trades with structural local demand and high retention, and treat any single-employer exclusivity as a cost to be minimised, not a growth shortcut — and into actions that follow from it without contradiction: renegotiating Falcon Crest to a large but non-exclusive contract, redirecting new-centre capital toward AC/HVAC and EV trades, and holding retail associate flat while its retention problem is fixed rather than scaled. Option A is tempting revenue that violates the diagnosis by concentrating risk in exactly the way the data warns against; Option B is the aspiration the board arrived wanting, dressed as a plan. A good answer need not reject growth — it must show the growth follows from a stated diagnosis the board can test against the same exhibits Devika has in front of her.

Jalsetu Traceability Systems: What the Lot Number Is For

An Indian-context decision case for the Product Strategy module — ISB Product Management

1. Sunday night, Piplod

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 18 October 2026, the third floor of the Jalsetu Traceability Systems office in Piplod, Surat, was empty except for Chaitali Bhanushali and a guard who kept asking about the corridor lights. Three documents were open: a nine-page board pre-read her co-founder had circulated on Friday, titled Jalsetu FY28: The Operating System for Indian Seafood Export; a draft memorandum of understanding from Jawhara Foodstuff Trading LLC in Dubai, worth ₹9.4 crore over three years, which Jawhara wanted signed before its family board met on 2 November; and a two-paragraph email from the quality-assurance head of Poortvliet Seafood BV in Rotterdam, which buys from six of Jalsetu's customers, asking whether Poortvliet's auditors might query lot data directly, and on what commercial basis.

The board met at ten the next morning. Behind it sat a Series B term sheet from Pushkal Growth Partners: ₹110 crore at ₹460 crore pre-money, with a condition she had read perhaps twenty times. Before signing, the company must present "a written product strategy identifying the segment in which the Company intends to be the category leader, and the segments it will not serve." Eight weeks of evidence-gathering had left her convinced that the three doors in front of her were not really three doors, and unable to say what they were instead.

2. Company history: the clause that is still in force

Jalsetu was founded in 2019 by Chaitali Bhanushali, who grew up in Veraval where her family ran an ice plant at the fishing harbour, and Hardik Parmar, who had sold industrial weighing systems to processors across Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh for a decade and knew every plant manager on the coast. The first product was narrow: a tablet-and-barcode system that recorded a catch lot or pond harvest at receipt, held its identity through peeling, grading, freezing and packing, and printed a carton code traceable to a pond or a landing. India's marine-products exports were then nearing ₹60,000 crore a year, and every processor they met had the same problem: European and American buyers asked questions paper registers could not answer in the hours a consignment could be held.

Then came the decision that shaped everything since. Prawaal Seafoods Exports, a Veraval exporter with three plants and roughly ₹700 crore of turnover, offered to standardise on Jalsetu — on conditions. It wanted the plant floor itself: yield per lot, peeling-line productivity, count-size reconciliation, packing and cold-store inventory. It wanted the system on servers inside its own plants, because its promoters would not put yield data in anyone's cloud. And its terms included a perpetual licence for the plant modules, source-code escrow, and a four per cent annual cap on support-fee increases for ten years.

Hardik argued the deal was existential, and it did buy credibility across the Kathiawar belt. Chaitali argued for a narrower version and lost. Five years on, as Exhibit 1 shows, Prawaal is 19 per cent of revenue at a fee rising 4 per cent a year against salary inflation of roughly 9; Jalsetu maintains on-premises installations at fourteen plants for six customers; and the modules built for Prawaal are what prospects ask to see first.

3. The industry

India exports frozen shrimp, and to a lesser extent fish, cephalopods and surimi, to buyers ever less willing to take a supplier's word for anything. Roughly three-quarters of the value is farmed vannamei from ponds across coastal Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Odisha, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, aggregated by hatcheries, feed dealers and commission agents and processed by several hundred plants of which perhaps eighty matter commercially. The listed comparators include Avanti Feeds, Apex Frozen Foods, Waterbase and Surat's own Zeal Aqua; the buyers are American and European importers and, increasingly, Gulf re-exporters.

The regulatory surface is dense. The Marine Products Export Development Authority registers exporters and collects consignment-level reporting; the Export Inspection Council certifies consignments for the European Union, where health certification moves through TRACES NT and a fixed share of Indian aquaculture consignments faces mandatory residue checks at border posts, adverse findings surfacing as RASFF notifications. The Coastal Aquaculture Authority registers farms, so a pond either has a registration number or it does not. The United States adds Seafood Import Monitoring Program reporting, FDA import alerts on antibiotic residues, and a tariff position that has pushed exporters to hedge toward Europe, the Gulf and East Asia. FSSAI governs the domestic side; the DPDP Act, 2023 governs whatever Jalsetu records about an identifiable farmer.

The competitive picture changed twice in eighteen months. Pratyaksh Trace Cloud, a Chennai rival that raised a large round in 2025, began giving its traceability module away free for two years with its plant-floor suite — the inverse of Jalsetu's pricing. Jaanch Compliance Systems, a Noida firm with some 4,000 exporter customers across DGFT and FSSAI filings, added MPEDA consignment reporting to its subscription free in June 2026.

4. The situation in detail

In January 2025 Jalsetu launched the Buyer Dossier: one compliance packet per consignment, assembled automatically, carrying lot genealogy back to pond or landing, antibiotic test certificates, temperature history and the EIA health certificate number. Buyers were asking for it, no competitor had it, and it could be priced per consignment rather than per plant — revenue that grew with export volume, not headcount. Sales priced it at ₹1,100 a dossier, free for the first year with every new plant deal.

Three things have since turned out otherwise. First, adoption looked excellent and was not. By September 2026, 36 of 41 customers were "using" the module, but as Exhibit 5 shows, only nine generated a dossier unaided, and services touched 71 per cent of the quarter's dossiers at a loaded cost of about ₹1,900 against the ₹1,100 price. Jalsetu had built a product and was delivering a service.

Second, the data underneath is thinner than the document implies. Genealogy is complete inside the plant and rests on a farmer declaration outside it. Anirban Dutta's team in Toronto matched pond identifiers against the Coastal Aquaculture Authority register in August: 58 per cent resolved to a valid registration; 19 per cent to one whose stated area was smaller than the harvest attributed to it; the rest did not resolve. No customer has been told. Fathima Rasheed has argued since June that the dossier asserts a chain of custody the company cannot verify, and that a European rejection traced to a Jalsetu dossier would be a different kind of event from a competitor's.

Third, buyers began asking for something Jalsetu had not planned to sell. Poortvliet does not want a PDF; it wants query access. Palmetto Coast Seafood Inc., a Charleston importer Bharat Menon has courted since February, says the same more forcefully and has mentioned paying. That is a different business: a buyer-side network sold in Rotterdam and Charleston, in which Jalsetu's processors become data suppliers rather than customers, and their yield, count-size recovery and rejection history become visible to the people who negotiate their prices. Girish Kotak, managing director of Prawaal, has made his view plain.

Underneath it all is the Gulf. Jawhara re-exports frozen seafood out of Jebel Ali and wants consignment-level traceability and grading for product from four origin countries. The product is not Jalsetu's — re-export documentation, not pond-to-plant genealogy — and Sabina Qureshi estimates it would absorb the two senior engineers who understand the dossier pipeline.

5. The people

Chaitali Bhanushali — Co-founder and Chief Product Officer, Surat. Believes Jalsetu's advantage is that it sits where physical product and paper meet. Has told no one on the board about the 58 per cent.
Hardik Parmar — Co-founder and Chief Executive, Surat. Author of the pre-read. Argues Jalsetu wins by becoming the operating system of the Indian plant, where switching costs are enormous and Pratyaksh is taking ground by giving traceability away. Holds 26 per cent, with a secondary in the term sheet that pays only at this valuation. Does not say the roadmap he defends is largely Prawaal's, nor that Girish Kotak calls him weekly.
Fathima Rasheed — Head of Regulatory Affairs, Kochi. Nine years at an EIA-notified laboratory. Wants verification before expansion: sampling protocols, laboratory integration, a dossier that distinguishes verified fields from declared ones. Her incentive is asymmetric — she carries a border rejection and none of the growth. Does not say two of her three staff have applied elsewhere.
Yogesh Kulkarni — Vice President, Engineering, Pune. Fifty-eight engineers, eleven of whom only maintain on-premises installations and per-customer modifications. Wants a decision so he can stop staffing every direction at once. Privately believes the multi-tenant rewrite any buyer-side product needs is eighteen months; wrote twelve in the pre-read because Hardik asked what it would be "if it went well".
Anirban Dutta — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Built the CAA reconciliation and the telemetry in Exhibit 5. Thinks the real asset is four years of lot-level grading, yield and rejection data across 41 exporters, and that risk scoring belongs to whoever has most to lose. Has not said his model's lift was measured on 314 rejection events, 180 from one customer.
Bharat Menon — Head of Sales, Edison, New Jersey. Carries an importer pipeline he values at USD 4.1 million, is paid on bookings, and argues India will never pay software prices. Does not mention that four of his eleven named importers are already on a buyer's own portal, or that two conversations opened with a request for free data.
Sabina Qureshi — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Brought in Jawhara. Argues the deal de-risks the Series B with non-rupee revenue this year. Has not circulated the clause requiring support for two origin countries where Jalsetu has no operations.
Mihir Vaidya — Partner, Pushkal Growth Partners, Mumbai; board observer. Wrote the strategy condition, is agnostic about which segment Jalsetu picks, and will not fund a company that has not picked one. His fund's thesis note calls Jalsetu "the compliance layer for India's USD 8 billion seafood export corridor" — a framing that assumes the buyer-side product he has not been told is eighteen months away.

7. Voices

"We are not a compliance company. We are the system the plant runs on; compliance is one report it prints. Forget that, and Pratyaksh takes the plant floor with a free module while we sell reports to people who already have a vendor."Hardik Parmar, board pre-read, 16 October 2026

8. The options as Chaitali currently sees them

Option A: the plant operating system. Concentrate on the Indian plant, ship the roadmap Prawaal and the Kathiawar cluster want, and defend traceability as a bundled feature. It is fundable on today's evidence; Exhibit 2 says the plant floor is nearly half of ARR. It also accepts 41 per cent margins, a services-heavy business, and the proposition that what makes Jalsetu hard to replace is switching cost, not anything a buyer values. It leaves the 58 per cent alone, because no plant manager has ever asked.

Option B: the buyer-side network. Build query access, verified fields and risk scoring for importers, sell in Rotterdam and Charleston, and let the processor become the data source. The margins in Exhibit 6 are the best on the page and the demand the least ambiguous. It also needs eighteen months Jalsetu cannot obviously fund, a rewrite that collides with six on-premises contracts, and the consent of processors whose largest fear is precisely this transparency — including the one that is 19 per cent of revenue and cannot be repriced until 2031.

Option C: the Gulf re-export platform. Sign Jawhara, take the ₹9.4 crore, buy time.
