She has written all three on one page and keeps returning to the same objection: each answers "which customer should we serve?", and none answers the question Fathima keeps asking — whether Jalsetu's central claim, that a lot can be traced, is presently true. There is a fourth shape she cannot cost: spend a year making a narrow set of assertions genuinely verifiable, in one species and one state, at whatever revenue that implies, on the theory that a verified lot is the only thing a buyer, a regulator or an insurer would ever pay differently for. She has no exhibit for it. It is in none of the columns of Exhibit 6, and it is not what Mihir Vaidya's condition asks her to write.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Monday, 19 October, expecting the document the term sheet requires; exclusivity expires on 30 November. Jalsetu holds ₹14.2 crore and burns ₹1.3 crore a month, or eleven months. The Jawhara MoU lapses on 2 November. Prawaal's three-plant renewal falls due in March 2027 at a fee capped at 4 per cent until 2031, with escrow and an on-premises system-of-record clause any query layer must be negotiated around; six perpetual-licence customers have weaker versions. Any product recording identifiable farmer data falls under the DPDP Act, and Fathima reads the current declarations as insufficient for onward disclosure to a foreign buyer. And the season peaks between Diwali and European Lent demand, so every plant is at capacity for fourteen weeks and no one will accept a disruptive release before February.

10. Questions for discussion

1. What, precisely, is the problem Jalsetu faces? State it in one sentence someone could disagree with, and name the exhibits for and against it.

2. Exhibits 4 and 5 point in different directions about why customers value Jalsetu. How was each produced, which would you rely on, and what would settle it?

3. Exhibit 2 sets ARR against engineering effort; Exhibit 3 offers four retention numbers from one set of books. What does a director who reads only the pre-read believe, and where is that belief wrong?

4. Hardik's pre-read commits to being "the operating system for Indian seafood export." Is that a strategy, a goal, or a slogan? What must be added — and given up — for it to survive being tested twice?

5. The 2021 Prawaal terms bind Jalsetu until 2031. Which options does that contract foreclose, which does it merely make expensive, and what is the cheapest way to find out before the exclusivity lapses?

6. The fourth shape has no sponsor, no exhibit and no revenue line. What would make it a real option by Monday? And what, in six sentences, should she tell the board about the 58 per cent, about Jawhara, and about the segment Jalsetu will not serve?

At twenty past midnight Chaitali opened a blank document and typed one word: Diagnosis. Below it she wrote three candidate sentences and deleted each. The first said Jalsetu's problem was that it had been paid by the wrong side of the chain for five years. The second said what it sold as software was a service performed by eleven people in Surat and Kochi. The third said it had built a document, not a fact. She could argue any of the three, and had done so in different meetings that week. She thought about Girish Kotak's yield data and the 4 per cent cap; about the nine customers out of thirty-six; about the way Mihir Vaidya said the word "segment". Then she saved the file without a name, closed the laptop, and told the guard to switch off the lights. The board would convene in nine hours and forty minutes.

Strategy & Business · Product Strategy · Expert reading

The Kernel Under Load: What Diagnosis, Guiding Policy and Coherent Action Demand of a Product Leader

1. Two Decisions, Twelve Weeks Apart

On 14 September 2026, Devika Raghunathan, Chief Product Officer of Moolbandh Instruments, found the number she had been avoiding. Moolbandh made battery-powered cold-chain data loggers — the sealed devices that ride inside vaccine cartons — and sold a compliance dashboard alongside them. FY2026 revenue was ₹94 crore: ₹71 crore of hardware at 28 percent gross margin, ₹23 crore of software at 79 percent, across 340 enterprise accounts. Software renewal, blended, was 68 percent and falling, and a Shenzhen logger of adequate accuracy was landing in Chennai at ₹1,900 against Moolbandh's ₹4,200 list. Her head of sales wanted a price-match programme approved before the December tenders. The board had asked for a strategy; what she had was an eleven-slide deck whose operative verbs were strengthen, expand and leverage.

Twelve weeks earlier and 570 kilometres south, Nandita Iyer faced another version of the same emptiness. Nandita ran product at Ankurvat Learning, a Bengaluru company tutoring class 6 to 10 students in spoken English and mathematics in Hindi, Marathi, Telugu and Tamil. Ankurvat had 2.1 million monthly actives, 190,000 subscribers at ₹399 a month, 9.4 percent monthly churn, and a margin improving for a reason nobody there controlled: inference cost per paying user had fallen from ₹210 to ₹58 in eighteen months. In June her team had written a one-line strategy — "own vernacular AI tutoring in India" — and three workstreams: train a proprietary speech model, sign state-board publishers, rebuild onboarding. Each had a director, a budget and a plausible business case. None came from the same argument, and by October two were competing for the same eleven backend engineers.

Both were about to learn the same thing from opposite ends of the product spectrum: the difficulty in strategy is rarely a shortage of good ideas, but the absence of a structure that says which good ideas are, here, the wrong ones. Richard Rumelt's kernel is that structure, taken below past the definition: the formal treatment of coherence, the conditions under which it misleads, the seams where it fails, and the points on which serious readers still disagree.

2. The Idea and the Argument It Was Built to Settle

The definition is minimal. A strategy has a kernel of three parts. A diagnosis simplifies an overwhelming situation by identifying which aspect is critical — not a list of challenges but a bet on which one is load-bearing. A guiding policy is the approach chosen to overcome that obstacle; a channel rather than a plan, it works by making certain actions illegitimate. Coherent actions are coordinated resource commitments, coordinated meaning designed to support one another rather than merely to coexist in a budget.

The intellectual history explains what the kernel argues against. Rumelt's Strategy, Structure, and Economic Performance (1974) found that related diversifiers outperformed both single-business firms and conglomerates; his 1991 paper "How Much Does Industry Matter?" found business-unit effects explained several times more profitability variance than industry membership. What a firm chooses, and how its pieces fit, dominates where it stands — grounding for treating strategy as design rather than positioning. By 2011, when Good Strategy/Bad Strategy appeared, the planning apparatus descended from Ansoff had been demolished by Mintzberg's The Rise and Fall of Strategic Planning (1994): planning is analytic, strategy synthetic. Mintzberg cleared the ground and left a vacuum; the kernel is the positive answer, and its target is bad strategy — fluff, failure to face the problem, goals mistaken for strategy. The provocation is that these are not weak strategies but the absence of one.

The proposition each school would and would not sign is more useful than a summary of positions.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Positioning (Porter)Strategy requires trade-offs; activities that fit beat activities that coexist.That the primary act is diagnosis; it is choosing a position given industry structure.
Resource-based view (Barney, Teece)That firm-specific configuration drives returns.That one obstacle should organise allocation; a kernel tuned to this year's constraint starves next decade's capability.
Integrative choice (Lafley & Martin)That most strategy documents are goal sheets.That strategy begins with a problem; framing one anchors you to the present. The cascade reasons from possibilities.
Discovery-driven (McGrath, Blank)That resources must be committed, not merely allocated.That diagnosis precedes experiment. The constraint is an output of cheap tests.
Simple rules (Eisenhardt & Sull)That a guiding policy should rule things out.That tight coupling suits high-velocity markets, where the action set stays thin.
Table 1. The dispute is over sequence, tightness, and whether the constraint is knowable before you act.

3. Mechanics: Diagnosis as Constraint Identification, Coherence as Complementarity

Diagnosis is, operationally, identification of a binding constraint — the one whose shadow price is non-zero, so that relaxing it changes the outcome and relaxing others does not. Devika's deck offered three candidates: import price pressure, an under-resourced field team, weak software renewal. Ask of each: fixed tomorrow, what would the financials do?

Price pressure dies on arithmetic. The logger carries ₹3,024 of COGS against ₹4,200 list, so matching the imported ₹2,600 turns ₹1,176 of contribution into a ₹424 loss on each of roughly 169,000 annual units — ₹7.2 crore a year. Price is not a constraint Moolbandh can relax; it is a wall. Renewal behaves differently. Splitting the 340 accounts by whether the dashboard was wired into the customer's quality-management or ERP system separated them cleanly.

Account segmentAccountsShareRenewalSaaS ARR
Integrated (connector into customer QMS/ERP)9628%94%₹7.1 cr
Not integrated (CSV export only)24472%58%₹15.9 cr
Blended340100%68%₹23.0 cr
Table 2. Moolbandh Instruments, FY2026. Integration status is observable before renewal: a leading indicator, not a post-mortem.

The gap is not proof of causation — larger customers both integrate more and stay longer — but it survives the obvious control: under ₹15 lakh of annual spend it is still 29 points. Devika's diagnosis was therefore a causal claim with a mechanism: the product is replaceable because it is not wired into anything; the loggers are a commodity and the dashboard is a destination the customer must remember to visit. The guiding policy followed: buy position inside the customer's system of record, treating hardware margin as the budget for it rather than as profit to defend. Discounting removes that budget and re-frames Moolbandh as a device vendor exactly when it is trying to stop being one, which makes the price-match not merely expensive but incoherent.

The arithmetic is checkable. Moving integrated share from 28 to 70 percent gives blended renewal of 0.70 × 94 + 0.30 × 58 = 83.2 percent, a 15-point gain on ₹23 crore, or ₹3.45 crore of retained revenue a year. The cost is 142 integrations at eleven engineer-days each and ₹18,000 a day fully loaded: ₹2.84 crore, once. Under ten months of payback — provided they are productised into self-serve connectors rather than delivered as consulting, which would make the cost recur. That proviso is the difference between a guiding policy and a services business.

Coherence has a formal definition, and standalone business cases cannot see it

Milgrom and Roberts formalised coherence as complementarity: two activities are complements when more of one raises the marginal return to the other. Write the value of an action set as standalone values plus pairwise interactions. A portfolio review that scores each initiative alone reads only the diagonal of that matrix, and is structurally blind to every off-diagonal term.

Figure 1. A3, the hardware price-match, has the second-highest standalone value and is the most destructive element in the set.

Total the sets. All five yields 11.2 of standalone value plus a net −2.2 of interactions, or 9.0. A1, A2 and A4 alone yield 7.1 plus 5.4, or 12.5; adding A5 takes it to 12.1, adding A3 instead to 9.0. A smaller plan with 37 percent less standalone value is worth 39 percent more — the arithmetic statement of what a guiding policy does. It also exposes the mechanism producing bad strategy inside competent companies: a review approving initiatives one at a time cannot, even in principle, detect incoherence, because the quantity it measures does not contain it.

4. Conditions: When the Kernel Binds and When It Misleads

The kernel is not universal, and an expert states its conditions as claims that could be checked rather than as caveats.

Condition, as a testable claimMoolbandhAnkurvat
C1. One obstacle dominates: its shadow price is at least 2× the second's.Holds. Renewal gap ~₹3.4 cr/yr; field capacity ~₹1.1 cr.Marginal. Retention and unit cost within 1.4× — not yet sharp.
C2. The constraint is stable over the action horizon.Holds. Integration behaviour moves over years; actions land in three quarters.Fails for cost — inference prices fell 72% in eighteen months — and holds for retention.
C3. Actions interact: one pairwise term exceeds 25% of a standalone value.Holds; A1×A4 = 2.1 against A4's standalone 2.6.Holds. Onboarding and the mastery graph reinforce; the speech model does not.
C4. Commitment is required: resources cannot be cheaply redeployed.Holds. Connector engineering is specific and sunk.Partly. Training is sunk; content is portable.
Table 3. Where a condition fails, the kernel narrows to a sub-problem.

Where the kernel actively misleads matters, because its popularity has made "what is your diagnosis?" a reflex that sometimes destroys value. When no constraint binds — abundant capital, no live threat, demand you cannot serve — forcing a diagnosis manufactures an obstacle, and that invention then organises real spending. When the environment moves faster than the action horizon, C2 fails and a coherent set becomes a correlated bet: Ankurvat's speech model was rational against ₹210 of inference cost and irrational by the time it would have shipped against ₹58. Where the situation is genuinely novel, diagnosis-first produces a confident fiction. In all three the honest expert says the kernel does not yet apply, and names what must change first.

5. Hard Edges: Portfolios, Two Sides, Regulators, Metal and Models

Multi-product firms are the first hard edge. A company with four lines cannot have one diagnosis unless the lines share a constraint; writing a single kernel and cascading it either forces a false commonality or produces a corporate policy so abstract it forbids nothing. The correct structure is nested: the corporate guiding policy becomes the diagnosis input one level down, and each unit writes its own kernel inside that channel. Rumelt's term for the nearer targets this produces is proximate objectives, chosen because achieving them removes the obstacle above.

Figure 2. Nesting works when each unit's diagnosis follows from the level above. The sharpest seam is compensation: a policy contradicted by a commission plan loses.

Two-sided businesses break the singular diagnosis differently: supply and demand constraints rarely bind at once, so one diagnosis starves a side. The competent handling carries an explicit sequence claim — which side binds first, what evidence shows it has stopped binding, what the policy becomes afterwards. Regulated products distort differently: compliance arrives as mandatory action derived from no guiding policy, so the action set carries a floor of work nobody chose. Experts separate the discretionary budget from the licence-to-operate budget, rather than letting compliance quietly consume the strategy while the roadmap is still called strategic.

Hardware-plus-software firms face a tempo problem: the hardware policy is locked by tooling and lead times eighteen months out while the software policy turns in a quarter, so a kernel written at one horizon is wrong for the other. AI-native products break a different assumption — that the firm controls the mechanism its advantage rests on. At Bijakosh Labs, a Pune company selling document extraction to insurers, two successive diagnoses ("extraction accuracy is the obstacle") were invalidated within a year by general model improvements Bijakosh neither caused nor paid for. Hence the expert requirement that a diagnosis name an obstacle whose removal is attributable: if a rising tide removes it for everyone, it was never your strategy.

How mature companies handle this, as distinct from how they describe it, is worth saying bluntly. Most large firms run an annual process that produces goals, plus a few genuine kernels living in three or four executives' heads and enforced through resource allocation and hiring rather than documents. The published strategy is a coalition artefact; the operating strategy is what survives the budget meeting, and an experienced product leader treats the discrepancy as data.

6. Eight Distinctions That Separate Command from Competence

A diagnosis is a causal claim, not a difficulty rating. Competent practitioners list challenges and rank them by pain; experts write a mechanism — this happens because that — with a measurable on each side. The tell is that the diagnosis can be wrong: they can name the observation that would refute it. Deep understanding produces long descriptions; a diagnosis is deliberate simplification.

A guiding policy is priced by what it forbids. Ask what it rules out and watch whether the answer names something wanted. Experts name an attractive option with regret rather than contempt — price-matching would have won Devika two December tenders worth ₹6 crore. Someone who can only cite bad options as the things rejected has written a policy that forbids nothing.

Coherence lives off-diagonal and is therefore invisible to good governance. A competent reviewer asks what an initiative returns; an expert asks what it makes easier and what it makes harder. This implicates rigorous processes, not sloppy ones: a stage-gate committee judging each project alone assembles an incoherent portfolio of excellent initiatives faster than a sloppy committee would.

Diagnosis belongs at the altitude where the obstacle is removable. Told the obstacle is the Chinese cost base, experts downshift and ask what nearer thing, removable in three quarters with resources actually available, would change the trajectory. The tell is a diagnosis a named team could start on next month. A truer diagnosis nobody can act against is a description of the world.

Diagnosis is adversarial before it is analytical. The useful test is not "is this true?" but "which competitor is most damaged if we are right and act on it?" A diagnosis every rival has reached buys parity, not advantage: the whole Indian cold-chain industry knew about cheap imported loggers. Non-obvious diagnoses are uncomfortable by construction, and comfort is the warning sign.

A guiding policy with no cost of being wrong is decoration. Experts state the falsifier and its date unprompted: Devika's was 45 connector activations by 31 March 2027. Coherence also has a shelf life, so the falsifier doubles as a re-diagnosis trigger tied to a metric rather than a calendar. Without one a policy cannot lose, and what cannot lose is not a choice.

The kernel is a test, not a generator. You cannot deduce a diagnosis from data; you invent candidates and then kill them. Experts separate the two activities visibly, running a session whose only purpose is four rival diagnoses before evidence enters the room. The tell is that they have discarded diagnoses they liked. Treated as a template, the kernel yields three headings and no strategy.

Bad strategy is usually a political equilibrium, not a cognitive failure. Naming one obstacle names one group as the constraint and names the initiatives that will not be funded; fluff persists because it is the only text a coalition can sign. The tell is that an expert treats a kernel as a sequenced negotiation, securing the diagnosis privately with the executives who lose most before it reaches a slide. The uncomfortable evidence: after fifteen years of near-universal teaching, strategy documents have improved in vocabulary far more than in content.

7. What Actually Differs by Product Type and Stage

What changes across product types is which of the three elements is hard, and that difference is real. In consumer products the hard part is diagnosis, because behaviour is the constraint and behaviour is opaque: Ankurvat could measure churn precisely and could not say why. In B2B the diagnosis is easier — customers will tell you at length what blocks them — and coherence is harder, because the action set spans product, field sales, services and pricing, four functions with four incentive systems. In platforms the diagnosis must carry a sequence, and a policy serving one side is often a tax on the other. In hardware the binding element is commitment: coherent action means tooling, inventory and shelf space, so incoherence is paid in written-off capital rather than wasted quarters — which is why such firms are often better at the kernel than software companies and worse at revising it.

AI products differ in one way and are otherwise unexceptional: the attribution problem, exogenous capability improvement fast enough that an obstacle can dissolve without your involvement. Everything else claimed as distinctive — faster iteration, harder evaluation — is a difference of degree.

Stage moves the centre of gravity. At seed the kernel collapses into diagnosis alone, since one real action is available and coherence is satisfied by nine people who eat lunch together. Between Series A and C the guiding policy becomes the hard part, because the company can afford several things and must choose; this is where most product strategy teaching lands and where Moolbandh sits. At scale the hard part is coherence across seams: the honest description of a large firm's problem is that the diagnosis has been known for two years and the organisation cannot hold a policy against its own compensation plan.

8. Three Worked Cases, One of Them a Failure

Vatvriksh Payments: a sequenced diagnosis on two sides

Vatvriksh Payments, a Jaipur merchant acquirer, put QR collection and a ₹2,000-a-year working-capital product into kirana stores. In FY25 it had 84,000 merchants and 61 percent 90-day retention, read as a merchant-quality problem. The sharper reading split by consumer-side density: where more than 18 percent of a pincode's transactions already ran through Vatvriksh QR codes, merchant retention was 88 percent; below that, 44 percent. The diagnosis became a sequence claim — consumer density binds first, merchant experience second — and the policy was to stop selling merchants nationally and saturate 40 pincodes. Merchant additions fell 63 percent for two quarters; 90-day retention rose to 79 percent; net revenue per merchant rose from ₹1,340 to ₹2,210, because the credit product underwrites well only on dense transaction history. The unforecast second-order effect: a commission plan still paying per activation resisted for five months until rewritten.

Jadmool Retail Cloud: a coherent kernel on a false diagnosis

Jadmool sold store-operations software to apparel chains. In 2024 net revenue retention slipped from 108 to 96 percent and leadership diagnosed an adoption problem: only 41 percent of store managers opened the app weekly. The policy was to make adoption structural rather than voluntary, and the actions were genuinely coherent — a head-office compliance dashboard, gamified streaks, task completion wired into the manager's appraisal, an offline-first rewrite for basement stockrooms. Each made the others more effective. Weekly adoption went from 41 to 88 percent in nine months.

Net revenue retention fell to 91 percent. Coherence had faithfully amplified a wrong diagnosis. The real obstacle, found in loss interviews across eleven churned chains, was that Jadmool improved task completion — a quantity regional heads were not evaluated on. They were evaluated on shrinkage and end-of-season markdown. Higher adoption moved neither number the buyer was paid on, so renewal got harder as adoption rose. An improving operational metric beside a deteriorating commercial one is the signature of a coherent plan attached to the wrong constraint — and coherence makes it worse, because a coherent plan executes fast.

Recovery took fourteen months and ₹9 crore. The re-diagnosis: Jadmool had built a compliance tool for a buyer with a margin problem. The new policy — instrument the two numbers the buyer is paid on, then earn the right to task management — forced abandonment of the gamification investment and a rebuild of the analytics layer around markdown attribution. Retention recovered to 104 percent by FY26. The executive who led both made the point worth carrying: nothing in the first violated Rumelt's test. It passed. It was false.

Kandmool Foods: where commitment changes the test

Kandmool Foods, a Coimbatore millet-snack maker, diagnosed in 2025 that its constraint was shelf velocity, not demand — 2.3 units per store weekly against a category norm of 6.1, so distributors deprioritised it. The policy cut the range from 22 SKUs to 6 and concentrated trade spend in 4,000 modern-trade outlets; velocity reached 5.4 in three quarters and reorders rose 71 percent. What coherence cost is the instructive detail: ₹3.1 crore of packaging tooling for the 16 discontinued SKUs written off, two the founder's originals. In physical goods the coherent-action test bites against sunk capital, so its discipline is felt as destruction rather than prioritisation — the reason such firms revise strategy late.

9. Failure Modes, Their Early Warnings and the Cost of Catching Them Late

Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late

Table 4. Each question is answerable in a meeting, and built so that hesitation, not a wrong answer, is the signal.

Two survive training. The stale kernel persists because reopening a diagnosis reopens the allocation that followed it, and everyone who won the last round wants the question closed. The incentive contradiction persists because product leaders do not own compensation, so a strategic obstacle sits in a function they can only influence. In both cases the expert response is not analytical: it is to secure sponsorship before writing the kernel rather than after.

10. Where Serious People Still Disagree

Does diagnosis come first, or does choice? Rumelt's strongest form: every strategy already contains an implicit diagnosis, so refusing to state it means adopting one unexamined, and stating it is what kills fluff. Roger Martin's counter: problem-framing binds you to the present. At P&G the choices that built Olay came not from diagnosing a defect in the existing line but from imagining a mass-prestige possibility and asking what would have to be true for it to work. Rumelt rests on the poverty of goal-based documents, Martin on cases where the winning move was invisible from the current obstacle. Rumelt is wrong if the dominant constraint is usually unknowable ex ante; Martin is wrong if possibility-based reasoning, in ordinary hands, reliably produces attractive fictions.

Is coherence a virtue or a concentration of risk? Rumelt holds that complementarity is the only source of returns that cannot be copied piecemeal, and his 1974 finding on related-constrained diversifiers is evidence for it. Rita McGrath's counter is that a tightly coupled action set is one correlated bet, and that under genuine uncertainty the right structure is a portfolio of low-correlation options converted to commitment as uncertainty resolves. The disagreement turns on environmental variance and nobody has a usable threshold. Coherence is wrong wherever the probability the diagnosis is false exceeds the ratio of the coherence premium to the total downside — a calculation everyone gestures at and nobody performs.

Does the kernel belong below the firm at all? One camp holds that product strategy is a category error — firms have strategies, products have plans — and that applying the kernel at team level yields four hundred micro-strategies pulling apart. The other holds that a team allocating irreversible engineering capacity against a real constraint is doing strategy whatever it is called. The defensible position is conditional: the kernel belongs at whatever altitude has both a real constraint and real discretion over resources — in most companies, fewer levels than the number of teams writing strategy documents.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has studied the kernel produces documents with three correct headings. Someone who has internalised it differs in four observable ways. They spend a disproportionate share of their time on diagnosis and treat it as generative work — rival candidates, then attacks on them — not as a summary written after the plan exists. They evaluate initiatives in pairs, and their standard review question concerns interaction, not return. They can state without notes the attractive option their policy forbids and what it was worth — the fastest test of whether a strategy exists. And they carry a live falsifier: a number and a date at which they have agreed to reopen the question. A subtler fifth marker: they treat the political work as part of the craft, because a diagnosis that cannot survive its own organisation is an essay.

12. The Decisions, and Three Questions

Devika took the argument to Moolbandh's board on 28 November 2026 and asked for the price-match programme to be rejected rather than deferred, because it would consume the ₹2.84 crore the connectors required while confirming to buyers that Moolbandh sold metal. She funded A1, A2 and A4, declined A3 and A5, and attached the falsifier: 45 connector activations by 31 March 2027 or the policy reverts. The hardest part of the meeting was not the analysis but the two December tenders, worth ₹6 crore, that the decision gave away — correctly the hardest part, since a policy that gives up nothing is not one.

Nandita concluded differently. She declined to write a kernel at all, because C1 failed: her two candidate constraints were too close in magnitude to justify one dominant diagnosis. Instead she ran an eight-week programme whose sole objective was separating them, using a cohort split she already had: learners completing six or more graded diagnostics in their first fortnight retained at 52 percent to day 30, against 24 percent for the rest. If that gap held under a controlled onboarding change, retention was the constraint, accumulation the mechanism, and the speech model a distraction the falling cost curve had already made irrelevant. Declining to write a kernel until the diagnosis sharpens is not a failure to have a strategy; it is the same discipline, exercised earlier.

1. Jadmool's first kernel passed every element of Rumelt's test and was false. If the test cannot separate a good strategy from a coherent mistake, what work is it doing, and what would you add without rebuilding a planning process?

2. Devika's policy is contradicted by a commission plan she does not control. Is a policy unenforceable through incentives a strategy, a proposal, or a diagnosis of a different obstacle?

3. When does deferring the kernel, as Nandita did, become an excuse rather than a discipline — and what would you require her to commit to on the day she defers?

13. Going Deeper

  1. What strategy is and isn't — the ground the kernel stands on.
  2. The product strategy document — the artefact carrying a kernel into an organisation.
  3. Playing to Win — the strongest live alternative to diagnosis-first.
  4. Strategic themes and outcome-based prioritisation — one policy, many teams.
  5. Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later — where coherence survives sequencing, or dies.
  6. Focus and sequencing — what is abandoned, and in what order.
  7. Strategic bets and reversibility — coherence and optionality at once.
  8. Risks and assumptions in strategy — building the falsifier in.
  9. From strategy to team goals — nesting, and the compensation seam.
  10. Wardley mapping — a disciplined generator of diagnosis candidates.
  11. Disruption theory — recurring diagnoses competitors misread.
  12. Product-market fit — where diagnosis is the whole kernel.
  13. Technology trend analysis — will the obstacle dissolve without you?
  14. AI as a strategy, not a feature — diagnosing an exogenous mechanism of advantage.
  15. Holding a contrarian product thesis — a shared diagnosis yields no advantage.
  16. Strategy narrative and memo — getting a diagnosis accepted by those it names.
  17. Strategy when you are the founder — when the author owns the sunk costs condemned.
  18. B2B vs B2C strategy — where diagnosis is hard versus where coherence is hard.

Rumelt's Kernel: What Separates a Strategy from a Wish

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Rhea Kapoor sat in a Bhopal conference room with a slide titled "Pavanpath 2027: Path to Category Leadership." She was VP of Product at Pavanpath Mobility, an electric two-wheeler ride-hailing service that had raised ₹180 crore in its Series B eleven months earlier and was burning roughly ₹6 crore a month across Indore, Bhopal, Nagpur and Surat. The board wanted a decision by month-end: launch in twelve more tier-2 towns, as the original pitch deck promised investors, or hold the line in the four cities Pavanpath already served. Her slide had three bullets — "expand footprint," "deepen driver network," "improve unit economics" — and every board member in the room had, at some point, said all three sentences out loud with approval. None of them told Rhea what to actually do on Monday morning. That gap, between a set of admirable intentions and an actual plan of action, is precisely what Richard Rumelt's kernel is built to close, and it is why Rhea's next draft looked nothing like her first.

The Idea

Richard Rumelt, a strategy scholar at UCLA who had spent three decades consulting to companies from Intel to the U.S. Department of Defense, published Good Strategy/Bad Strategy in 2011 to name a problem he had watched repeat for years: executives were producing documents that used the word "strategy" to describe goals, values, and financial targets, with no actual strategy inside them. His fix was a minimal, testable definition. A strategy, Rumelt argued, has a kernel — a logical core — made of exactly three parts: a diagnosis that names the single most important obstacle standing in the way, a guiding policy that states the overall approach chosen to deal with that obstacle, and a set of coherent actions — resource commitments and specific steps, coordinated with each other — that carry the guiding policy out. Strip any one of the three away and what remains is not a weaker strategy; it is not a strategy at all. The sentence Rhea could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: a real strategy diagnoses the obstacle, chooses one way of overcoming it, and backs that choice with actions that reinforce rather than contradict one another.

Figure 1. The kernel is not a template to fill in — each part is a load-bearing claim the other two depend on.

How It Actually Works

The mechanics begin with a discipline most teams skip: separating the diagnosis from the goal. A goal — "become the leading mobility platform in central India" — describes a destination. A diagnosis describes why the destination is hard to reach right now, stated as a specific, falsifiable claim about the world: which constraint binds, which force is working against you, which piece of the situation, if left unaddressed, will defeat any plan. Rumelt's insight was that most obstacles are compound and messy, and the diagnostic work is to simplify that mess into one dominant challenge without pretending the mess wasn't there — his phrase for this was that a good diagnosis "defines a challenge," it does not simply list symptoms.

Once the obstacle is named, the guiding policy answers a narrower question: given this obstacle, what is our overall approach? A guiding policy is not itself a plan — it is closer to a channel that action must flow through. It works by ruling things out: a real guiding policy makes some obvious, tempting moves illegitimate. If Pavanpath's diagnosis is that unsubsidized driver supply cannot reach viable density in more than a handful of cities at once, a guiding policy of "concentrate density before expanding" rules out launching in twelve towns simultaneously, no matter how attractive each one looks in isolation. The step practitioners most often skip here is stress-testing the guiding policy against an alternative diagnosis — asking, if the obstacle were actually something else, would this same policy still make sense, or did we just back into our preferred answer and call it a diagnosis afterward.

The coherent actions are where most strategy documents quietly turn into wish lists again. Coherence is a specific, checkable property: each action should make the others more effective, and removing any single one should visibly weaken the rest. A pile of initiatives that are each individually sensible but were not derived from the same guiding policy is not a strategy — it is a budget.

A Worked Example

Rhea's team pulled the actual numbers. Across the four live cities, Pavanpath ran 40,000 rides a day at an average fare of ₹42. In the two newer cities, Nagpur and Surat, the cost of serving each ride — driver payout, EV charging-swap fees, and a ₹9 per-ride bootstrap incentive paid to keep drivers online during low-demand hours — came to ₹47, a loss of ₹5 per ride. Those two cities alone generated 14,000 of the 40,000 daily rides, so the bootstrap subsidy was costing Pavanpath roughly ₹5 × 14,000 = ₹70,000 a day, or about ₹21 lakh a month, just to hold supply together in markets that had not yet reached self-sustaining driver density.

Indore15,0001,6509.1No
Bhopal11,0001,5107.3No

Surat6,00051011.8Yes, ₹9/ride

The diagnosis that fell out of this table was not "we are underfunded" or "competition is fierce" — both true but too vague to act on. It was sharper: driver density above roughly 1,500 active drivers per city let supply self-regulate without cash incentives, and Pavanpath had reached that threshold only in Indore and Bhopal. The guiding policy Rhea proposed was to treat driver density, not city count, as the resource to allocate: pause the twelve planned launches, and only greenlight a new city once its driver waitlist passed 2,000 names — a proxy that could be verified before spending a rupee. The coherent actions followed directly: redirect the ₹21 lakh monthly subsidy plus an additional ₹1.5 crore of planned launch marketing into referral bonuses inside the two dense cities, renegotiate the charging-swap contract from per-swap pricing to a volume rate now that Indore and Bhopal justified the minimum commitment, and instruct the city-launch team to build a waitlist product for four candidate towns without spending on driver acquisition until the 2,000-name threshold showed real pull.

The second pass tested how much of this depended on the assumption that ₹180 crore of runway was available. If the funding environment tightened and only ₹80 crore remained on the balance sheet — a real possibility the board was discussing that same quarter — the diagnosis itself changed. The binding obstacle was no longer driver density; it was runway measured in months at current burn, which fell from roughly 30 months to about 13. A guiding policy built for a density problem does not automatically survive a runway problem: the coherent actions under the tighter scenario would need to include cutting the referral-bonus reallocation itself, since it still spent cash, in favour of raising Indore and Bhopal fares by a testable 8 percent to see whether demand held. The arithmetic did not just get smaller — the correct guiding policy changed, which is the entire point of doing the diagnosis explicitly rather than assuming last quarter's approach still applies.

Nuances a Learner Must Sit With

Diagnosis is not the same sentence as ambition.

"We must become more competitive" describes a wish, not an obstacle. A diagnosis names a specific mechanism — a threshold not yet crossed, a force actively working against you — that a reader could, in principle, prove wrong.

A guiding policy is not a plan, and testing it as one misses the point.

Its job is to make certain actions obviously wrong, not to specify every step. If a guiding policy could justify almost any initiative a team wanted to run anyway, it was never doing the ruling-out work a real policy does.

The kernel cannot tell you whether your goal is worth pursuing.

It only tests whether your approach to a stated obstacle is coherent. Pavanpath could build a perfectly coherent kernel around a category-leadership goal that was itself a poor use of investor capital; the kernel is silent on that question by design.

Coherence is falsifiable, and that is what makes it useful.

Ask of any action list: if we deleted this one line, would the others get weaker? If the answer is no, that line was never part of the strategy — it was added because someone wanted it funded.

The kernel presumes a genuine obstacle exists.

When no real constraint binds — a monopoly facing no competitive threat, say — forcing a kernel produces an invented obstacle dressed up in the vocabulary, which is worse than admitting no strategic choice is currently required.

Kernels nest.

A company-level guiding policy becomes the diagnosis one level down for a business unit, which is why Rumelt calls the intermediate targets this produces "proximate objectives" — close enough to be achievable, chosen because hitting them removes the obstacle above.

The kernel is a logic test, not a truth detector.

A beautifully coherent kernel built on a wrong diagnosis is still wrong. Judgment and evidence must supply the diagnosis; the kernel only checks what follows from it.

Consumer, B2B, Marketplace — and Scale

The three parts of the kernel stay fixed, but what typically binds differs by business type. In a consumer product like Pavanpath, the obstacle is usually behavioural or structural — a density threshold, a habit not yet formed, a switching cost not yet built. At Samirna Freight Technologies, a Pune-based B2B logistics software firm selling to manufacturing plants, the obstacle Rhea's counterpart there diagnosed was procurement friction: an eleven-month average sales cycle caused by plant-level buyers needing corporate IT sign-off, not product quality. Their guiding policy — sell first to plants where a pilot could run on existing infrastructure without IT approval — looked nothing like a density policy, though the underlying kernel logic was identical. In a two-sided marketplace such as Meghavaran Bazaar, an agricultural produce marketplace connecting mandi traders to retailers, the diagnosis frequently has to be split in two, since supply-side and demand-side obstacles rarely coincide; the guiding policy then has to specify a sequence — which side gets seeded first — because a single undifferentiated policy usually starves one side while serving the other. Company stage matters as much as business type. An early-stage team's kernel is typically built around a single survival-defining obstacle, and the coherent-action problem is small because few people can contradict each other. A large, multi-business organisation's hardest work is rarely diagnosis at all — it is coherence, because divisions with their own incentives will happily fund actions that quietly undercut a guiding policy set two floors above them.

Common Mistakes

The wish-list diagnosis. Symptom: a strategy document whose "diagnosis" section is a list of good outcomes — "improve retention, launch new markets, raise NPS." Underlying error: goals have been relabelled as obstacles. Cheapest diagnostic: ask what specifically breaks if we do nothing; if the answer is vague, the diagnosis has not actually been done.

The generic guiding policy. Symptom: a policy statement — "focus on quality" or "put the customer first" — that could be pasted unchanged into a rival's deck. Underlying error: the policy names a virtue instead of ruling anything out. Cheapest diagnostic: ask what a good, tempting idea this policy forces you to reject; if nothing comes to mind, the policy is decorative.

The incoherent action pile. Symptom: initiatives from different teams that visibly work against each other — marketing increasing city launches while finance freezes the same cities' budgets. Underlying error: actions were approved independently rather than derived from one guiding policy. Cheapest diagnostic: ask each team lead which guiding policy their initiative serves, in one sentence; hesitation reveals the gap.

The kernel treated as an annual ritual. Symptom: a kernel written in January that nobody revisits even after the facts underneath it change materially by June. Underlying error: mistaking the document for the discipline. Cheapest diagnostic: ask when the diagnosis was last re-tested against current numbers, not when the slide was last edited.

What Good Looks Like

Rhea's second draft, the one she actually brought to the board, fit on a single page and read nothing like the first. The diagnosis stated, with the driver-density table attached, that Pavanpath's binding constraint was reaching self-sustaining supply density before cash-subsidised growth became unaffordable at scale, and that only two of four cities had crossed that line. The guiding policy stated plainly that city count would be sacrificed to city depth until the waitlist threshold was met, and named the twelve-city expansion, as originally pitched to investors, as the specific plan being abandoned — not softened, abandoned. The coherent actions were four in number, each traceable back to the density argument, each with a named owner and a rupee figure, and each one made harder to justify if any other were removed. No bullet used the words "leading," "innovative," or "best-in-class." A board member who had approved the first draft without much comment spent twenty minutes with the second one arguing about the 2,000-name threshold — which was, Rhea later said, the first real strategy conversation Pavanpath's board had had in a year, because for the first time there was something concrete enough to disagree with.

Closing

The board approved the density-first guiding policy on a split vote, with two directors asking for the runway-tightening scenario to be reviewed again in ninety days — itself a sign the kernel had done its job, since a document with a genuine diagnosis invites genuine argument about facts rather than polite agreement with aspiration. Rhea's own reasoning, recorded in her notes afterward, was simple: she would rather defend one falsifiable bet in front of her board than a dozen plausible-sounding intentions that could not tell her, or them, what to do differently on Monday. The next topic worth studying from here is how a chosen guiding policy gets translated into strategic themes and outcome-based priorities across a roadmap — because a kernel that stops at "coherent actions" on a single page still has to survive contact with a quarterly planning cycle. Two questions worth sitting with: when you last wrote a strategy document, could you point to the one sentence that was your diagnosis, distinct from your goal — and if a colleague deleted one action from your current plan, would anything else in it actually get weaker?

Ekatra Solar Cloud: The Wedge That Was Legislated Away

Thiruvananthapuram, Sunday 27 September 2026 — a vice-president of product must hand a board an eighteen-month roadmap, on evidence that may measure the wrong thing.

1. The night before

The Technopark campus at Kazhakkoottam was dark except for the fourth floor of Ekatra Solar Cloud's building, where Uthara Menon had switched the air-conditioning off and slid the balcony door open to the late September rain. On Friday, 2 October, Ekatra's board would approve an eighteen-month product roadmap, and Balachandran Nair, the co-founder and chief executive everyone called Bala, had been explicit: one roadmap, one story, one number the bridge investors could underwrite. Not three options with footnotes.

Three documents lay on the desk. A retention analysis from Jerome Fernandes, Ekatra's data scientist in Toronto, sent at 3 a.m. Indian time with a covering note that read only: read exhibit 4 before exhibit 1, or you will draw the wrong conclusion. An unsigned white-label licence from Nafahaat Energy Trading LLC of Abu Dhabi, worth ₹9.5 crore over three years, expiring 9 October. And two lines from the operations director at Nishkam Rooftop Energy, the anchor customer, asking whether Ekatra would quote for a January renewal, and whether the quote would reflect “the reduced scope of the compliance module.”

Ekatra had ₹19.4 crore in the bank and was burning ₹1.7 crore a month: eleven months, for 78 people across four countries, in a company that grew 140 per cent in the year to March 2025 and 21 per cent in the year to March 2026. Uthara had spent the week on a question she had assumed was settled: did Ekatra have fit, and if so, in what?

2. Company history, and one decision that still binds

Ekatra was founded in 2019 by Bala Nair, who had spent nine years running delivery for a Kerala rooftop engineering-procurement-construction contractor, and Devyani Kulkarni, a Pune engineer who had built field dispatch software. Their observation was mundane and correct: a 25-kilowatt rooftop installation took eleven to nineteen weeks from order to commissioning, and less than a fifth of that was construction. The rest was paper: surveys, ALMM eligibility checks, a subsidy application, a net-metering application, feasibility approval, inspection, meter change, commissioning certificate. And every utility — KSEB, TANGEDCO, MSEDCL, BESCOM — wanted the same facts in a different order on a different form.

Ekatra's first product was a survey app and a paperwork engine: a technician photographed a roof, captured tilt and shading, and the platform returned a bill of materials, a generation estimate and a filled application pack for that state. By 2022 it had 210 paying installers and a reputation for one thing. It made the paperwork go away.

That year came the decision that shaped everything since. Rather than a generic workflow engine with regional configuration, Devyani's team rewrote the platform around a single project object whose fields were the union of every Indian utility form Ekatra had met: sanctioned load, phase, consumer number, subsidy category, DISCOM circle, inspection slot. It was a bet that Indian paperwork was the moat, and for four years it was. It also means the engine cannot be separated from Indian regulatory semantics without roughly eight months of platform work — an estimate Devyani has twice revised upward and Uthara privately doubts.

In March 2023 came the decision that binds hardest. Nishkam Rooftop Energy, a Chennai developer then building 60 MW a year, moved its execution stack to Ekatra and co-developed the operations-and-maintenance monitoring module, committing ₹6 crore over three years — transformational money then — for two clauses. Until 31 March 2027 Ekatra may not licence that module to any Indian installer or developer commissioning more than 25 MW a year, and Nishkam's generation data may not appear in any benchmark. Bala signed both in a week; Uthara, who joined in 2024, has read them forty times.

3. The industry

India's rooftop market changed shape in February 2024, when the Government of India launched PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, with a central subsidy of up to ₹78,000 for residential systems and a national portal routing applications, vendor registration and disbursement. Residential rooftop became a volume business: thousands of small installers registered, and district electrical contractors began selling 3-kilowatt systems off a subsidy leaflet. Supply was not the constraint — Waaree Energies, Premier Energies, Tata Power Solar and Adani Solar had more capacity arriving than the market could absorb, and inverter brands from Luminous to Enphase competed hard on installer margin. The constraint was execution.

Above that sat a different market. In commercial-and-industrial rooftop, developers such as CleanMax, Fourth Partner Energy, Amplus and ReNew own the asset and sell power to a factory under a long-term agreement. They care little about residential subsidy paperwork, for which they are ineligible, and greatly about generation, availability and DISCOM reconciliation under state net-metering rules. Between the two sat Ekatra's competition: Naipunya Power Software, a well-funded Bengaluru installer CRM; the in-house modules larger developers build; and spreadsheets and WhatsApp, still running most Indian rooftop projects.

Two forces now bore on the product. The national portal was maturing, absorbing functions Ekatra charged for: standardised vendor registration, auto-populated consumer details and, from January 2026 in eleven states, a linked utility application flow that removed most re-keying. And the Gulf was opening: the UAE and Oman were expanding distributed solar under net-metering programmes with no subsidy layer and utility interfaces nothing like a KSEB form. Nafahaat Energy Trading LLC, an Abu Dhabi distributor with an installation arm and a joint venture with Nasaq Contracting LLC, wanted Ekatra's field, scheduling and monitoring product white-labelled in Arabic and English, one emirate live by April 2027. Their proposition was simple and awkward: they wanted everything except the moat.

4. The situation in detail

Through 2024 and early 2025 every internal number said Ekatra had found its market: installer accounts rose from 260 to 1,140 and per-project fee income tripled. In March 2025 Bala called Ekatra “the operating system of Indian rooftop,” and the board took engineering from 19 to 41 people.

The first crack appeared in the cohort data late in 2025: twelve-month logo retention for installers acquired in FY2025 was 56 per cent (Exhibit 1). Hui Min Goh, customer-success lead in Singapore, insisted it was misread. Tracing churned accounts, her team found 58 per cent had not switched to a competitor but had stopped installing solar, or gone quiet after a proprietor's GST registration lapsed. On that reading the churn was the market's mortality rate, not a product failure — which Jerome could neither confirm nor refute, since a reason was recorded in only 44 per cent of cases.

The second crack was slower and, Uthara had come to think, worse. From January 2026 the portal's linked application flow went live in eleven states. Ekatra's instrumentation (Exhibit 4) shows median time in the subsidy module falling from 5 hours 50 minutes per project in January 2025 to 44 minutes in August 2026, and projects skipping it entirely rising from 4 to 38 per cent. Installers were still paying, and no longer using what they had bought Ekatra for.

In June 2026 a third crack opened from the other side. Eshanya Renewables, one of the five largest C&I accounts, was absorbed into a larger platform and signalled that its January 2027 renewal would probably not proceed, the acquirer having its own stack. A fortnight later Nirdesh Energy Projects, a Rajkot developer, renewed at a 9 per cent uplift, telling Vikrant Sabharwal, sales head in New Jersey, that switching would cost a year of project history and was never seriously considered. Both facts reached the monthly report under one heading: “C&I retention: 91 per cent.” The ten largest accounts carry 47 per cent of revenue, nearly all renewing in the first quarter of 2027 (Exhibit 5).

In August, at Uthara's request, Lena Brandt in Berlin fielded a Sean Ellis-style survey (Exhibit 2). The headline was excellent: 52 per cent of installer respondents would be very disappointed to lose Ekatra, above the 40 per cent usually read as evidence of fit. Jerome raised two things. It was fielded in-app to accounts active in the previous thirty days, excluding 71 per cent of paying accounts. And the most cited reason for the disappointment was the subsidy paperwork — the module Exhibit 4 shows emptying out.

5. The people

Uthara Menon — Vice-President, Product; Thiruvananthapuram
Joined in 2024 from field-services software. Holds that Ekatra must name the job it is best in India at before choosing a segment, and cannot yet name it in one sentence.
Not saying: she now believes the 2022 data-model decision, which she has publicly defended, is the binding constraint — and suspects eight months is nearer four.
Balachandran Nair — Co-founder and CEO; Thiruvananthapuram
The installer base is the asset and PM Surya Ghar a decade-long tailwind: widen Ekatra into the installer's whole business. He must price a bridge in November on the FY2025 curve.
Not saying: two funds have declined to lead, citing revenue quality, and he has taken an exploratory call about an acquisition.
Devyani Kulkarni — Co-founder and CTO; Pune
No international work before March 2027; the platform carries four years of India-specific debt. She is measured on the Indian roadmap and a reliability target missed twice.
Not saying: two of her three senior backend engineers would leave rather than spend a year on “form plumbing.” The eight months protect them too.
Hui Min Goh — Customer Success Lead; Singapore
Installer churn is business mortality, not dissatisfaction, and Exhibit 1 is being used to abandon a segment that loves the product. Her team of nine exists for that segment.
Not saying: her model gives an installer paying ₹1.24 lakh a year some forty minutes of attention a quarter, so she cannot know why most go quiet.
Jerome Fernandes — Data Scientist; Toronto
No fit measure in use is clean: retention is contaminated by account mortality, the survey by sampling, net revenue retention by a fee boom. Wants a quarter to instrument properly.
Not saying: he ran the mortality test against public registry data, found it ambiguous, and will not hand Bala a number he cannot defend.
Vikrant Sabharwal — Head of Sales; New Jersey
Take the Nafahaat licence: cash, a second geography, proof the product travels. His FY2027 quota already assumes ₹3.1 crore of Gulf revenue.
Not saying: Nasaq Contracting LLC wants source-code escrow and a buy-out option after year three, a clause he has not circulated.
Thomas Kurien — Head of Implementation; Thiruvananthapuram
The only durable thing Ekatra owns is commissioning throughput, survey to meter. Paperwork was one obstacle; there are five others and nobody has built for them.
Not saying: his team quietly files utility applications by hand where the portal flow is unreliable — part of why C&I retention reads 91 per cent.
Purnima Raje — Partner, Ekagra Growth Partners; Mumbai (board)
Pick the segment with the best net revenue retention; do not start a platform rebuild on eleven months of cash.
Not saying: her fund is itself raising, and a signed Gulf licence reads well in a portfolio update whatever it does to the roadmap.

7. Voices

“We are not losing customers because they dislike us. We are losing them because their businesses close. Show me one exit interview saying the product failed.”

Hui Min Goh, product review call, 16 September 2026

“We have exit reasons for 44 per cent of churn, typed by the people whose jobs depend on the answer. I am not saying you are wrong. I am saying we do not know, and the deck treats not-knowing as good news.”

Jerome Fernandes, same call, 06:15 in Toronto

“Fifty-two per cent very disappointed. Anywhere else that is the opening slide. Why are we explaining it away?”

Balachandran Nair, internal thread, 17 September

“Because they are disappointed about the paperwork, Bala, and the portal does the paperwork now — in eleven states, better than we do. We are measuring affection for a feature that is being retired, and it is good for the country that it is.”

Uthara Menon, reply, 17 September

“Eight months means eight months. Every field in that schema assumes a consumer number, a circle office, a subsidy category. Nafahaat has none of them. You are not asking for a translation, you are asking for a second product.”

Devyani Kulkarni, architecture note, 21 September

“My crews do not care about fit. They care that a project takes fourteen weeks and nine of them are waiting. Paperwork was one wait. Inspection slots, meter availability, structural sign-off, customer payment, crew travel — five more, and we have built for none.”

Thomas Kurien, Technopark canteen, 24 September

8. The options as Uthara currently sees them

Option A — Widen the installer product. Accept Hui Min's reading of Exhibit 1, treat the 52 per cent as real, and build the installer's business operating system: lead capture, lender tie-ups, crew scheduling, collections over UPI. The exposure is a segment paying ₹1.24 lakh a year, whose fee income tracks a government scheme, and whose affection is anchored to a module that is emptying out.

Option B — Commit to C&I and monitoring. Exhibit 3 puts 57 per cent of ARR there at ₹36.4 lakh an account, and Exhibit 4 shows monitoring as the one engagement series rising for the right reasons. But the segment is consolidating, Eshanya being the second such loss in eighteen months; the Nishkam exclusivity blocks the natural buyers until 31 March 2027; the benchmark clause removes the most defensible analytic Ekatra could build; and Nirdesh renewed on switching cost.

Option C — Take the Nafahaat licence. ₹3.1 crore in year one, a second geography, and a forcing function to separate the workflow engine from Indian regulatory semantics — work that must happen anyway. Against it: eight contested months on eleven months of cash, an escrow and buy-out clause Vikrant has not circulated, and no Indian roadmap while it runs.

Uthara had written those three on a whiteboard on Thursday and been dissatisfied since. Each names a customer segment as the unit of the decision. Thomas Kurien's five waits do not fit that frame; nor does the possibility Jerome raised and nobody took up, that Ekatra's real asset is four years of commissioning data on 41,000 projects, which the Nishkam clause restricts but does not extinguish. Nor does the option nobody wrote down: that Ekatra is a sound business with an eroding wedge, worth more to an acquirer with a distribution engine than to itself.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Friday, 2 October, in Mumbai. Cash: ₹19.4 crore, burn ₹1.7 crore a month. People: 78, of whom 41 are engineers and eleven sit in Pune; two senior backend engineers are flight risks; Ekatra cannot run two platform programmes at once and has never shipped outside India. Contracts: the Nafahaat licence lapses on 9 October and its April 2027 milestone is called a good-faith target in one clause and a payment trigger in another; the Nishkam exclusivity runs to 31 March 2027 and its benchmark restriction never expires; ₹12.4 crore of ARR renews between 15 January and 31 March 2027. Regulation: the portal will keep absorbing paperwork, state regulators will keep revising net-metering rules, and any product built on customer generation data must satisfy the DPDP Act's consent requirements — a point counsel has raised twice and nobody has costed.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Taking Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 together, where — if anywhere — does Ekatra have fit today? Which number would you most want to replace, and with what?
  2. Exhibit 1 shows 56 per cent installer logo retention; Exhibit 3 shows 112 per cent net revenue retention in the same segment. Both are correct. What is each measuring, and which should the board trust?
  3. Hui Min argues that churn caused by customers' businesses closing is not a fit problem. When is she right, and when does it make no difference here?
  4. Exhibit 2 clears the conventional threshold, yet the cited reason is the module Exhibit 4 shows emptying out. What does that imply about a delight survey as a leading indicator when the market, not the product, has changed?
  5. Was the 2022 decision to build around Indian form semantics a good one that has aged, or a bad one that paid for four years? What follows for how Ekatra treats the eight-month estimate?
  6. It is Monday morning, 28 September. What does Uthara do first, what does she refuse to do, and what does she say to the board on Friday — including what she admits she does not know, and how she will find out before January?

Sunday, 11:40 p.m.

Uthara opened the whiteboard photograph on her phone: three boxes in her own handwriting. She thought about Thomas's sentence in the canteen — nine weeks of waiting out of fourteen — and that no exhibit in Friday's pack measured it. She thought about the Nafahaat term sheet, and how much easier eight months would be to defend if she believed the number. She thought, last and least comfortably, about the possibility that Ekatra had genuinely had fit in 2024, and that nothing it did wrong had taken it away.

The rain started again. She did not add a fourth box.

Sanhita Legal Cloud: Which Fit Is Real?

Visakhapatnam, September 2026 — a product-market-fit decision ahead of a Series B term sheet

A deadline on Beach Road

On the morning of Monday, 28 September 2026, Ruchira Bhandari sat at her desk on the fourth floor of Sanhita Legal Cloud's office on Beach Road in Visakhapatnam, looking out at container ships queuing for the port and at a slide she had rewritten four times. In fifteen days, on 13 October, the board would meet to approve the product roadmap Sanhita would show the two venture funds negotiating its Series B term sheet. Srinivas Kotamraju, the co-founder and chief executive, had asked her for one recommendation, not three options with footnotes: where should the next eighteen months of engineering effort go. Ruchira had spent three weeks with a data scientist in Toronto pulling apart what Sanhita's numbers actually said about product-market fit, and the answer was more uncomfortable than the growth story the fundraise deck wanted.

Codifying the contract

Srinivas had started Sanhita in 2019 after years running legal operations at a large IT-services firm, watching contract drafts move between lawyers as tracked-changes Word files, with renewal dates kept on a shared Excel sheet nobody trusted. Sanhita — Sanskrit for a codified collection — let in-house legal teams draft from an approved clause library, route drafts through configurable approval workflows, and track obligations and renewal dates after signature, integrating with e-signature platforms such as Leegality and Digio. Its libraries stayed current with regulatory change: data-processing-agreement clauses for the DPDP Act, related-party language for SEBI's listing norms, GST references in vendor terms. Sanhita competed for mid-market attention against SpotDraft and Leegality's own CLM module, and against Icertis and DocuSign CLM further up-market; below it, most small firms still ran contracts through Word and Outlook. By September 2026 Sanhita served 545 paying customers — mostly firms with 300 to 3,000 employees across D2C consumer brands, NBFC and fintech lenders, and IT-services boutiques — and had reached roughly ₹32 crore in annual recurring revenue.

The numbers Ruchira cannot ignore

Quarter-on-quarter growth had slowed from above 30 per cent through 2023 and 2024 to 9 per cent in the June 2026 quarter, and renewal conversations that used to be formalities were turning into negotiations. Daniel Cho, Sanhita's data scientist in Toronto, had built a cohort-retention analysis (Exhibit 1) that worried Ruchira more than the growth number itself: the core mid-market cohort's logo retention did not flatten early and high, the pattern associated with durable fit; it kept eroding until month nine and settled at only 57 per cent. A second cohort told a different story. In 2024 Sanhita had opened a free clause-library tier that caught on among ONDC-registered D2C sellers needing standard vendor and marketplace agreements; the 240 customers who converted to a paid self-serve plan showed retention flattening by month six and holding at 81 per cent. Mei Lin Tan, Sanhita's customer-success lead in Singapore, had watched the mid-market pattern up close: renewal calls that opened with "we need a discount" and closed with a shorter term. Meanwhile Priyanka Oberoi, Sanhita's sales head in New Jersey, had spent four months negotiating with Farid Al-Rashidi, general counsel of a trading and logistics group headquartered in Dubai, who was prepared to sign a three-year contract worth ₹4.2 crore a year — about 13 per cent of current ARR from one logo — if Sanhita built the multi-entity approval hierarchies and board-resolution workflows his group's seven subsidiaries required. Elena Krause, Sanhita's product designer in Berlin, estimated the module would occupy the entire nine-person team for two quarters, crowding out everything else. A Sean Ellis-style survey run in August (Exhibit 2) sharpened the picture: only 28 per cent of mid-market users said they would be "very disappointed" without Sanhita, below the 40 per cent benchmark read as evidence of fit, while self-serve cleared 46 per cent. Eighteen enterprise pilot users, three at Al-Rashidi's own subsidiaries, scored 61 per cent, but Daniel Cho flagged eighteen respondents as far too small a sample to trust with a fundraise on the line.

The people in the room

Ruchira Bhandari, VP Product, Visakhapatnam
Wants a recommendation she can defend to the board with evidence, not a slide chosen to flatter the fundraise story.
Srinivas Kotamraju, co-founder and CEO, Visakhapatnam
Wants a growth number investors can underwrite by 13 October, and is drawn to the Dubai contract because one large, name-brand logo is easy to explain to a term-sheet committee.
Priyanka Oberoi, Head of Sales, New Jersey
Has invested four months in Farid Al-Rashidi and does not want to walk away from a ₹4.2-crore, three-year contract that would make her quarter.
Mei Lin Tan, Customer Success Lead, Singapore
Wants engineering time spent on why mid-market customers disengage after month six, and believes self-serve is starved of attention its numbers deserve.

Exhibit 1 — Twelve-month logo retention by cohort

Exhibit 1. Logo retention by month since first invoice, indexed to 100% at month 0. Enterprise-pilot accounts are excluded: the segment is nine months old and has five customers, too few and too young for a curve.

Exhibit 3 — Segment economics, year to date

Three paths forward

Option A: Repair the core

Freeze new-segment commitments and put the product team on the mid-market drop-off itself — the stretch between month three and month nine where Exhibit 1 shows customers disengaging. Ruchira's early diagnosis, drawn from tickets Mei Lin Tan has logged, points to weak onboarding: legal teams buy Sanhita after a persuasive demo but never migrate their existing clause library in, so usage never becomes habitual. The upside is that this addresses the segment carrying 84 per cent of ARR with a fix that is squarely a product problem, not a market one. The cost is no new growth story for the board on 13 October, and telling the Dubai team to wait, risking the deal going to a competitor.

Option B: Take the Dubai deal and build enterprise

Sign Farid Al-Rashidi's contract, commit the engineering team for two quarters to the governance module, and use the logo to open enterprise conversations elsewhere. The upside is an immediate, contractually locked 13 per cent addition to ARR and a marquee name for the fundraise deck. The cost is that eighteen respondents and five accounts, three from the same client relationship, is a thin basis for believing Sanhita has found enterprise fit rather than simply won one negotiation; two quarters of the whole product team is two quarters the mid-market drop-off goes unaddressed.

Option C: Lean into self-serve

Redirect investment toward the startup segment, where Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 agree something real is happening: retention flattens early and high, and delight scores clear the classic benchmark. The upside is a genuine, repeatable signal and a product-led motion that could scale efficiently off the existing free tier. The cost is scale: at ₹60,000 average revenue per account, rebuilding today's ARR through this segment alone would take years, and it would mean telling Srinivas and Priyanka that this fundraise's growth story is a small, young segment rather than either larger, more familiar lever.

Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 suggest about where Sanhita truly has fit today, and where it does not, even though both segments show revenue?
  2. How much weight should the enterprise pilot's 61% score carry, given eighteen respondents and Al-Rashidi's dual role as prospect and reference?
  3. If mid-market retention is a product problem, what does that imply about spending two quarters of engineering time on the Dubai module instead?
  4. Which option should Ruchira recommend on 13 October, and what would she need to tell Srinivas and Priyanka to make it defensible?

A note for the learner

Product-market fit is segment-specific, not a single company-wide switch; a company can hold real fit in one pocket of its customer base while having lost it, or never found it, in another. The leading indicator is not revenue or logo count but the shape of the retention curve: a curve that flattens early and high, as the self-serve cohort's does at 81 per cent by month six, signals a market pulling the product toward itself. A curve that keeps eroding for nine months before settling at 57 per cent, as the mid-market cohort's does, signals a product customers buy but never build a habit around — and the Sean Ellis survey (28 per cent "very disappointed") corroborates rather than contradicts that reading. The Dubai contract deserves different scrutiny: closing one large, heavily customised deal after a long, relationship-driven sale is evidence that a skilled salesperson and a generous client found each other, not evidence that Sanhita has found enterprise-market fit; eighteen respondents, three inside the same buying group, cannot bear the weight the fundraise deck wants to put on them. A well-reasoned answer treats the mid-market retention problem as most urgent, because it sits under 84 per cent of current ARR and, on Mei Lin Tan's evidence, has an identifiable product cause. The defensible path is Option A, narrowed rather than absolute: commit the product team to fixing mid-market onboarding and activation, take a smaller, tightly scoped version of the Dubai contract that funds itself without consuming the whole roadmap, and fund self-serve as a separate, small, long-horizon bet rather than a pivot. What Ruchira should not do is let one large, persuasive logo stand in for a fit signal the company's own data says has not yet arrived.
