Product-Market Fit

Fit is not a milestone a company passes but a claim about a flow system — and most of the arithmetic that appears to confirm it is produced by contracts, switching costs, subsidised prices and compliance deadlines rather than by demand.

1. Two rooms, one question

On 14 October 2026, in a converted bungalow off Cenotaph Road in Chennai, Revathi Balasubramanian was preparing a board note she did not believe. She was chief product officer of Ishaara Clinical Systems, which sold inpatient-flow software — bed allocation, discharge coordination, nursing handover — to mid-sized hospital chains. Ishaara had closed the year at ₹19.4 crore of recurring revenue, up from ₹14.2 crore across thirty-four accounts, with net revenue retention of 104.2 per cent. The board had drawn the obvious conclusion: the product had found its market, and the next act was to take the sales team from nine to twenty-eight and spend ₹22 crore doing it.

Revathi's discomfort had a specific source. Her revenue operations lead, Faizal Rahman, working out of Kochi, had spent three weeks reading contracts rather than the billing system. Thirty-four accounts is too small a population for a retention curve to mean anything; one chain standardising on a rival moves the whole metric. So Faizal took expansion revenue apart line by line, and found that most of it had not been chosen by anyone.

Eleven hundred kilometres north-west, outside Ahmedabad, Ipsita Mahanta faced the opposite shape of the same problem. Her company, Yamini Cold Chain Systems, put temperature and door-state sensors into the cold rooms and reefer vehicles of pharmaceutical distributors and sold a dashboard and alerting service on top. In September 2026 Yamini had 1,180 devices live across ninety-six distributors, was installing ninety-five a month, and was on track for ₹20 crore of hardware revenue. Her Series B investors were unambiguous that this was fit. Ipsita, trained as a control engineer, kept returning to a figure nobody else found interesting: 2.4 per cent of installed devices came out every month. She suspected, correctly, that this number had already decided how big her company could ever be.

Both were asking the question this topic exists to answer — do we have fit, how would we know, could we lose it? Both had strong-looking evidence; neither had evidence that survived being taken apart.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Product-market fit is the condition in which a defined product, sold at a price that can fund the business, satisfies a defined need well enough that the market pulls the product forward rather than the company having to push it. Every clause is load-bearing, and the disagreements in the field are disagreements about which clause matters most.

The phrase was popularised by Marc Andreessen in 2007, in an essay arguing that market quality dominates team and product quality — that in a great market "the market pulls product out of the startup," and in a bad one nothing a good team does rescues it. He was writing against an error of his era: founders reading weak traction as an execution problem and answering it with marketing spend. Two years later Sean Ellis gave the idea an instrument, asking active users how they would feel if the product vanished and treating the share saying "very disappointed" as a leading indicator, with roughly 40 per cent as a threshold. Andy Rachleff formalised the sequencing: validate the value hypothesis before funding the growth hypothesis.

Four schools now disagree, and about signable propositions rather than emphasis. The market-first school (Andreessen, Rachleff) will sign that fit is found by choosing a market, not manufactured by iterating a product; it will not sign that any single metric detects it. The instrumentation school (Ellis and the growth practice downstream of him) will sign that fit has measurable leading indicators and that a company unable to produce them is guessing; it will not sign that clearing a threshold guarantees a business. The systems school, sharpest in Brian Balfour's argument that four fits must hold at once — market-product, product-channel, channel-model, model-market — will sign that a product can satisfy its users completely and still be unbuildable, because no channel delivers those users at a price the model can bear. The jobs school will sign that the unit of fit is a job in a circumstance, not a segment, and will not sign that fit can be read off telemetry.

3. Mechanics: what fit looks like when you take the aggregates apart

Expert practice begins not with a metric but with a decomposition, and the decomposition depends on whether the population is large or small. Ishaara's is small, so Faizal used growth accounting: a bridge from opening to closing recurring revenue in which every rupee is labelled new, expansion, contraction or churn. The step usually left implicit is the second pass, in which expansion is split by who decided it.

Figure 1 — Read left to right it is a healthy year. The dashed line marks the closing base once unchosen expansion is stripped out.

Of Ishaara's ₹2.9 crore of expansion, ₹0.9 crore was a price-indexed escalator written into nineteen contracts at signature; ₹0.7 crore was seat growth triggered automatically when a hospital added beds, which measures the customer's growth rather than the product's pull; only ₹1.3 crore was a customer choosing to buy something more. Recomputing retention on that ₹1.3 crore gives 93.0 per cent rather than 104.2 — absent contract mechanics, the same customers are shrinking. And ₹1.0 crore of it came from three accounts: thirty-one of thirty-four hospitals bought nothing new all year.

The second-order effects decide the enterprise reading, because with thirty-four accounts the revenue signal is too coarse. Genuine fit in complex sales leaves a signature in the sales process, and it has three parts that must move together: the cycle shortens, the discount off list narrows, and the win rate against the status quo rises. Ishaara had one of three. Median cycle had fallen from 214 days to 187, which the sales head called momentum; median discount had widened from 11 to 19 per cent, and the win rate against status quo had fallen from 38 to 29 per cent. The cycle had shortened because Ishaara had stopped bidding for tenders it always lost — selection, not pull.

Faizal's last cut was the most uncomfortable. Twenty-six of thirty-four accounts had exactly one named internal champion, usually a chief nursing officer or a quality head. Seven changed jobs in FY26, and five of those seven accounts contracted or churned, accounting for ₹1.7 crore of the ₹2.3 crore of downward movement. Ishaara had fit not with thirty-four hospitals but with twenty-six individuals who happened to work at hospitals that paid.

Ipsita's population is large enough for a more powerful formalism. Treat the installed base as a flow system: if a company installs a devices a month and loses a fraction c of its base each month, the base does not grow without limit — it asymptotes to a/c. At ninety-five installs and 2.4 per cent attrition, Yamini's ceiling is 95 ÷ 0.024 = 3,958 devices, and at ₹640 per device per month that is about ₹3.0 crore of recurring revenue, forever. The ₹20 crore of hardware revenue that impressed her investors is a flow proportional to gross installs, and says nothing about the ceiling.

Figure 2 — Halving attrition doubles the ceiling; doubling the sales team does not raise it at all. Note also that even the favourable curve reaches only about 4,600 devices in five years.

This is the formal core of the topic, and the reason fit is better understood as a rate than a state. A retention floor is the same claim drawn as a picture: the base stops falling when losses equal replacement. Two companies with identical revenue and different values of c have different maximum sizes.

4. Conditions, stated as testable claims

The idea applies where four claims hold, each checkable rather than assertable. First: usage is voluntary and repeatable, so that continuing to use the product carries information. For Ishaara this fails partially — nurses use the software because the hospital bought it. For Yamini it fails harder: distributors keep the sensors to satisfy state drug-control inspectors who require temperature logs, and retention under compulsion measures the compulsion. Second: the price tested can fund the business. Third: the population is large enough for the instrument. Yamini's 1,180 devices support cohort arithmetic; Ishaara's thirty-four accounts do not, which is why Faizal read contracts. Fourth: the decision is not forced by an exogenous deadline. Ipsita's fastest quarter coincided with a state licensing renewal cycle.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. In genuinely episodic purchases — a wedding, a house, a corporate restructuring — buyer retention is meaningless, and measuring it produces confident nonsense. Where the regulator rather than the user is the effective buyer, a flat retention curve is a compliance curve. And in a market that does not yet exist, absence of pull is the expected state rather than a verdict.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Yaadgaar Event Networks, a Jaipur marketplace matching wedding and event buyers with caterers, decorators and photographers, is the two-sided case at its hardest. Demand is once-in-a-lifetime: buyer retention does not exist, so fit must be read from the supply side and from liquidity. Last quarter 8,900 buyer briefs drew three or more quotes within forty-eight hours 61 per cent of the time. Of 2,300 vendors, 640 won two or more paid jobs and returned next quarter 78 per cent of the time; vendors winning one or none returned 22 per cent of the time. Blended vendor retention is therefore 37.6 per cent, so Yaadgaar must re-recruit three-fifths of its supply every quarter to stand still. Real fit sits inside this business — for the 640 — with a recruitment treadmill wrapped around it.

The AI-native case breaks differently. Inkishaf Contract Intelligence, in Gurugram, reviews commercial contracts for corporate legal teams at ₹65,000 per account per month against variable inference and retrieval costs of about ₹34 per document. At the average account's 1,450 documents a month that is a 24 per cent gross margin; at the top usage band it inverts completely.

Figure 3 — Three accounts sit in the right-hand band. They also have the longest tenure and the warmest references.

Inkishaf's most devoted customers are its least viable, and its thirty-day retention is flattered further by a free credit pool: of 120 trial accounts, 78 per cent were active at day thirty, but of the forty-one whose credits ran out and who were asked for a card, eleven converted — 26.8 per cent. The rest was the subsidy talking.

The organisational seam is where mature companies behave differently from how they describe themselves. Publicly, large firms re-test fit for each new product line. In practice a second module inherits the first's distribution, brand, procurement relationship and renewal date, so its retention measures the bundle rather than the module. Ishaara's discharge module renewed at 100 per cent because it sat on the same purchase order as bed management. The honest test is counterfactual: would this have been bought, at this price, by someone who did not already own the first module?

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The unit of fit is a job in a circumstance, not a customer segment. Competent practitioners segment by industry, size or geography because that is how the CRM is organised. The tell is that a segment cut explains less variance in retention than a cut by triggering event: Yamini's distributors split far more cleanly by "has failed an inspection in the last eighteen months" than by state or revenue band. Demand is produced by a situation, and situations cross segments.

Retention floors can be manufactured. A floor made of switching costs, annual contracts, regulatory logs or a below-cost price looks identical in a chart to a floor made of love. The tell is timing: manufactured floors churn when the constraint lifts — renewal dates, the start of a financial year, the end of a credit pool — while genuine floors churn evenly.

Net revenue retention above 100 per cent is frequently contractual. The tell is that expansion revenue is smooth, arrives in April, and correlates with the escalation clause rather than with usage. Splitting expansion into chosen and automatic takes an afternoon and routinely moves the number ten points or more.

Fit is a rate, and the ceiling is already visible. The most useful arithmetic in the topic is a/c. Competent practitioners forecast growth from a plan; experts compute the steady state implied by today's behaviour and treat the gap between it and the plan as the thing requiring explanation. The tell of someone who has internalised this is that they greet a churn improvement more warmly than a hiring plan.

In complex sales, fit is often person-fit. The tell is champion concentration: count accounts with one advocate, then count renewals that survived that advocate leaving. Ishaara's five of seven says the product had not become institutional. The obvious reading, that enthusiastic champions evidence fit, is half right — they evidence fit with a person, which is the fit that walks out of the building.

The denominator of a satisfaction survey does more work than its threshold. Practitioners argue about 40 per cent while surveying only currently active users, which excludes everyone the product has already failed. The tell is a stable score alongside a falling base. The more informative population is the lapsed one.

Fit decays because the alternative improves, not because the product worsens. Fit is relative to the best available substitute, including doing nothing. The tell is a stable satisfaction score with a falling win rate against status quo: customers still like you, and new buyers no longer need you. This is how incumbents lose fit while every internal metric holds steady.

Enthusiasm and unit economics can point in opposite directions. Where marginal cost is real — inference, delivery, field service, support — the most engaged cohort can be the least profitable, and a company optimising for engagement optimises its way into a loss. The tell is a negative correlation between usage intensity and account margin, which almost no dashboard computes.

Fit is necessary and nowhere near sufficient. A product can satisfy its users completely and still have no viable business, because the market is too small, the channel too expensive or the willingness to pay too low. The tell is a team that has proven fit and still cannot say how the next ten thousand customers get reached at a cost the model absorbs.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

The real differences are differences in instrument, not in concept. In consumer products the user is the buyer and usage is frequent, so cohort retention and direct survey are cheap and work well. In enterprise software the buyer, the champion and the user are three different people; the instruments become expansion decomposition, win rate against status quo, discount depth and champion resilience, and samples are too small for curves. In marketplaces fit is a conjunction of two conditions plus a liquidity threshold, and the side with episodic demand cannot be measured on retention at all. In hardware-plus-software the decisive quantity is attrition of the installed base, because revenue arrives at installation and hides the ceiling. In AI products every retention figure must be read net of inference cost and of any credit subsidy.

Where the difference is overstated: the underlying question — would this customer, unforced, choose this again at a price that funds us — is identical in all five, and so are the failure modes. By stage, a seed company asks whether fit exists anywhere; a growth company asks whether the fit it has is large and reachable enough to justify the spend, which is Revathi's question; a mature company asks, per product line, whether fit is re-earned or inherited.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

The first two are worked through above. Ishaara resolves into a measurable claim: narrow institutional fit, ₹1.3 crore of volitional expansion concentrated in three accounts, gross retention of 83.8 per cent, and a thirty-three-month payback that cannot support tripling a sales team. Yamini resolves into a ceiling of 3,958 devices and the discovery that ninety-six distributors are two products: twenty-one who buy the analytics tier and lose 0.4 per cent of devices a month, and seventy-five who buy a compliance log and lose 3.1 per cent. Aimed only at analytics buyers, the same ninety-five installs a month imply a ceiling of 23,750 devices — six times the business from the same sales effort.

The failure is Ikhtiyaar Payroll Cloud of Noida, which sold payroll and provident-fund compliance software to small firms at ₹49 per employee per month from 2019. Its cohorts flattened at 71 per cent by month nine and stayed there for three years — as clean a floor as any textbook shows. On that evidence it raised capital, hired, and in the third quarter of FY24 raised the price to ₹99 to fix a gross margin that had never worked.

Figure 4 — A floor that was never load-bearing: held up by a below-cost price and by the fact that nobody migrates payroll mid-year.

Within two quarters, month-thirteen retention of the repriced cohorts fell from 71 to 38 per cent, and recurring revenue fell from ₹31 crore to ₹19 crore over four quarters. The post-mortem found two supports, neither of them fit. The price had been below the cost to serve, so the floor was partly purchased. And 58 per cent of annual churn had always fallen in March and April, because no small firm changes payroll provider mid-financial-year — a seasonality a blended monthly rate had smoothed into invisibility. The recovery was a re-cut rather than a pivot: the accounts that absorbed the rise without complaint were staffing and facilities-management firms with very high workforce turnover, constant users of the onboarding and exit modules, 14 per cent of accounts and 41 per cent of surviving revenue. Ikhtiyaar repriced to ₹149 with a filing guarantee, stopped selling to everyone else, and rebuilt to ₹27 crore over five quarters at more than twice the gross margin.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Reading a manufactured floor as fit. Early sign: churn clustered in one or two months of the calendar. Diagnostic: what would have to become easier for a dissatisfied customer to leave tomorrow? Caught late, the cost is a two-year revenue decline — Ikhtiyaar's case.

Scaling distribution on inherited retention. Early sign: a new module's renewal rate equals the flagship's to the decimal. Diagnostic: would this have been bought standalone, at this price? Caught late, a sales organisation is built on a demand signal that does not exist.

Confusing customer growth with product pull. Early sign: expansion tracks the customer's headcount or bed count rather than usage. Diagnostic: strip automatic expansion and recompute. Caught late, a downturn in the customer's industry reads as a product failure.

Optimising for the most enthusiastic cohort. Early sign: the highest-usage accounts have the lowest margins. Diagnostic: rank accounts by margin and by satisfaction and look at the correlation. Caught late, growth accelerates losses.

Measuring fit on a population that cannot leave. Early sign: the buying trigger is an audit or licensing deadline. Diagnostic: what share of renewals fall within sixty days of a compliance date? Caught late, a change in the rule removes the business overnight.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Three disagreements are live and none is settled by available evidence. The first is whether fit is a phase change or a continuum. The threshold camp points to observed discontinuities in retention floors and founders' near-universal report that something changed in an identifiable month. The continuum camp notes that almost every published inflection is visible only in hindsight; for it to be wrong, someone would have to show a discontinuity predicted in advance rather than named afterwards. Nobody has published that.

The second is whether the 40 per cent benchmark means anything. Its defenders note real predictive content in consumer software and that practitioners need a usable prior. Its critics observe that the sample came from companies already engaged with a growth consultant, with no published control group of failures scoring above 40 — a survivorship problem no public dataset can currently settle.

The third, with the most money riding on it in 2026, is whether fit can be declared at negative gross margin. One camp holds that demand is demand: if buyers would be distraught without the product, fit exists and cost curves fall. The other holds that a product sold below marginal cost has tested a price that cannot fund the business, and so has not tested fit at all. The first is right whenever cost falls faster than competition erodes price; the second whenever it does not, and which obtains for AI inference is an article of faith on both sides.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic reports a metric. Someone who has internalised it reports a decomposition and names the mechanism behind each part. They ask for churn plotted against the calendar before churn plotted against tenure. They compute a/c early in any recurring-revenue conversation and treat the answer as a constraint rather than a forecast. They distinguish, in every renewal, between a customer who chose and a customer who did not decline. And they are unembarrassed to say “we have fit with this job at this price and not with that one.”

12. The decisions, and three questions

Revathi did not present the 104.2 per cent. She presented Figure 1, Table 1 and the champion-turnover count, and argued that Ishaara had institutional fit with a narrow class of hospital — two-hundred-to-five-hundred-bed chains with a dedicated quality function — and personal fit with everyone else. She asked for six sales hires rather than nineteen, all aimed at that class, and for the discharge module to be priced separately from April. The board approved ₹9 crore instead of ₹22 crore.

Ipsita stopped the Series B expansion plan for a quarter, moved her field team from installations to reducing attrition in the log-only base, and repriced so the analytics tier was the default rather than an upsell — accepting a lower first-year hardware number for a ceiling six times higher. Her board found this harder to accept than Revathi's did, because the number that fell was the one investors had been rewarding.

Three questions for discussion. First: Ishaara's volitional retention is 93 per cent and its gross retention 83.8 per cent — at what level of either would you tell Revathi she has no fit at all, and what makes that threshold defensible rather than arbitrary? Second: Ipsita's attrition could be cut by product work, by pricing, or by refusing compliance-only buyers — which of those is a fit intervention and which are selection? Third: if Inkishaf's most devoted customers destroy the most value, has it found fit, a pricing error, or neither?

13. Going deeper

  • Retention curves and the PMF signal — the steady-state argument drawn as a picture; teaches you to read shape rather than level.
  • The Sean Ellis PMF survey — the leading indicator and its sampling assumptions; the denominator decides the answer.
  • Searching for product-market fit — what to do before the signal exists; the discovery loop that makes measurement worth taking.
  • What strategy is and isn't — fit says where you are, not what to do about it.
  • Rumelt's kernel — the natural container for a finding like Revathi's.
  • The product strategy document — where a fit decomposition becomes a commitment.
  • Risks and assumptions in strategy — writing down what would falsify your fit claim.
  • Playing to Win — turning a narrow fit into a defensible position.
  • Wardley mapping — why fit erodes as components commoditise.

Product-Market Fit

Do we have it, how would we know, and could we lose it — the question Devika Rao had eleven weeks to answer before her Series A term sheet expired.

1. A term sheet with a clause she didn't like

On the second Monday of September 2026, Devika Rao sat in her Pune office with a term sheet from a Bengaluru growth fund and a clause she kept re-reading. The fund would lead a ₹38 crore Series A for Qismat Learning Cloud, the exam-preparation app she had founded in early 2024 for aspirants preparing for the SSC CGL clerical exam, bank probationary-officer exams under IBPS, and Railway Recruitment Board postings. The clause said the first tranche of ₹22 crore would close only after Qismat's board reviewed "evidence of durable product-market fit," at a diligence session in six weeks.

Fourteen months after launch, Qismat had real numbers: 210,000 downloads, 48,000 monthly active users, ₹1.6 crore in monthly revenue from a ₹499-a-month plan. Devika's instinct was to walk in with the growth chart. Her data lead, Farhan Sheikh, working from Lucknow where a large share of users lived, had been warning her that growth and fit were not the same fact, and that the diligence team — having just walked away from another edtech deal over exactly this confusion — would ask whether users would be genuinely upset if the app disappeared tomorrow, and whether that feeling was strengthening or eroding as the cohort aged. She did not yet have a confident answer, and had eleven weeks to get one.

2. The idea: fit is a relationship, not a milestone

Product-market fit — PMF — is the condition in which a specific product satisfies a specific market so well that the market pulls the product forward rather than the company having to push it. The phrase was popularised by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen in a 2007 essay, written after he had lived through the difference at Netscape and his own earlier startups: he distinguished sharply between a good team executing brilliantly against a market that doesn't want the product ("nothing you do matters") and a mediocre team with a product a hungry market wants ("the market pulls product out of the startup"). It was not a formula but a reorientation, telling founders to stop treating weak growth as an execution problem solved with more marketing spend, and start asking whether offering and need were matched well enough to justify that spend at all.

Two years later, growth consultant Sean Ellis turned that qualitative idea into something measurable: ask active users how they would feel if they could no longer use the product, and treat the share who say "very disappointed" as a leading indicator of fit, with roughly 40% as the threshold above which companies in his sample tended to have durable, defensible traction. The sentence Devika could say in the diligence session without sounding glib is this: product-market fit is not a size you reach, it is a signal you keep checking, because a market that wants you today can stop wanting you as competitors, prices, and habits shift.

"Product-market fit is not a size you reach, it is a signal you keep checking."

3. How the signal is actually built

Practitioners talk about PMF as though it announces itself, but assembling real evidence takes steps usually left implicit. The first is choosing the right unit of analysis: not "Qismat" as a whole but a specific product serving a specific segment, since a company can have strong fit with bank-exam aspirants and weak fit with railway-exam aspirants inside the same app. The second is picking a cohort and holding it fixed — everyone who signed up in a given month — so later months compare against a stable starting population, not one inflated by fresh signups, the commonest way founders accidentally flatter their own retention chart.

The third step is plotting retention, not signups or revenue, month by month, watching the shape rather than the level: a curve that keeps falling toward zero says the product is a novelty that wears off, while one that settles onto a horizontal line — sometimes called the "smile" or the retention floor — says a real core has decided to stay, the closest thing to hard, revealed-preference proof of fit. The fourth is running the Sean Ellis survey only on users with enough time to feel the product's value, typically two or more weeks, since day-one signups mostly measure curiosity. The final step, the one Farhan kept pressing on, is refusing to trust the aggregate number until it has been cut by the segments a serious investor would ask about, since an average can hide two very different stories stacked on top of each other.

4. Reading Qismat's own numbers

Farhan pulled the January 2026 signup cohort, 10,000 aspirants, and tracked how many opened the app at least three times each following month. The aggregate line was discouraging: from 3,750 active users in month one (37.5%) it fell to 2,725 (27.3%), 2,075 (20.8%), 1,675 (16.8%), 1,450 (14.5%), and 1,275 by month six (12.8%) — still sliding, no floor in sight. Read on its own, that curve argues against a Series A.

Fig. 1 — Six-month retention of the January 2026 signup cohort (n=10,000), disaggregated by exam category. The aggregate line looks like slow decay; the banking-exam sub-cohort has already flattened.

The second pass changed the input Farhan and Devika had been holding fixed: instead of one cohort, they split it by exam category. The 2,500 banking-exam users moved from 1,125 active in month one (45.0%) to 1,000 (40.0%), 950 (38.0%), 925 (37.0%), 925 (37.0%), and 900 by month six (36.0%) — a curve that stopped falling in month four and sat there. The remaining 7,500 users, mostly railway and other state exams, told the opposite story: 2,625 in month one (35.0%) collapsed to 1,725 (23.0%), 1,125 (15.0%), 750 (10.0%), 525 (7.0%), and 375 by month six (5.0%), no floor in sight. The Sean Ellis survey, sent that week to 1,200 users active a month or more, confirmed the split: of all respondents, 396 said they would be "very disappointed" without Qismat — 33%, short of the 40% benchmark. Among the 300 banking-exam respondents, 150 said very disappointed, exactly 50%; among the 900 railway/other respondents, only 246 did, 27.3%.

Changing that one input — the level at which the data was cut — reversed the aggregate's conclusion. Qismat did not lack product-market fit; it had strong, measurable fit with one beachhead and none yet with a second market it had expanded into too early — a fundamentally different, and far more fundable, problem than "the product doesn't work."

5. Six distinctions a learner has to sit with

Fit is a segment property, not a company property

The most common error is speaking as though a company either "has PMF" or doesn't. Qismat's numbers show why that breaks down: fit lives at the level of a specific product serving a specific group of people, and a single app can carry a floor for one segment while free-falling for another underneath the same aggregate metric.

The survey is a leading indicator, not proof

A 50% "very disappointed" score signals latent attachment, but it is stated preference from people who chose to respond — the 1,200 who answered were a quarter of Qismat's active base, and the quieter three-quarters are likely more lukewarm. The retention curve, what people actually did with their time, is the harder evidence; treat the survey as an early warning, read alongside its response rate, not a verdict on its own.

PMF, growth, and revenue are three different questions

A product can have a loyal core and still grow slowly for lack of an acquisition engine, or grow quickly on paid marketing while almost nobody stays once the coupon expires. Confusing the two leads founders to abandon a fit they already have, or keep spending on growth for one they don't. Revenue is a third signal: ₹499-a-month payments are encouraging, but can rise for reasons unrelated to fit — a festival discount, a placement season — so read it alongside retention and the survey, never alone.

Fit can be lost as quietly as it was won

A curve that flattened last year can start eroding this year if a well-funded rival enters the same beachhead, the syllabus changes, or habits move to a channel the product doesn't reach. PMF is a standing question to be re-asked, not a badge earned once.

The 40% threshold is a heuristic, not a law

Sean Ellis's benchmark came mostly from consumer software; it travels reasonably well but shifts by category — a habit-forming exam app should expect a higher bar than enterprise software used a few times a month.

PMF cannot tell you how big the market is

Fifty percent "very disappointed" says the relationship is strong; it says nothing about whether that population can support a venture-scale business, a separate market-sizing question Devika still had to answer before betting the company on that beachhead.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and company stage

The mechanics change with context. In a consumer app like Qismat, retention and the Sean Ellis survey are cheap to run at scale, since usage is frequent and the user is also the buyer. In B2B software, the buyer and daily user often differ, accounts are few, and a more useful signal is expansion — whether accounts add seats or renew without a discount fight — supplemented by candid reference customers rather than a thousand-response survey. In a marketplace, fit is a double condition: supply and demand must each independently want to stay, and buyer retention can look excellent while sellers quietly leave, invisible unless both sides are measured on their own cohort curves.

Company stage matters too. A young startup asks whether fit exists at all, for any segment; a company as large as India's established edtech names — Byju's, Unacademy, Physics Wallah, Testbook — mostly does not ask that about its flagship product anymore, but must ask it fresh with every new subject or price tier, since each is effectively a new product-market pair earning its own retention curve.

7. Three mistakes to watch for

Averaging away the good news. Symptom: a blended retention number that has looked mediocre for a year. Misunderstanding: treating the company, not the segment, as the unit of fit. Diagnostic: cut last month's cohort by channel or use case and look for a slice that has already flattened.

Surveying too early. Symptom: a Sean Ellis score that swings wildly month to month. Misunderstanding: including brand-new signups who haven't yet felt the product's value. Diagnostic: restrict the survey to users active two to three weeks or more.

Mistaking a growth spike for fit. Symptom: a jump in signups after a marketing push, followed months later by an unexplained slump. Misunderstanding: reading acquisition success as product validation. Diagnostic: track the retention curve of that campaign's cohort separately from organic signups.

8. What good looks like

A rival firm, Qudrat Prep Networks, offers the contrast Devika wished she'd seen a year earlier. Qudrat launched eight months before Qismat but committed from day one to a single beachhead — bank-exam aspirants only — refusing pressure from an angel investor to "cover all exams and look bigger." By month six its cohort retention had already flattened near 40%, and its Sean Ellis score cleared the benchmark on the first survey wave, because every design decision had been built for one job and one audience rather than stretched across several. Qudrat's Series A closed in four weeks with no diligence clause attached, on a smaller valuation than Devika hoped for, but on evidence nobody in the room needed to argue about.

9. What Devika decided

Devika went into the diligence session with Figure 1 and Table 1, not the growth chart. She proposed narrowing Qismat's roadmap and marketing spend to the banking-exam segment for two quarters, treating railway and "other exams" users as a holding pattern, and re-running the cohort analysis and survey in December before expanding into a second beachhead. The fund took the first tranche of ₹22 crore on those terms, with the diligence clause rewritten around banking-segment retention rather than the company-wide number. The lesson she repeated to Farhan was not that Qismat had been failing — it was that she had almost let one poorly chosen average talk her out of a real, well-earned pocket of fit. The natural next topic is how a founder actively searches for fit before it exists, rather than merely measuring it once a product is live. Two questions worth sitting with: what is the smallest, most defensible segment you could re-cut a discouraging retention number by before concluding the product doesn't work — and how would you know if a fit you already have is quietly eroding before your growth chart tells you?

Strategy Narrative and Memo

Near-expert treatment: writing a strategy that survives being retold by people who were not in the room.

1. Two rooms, two decisions

On 12 November 2026, in a converted warehouse off the Indore bypass, Nandita Karve, Chief Product Officer of Fasal Kendra Agri Exchange, read a one-line note from her chairman before the quarterly board call: "GMV story or margin story? Pick one before Thursday." Fasal Kendra matched farmer producer organisations to institutional buyers — mills, food processors, two packaged-goods majors — across twelve procurement corridors, from soyabean in Malwa to maize in the Krishna delta. FY26 closed at ₹1,048 crore of gross merchandise value and ₹19.9 crore of platform revenue at a blended 1.9% take rate. Her engineering capacity for the next eighteen months was fourteen people and would not grow. Two credible plans sat on her desk, sponsored by executives who had stopped speaking about it: Balwinder Sahni in Ludhiana wanted eight new corridors; Revathi Iyer in Chennai wanted grading, escrow settlement and a working-capital line in the four she already had.

That same week in Coimbatore, Sridhar Venkataraman, VP Product at Falak Metering Systems, was defending a different sentence. Falak shipped energy sub-meters into textile mills in Tiruppur and Erode — 2,100 units in FY26 — with an analytics subscription alongside. His CEO, Kalpana Rao, had asked a question that sounded rhetorical and was not: "Are we a hardware company that sells software, or a software company that ships a sensor?" Sridhar's firmware lead, Arunabha Sen in Kolkata, had a roadmap for a cheaper second-generation meter. His channel head, Imtiaz Qureshi in Surat, was paid on meter volume and had heard a rumour of an open ingest letting Falak's analytics run on a rival's hardware. Both faced the same problem: not what to decide, but how to write the decision so it stayed intact, and refused correctly, when a district sales manager repeated it to a customer in March.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A strategy narrative is a short written artefact — one to six pages of connected prose, not bullets — stating a diagnosis, the choice it forces, what that choice excludes, when the exclusion would be revisited, and what would count as being wrong. Its distinguishing property is transmissibility under loss: it must survive being retold, imperfectly, by someone who read it once and was not in the room. The memo is the document; the narrative is the structure inside it that makes retelling faithful.

Three lineages are usually blurred together. The consulting lineage runs through Barbara Minto's pyramid work at McKinsey, which formalised situation–complication–question–answer and insisted the answer come first. The operating lineage runs through Andy Grove's plan-of-record discipline and Amazon's 2004 replacement of slide decks with six-page memos read in silence, on the theory that prose exposes the joins bullets hide. The market-framing lineage — Horowitz on the CEO as keeper of the story, later Dunford on positioning — treats the narrative as an instrument for moving people. The three want different things from one document, and that is where practitioners divide.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Rumelt's kernel"A narrative without a diagnosis is a wish list in better prose.""A memorable line is part of the strategy."
Minto / SCQA consulting"Answer first; structure is the argument.""It needs an arc or an emotional register."
Amazon narrative-memo"Prose is the thinking, not its packaging.""Optimise the memo for hallway retelling."
Playing to Win"Where we will not play is first-class text.""One narrative can serve a multi-business portfolio."
Market-framing / positioning"Its job is to move people who owe you nothing.""It is primarily an internal artefact."
OKR / plan-of-record"People repeat what they are measured on.""A story moves behaviour more than a pay line."

The disagreement is not cosmetic. The Amazon school and the retelling school pull opposite ways: a document built for silent reading rewards qualification, while one built for retelling must shed it to travel. Nandita, facing a field organisation in eleven states, and Sridhar, facing one CEO and one channel head, need not make the same trade.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice has a quantitative core usually left implicit. The narrative's force comes from one number the chosen path makes worse, and from which single assumption, if wrong, flips the ranking. Everything else is scaffolding. Consider the model built by Fasal Kendra's CFO, Sarvesh Menon, in Mumbai.

Corridor throughput is governed by fill rate — the share of listed lots clearing within 48 hours — which rises with buyer density and saturates. The fitted relationship is f = b / (b + 6), where b is active buyers per corridor per month. At today's four buyers, f = 0.40. Each corridor lists about 1,400 lots a month at ₹1.30 lakh a lot, so potential monthly GMV per corridor is ₹18.2 crore. Twelve corridors over twelve months give ₹2,620.8 crore of potential; at f = 0.40 that realises ₹1,048.3 crore, and at 1.9% the ₹19.9 crore Nandita reported.

Revathi's plan deepens four corridors: grading and escrow lift buyer density from 4 to 12, taking f to 0.667, and — the second-order effect — justify a 2.9% take rate rather than 1.9%, because the platform now carries settlement and quality risk rather than merely introducing parties. Those four corridors hold ₹873.6 crore of annual potential; at 0.667 they realise ₹582.4 crore, which at 2.9% yields ₹16.89 crore against ₹6.64 crore today. The untouched eight continue at ₹698.9 crore of GMV and ₹13.28 crore. Total: ₹1,281.3 crore of GMV and ₹30.17 crore of revenue, less ₹1.2 crore of assay-laboratory cost — ₹28.97 crore of contribution.

Balwinder's plan widens. Eight new corridors reach roughly 70% of mature listing volume within eighteen months: ₹152.9 crore of potential each, ₹1,223.0 crore in all, realising ₹489.2 crore at f = 0.40 and ₹9.30 crore at 1.9%. The existing twelve are unchanged at ₹19.92 crore. Total: ₹1,537.5 crore of GMV and ₹29.21 crore of revenue — but launch costs of ₹85 lakh a corridor, ₹6.8 crore in all, leave ₹22.41 crore of contribution.

Eighteen-month pathGMVRevenueDirect costContribution

Widen to twenty corridors₹1,538 cr₹29.21 cr₹6.80 cr₹22.41 cr

Two things fall out that no slide would have surfaced. First, deepening deliberately produces ₹257 crore less GMV — the number the board has quoted to investors for three years. A narrative that does not say so will be reversed the first quarter GMV misses. Second, the sensitivity rows identify the load-bearing assumption, and it is not the one the room argued about. If density reaches only 8 rather than 12, deepening still wins comfortably, ₹26.55 crore against ₹22.41 crore. If the take rate cannot be lifted, deepening falls to ₹23.15 crore and the plans sit within ₹74 lakh of each other. The strategy is a bet on pricing power, not liquidity — and the memo must say so in the sentence a district manager will repeat, naming Revathi as owner of the first three renegotiated contracts by 31 March.

4. When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

Three testable conditions govern whether a narrative is worth the fortnight it costs. First: the decision must be reversible by people who did not make it. Fasal Kendra passes emphatically — field staff in eleven states can quietly keep selling the widened footprint. Falak is borderline: three people can reverse Sridhar's choice, and all three sit in one building. Second: the choice must exclude something a reasonable colleague wants. Both pass; Balwinder and Imtiaz are the excluded parties, which is why both memos will be tested. Third: the analysis must stay stable longer than the retelling cycle. Fasal Kendra passes, since corridors move on agricultural seasons; an AI-native firm may fail outright.

The discipline actively misleads in two situations. When the analysis is genuinely unsettled, a narrative converts uncertainty into apparent conviction, and conviction travels faster than its caveats; the honest artefact is a list of open questions with owners. And when the real constraint is capability rather than choice — neither option can be executed — a well-argued allocation memo is a way of not discussing the hiring problem.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product portfolios break the single-narrative assumption. Odhani Apparel Networks, a Jaipur direct-to-consumer group, runs ethnic wear, workwear and kidswear at ₹128 crore, ₹54 crore and ₹28 crore of revenue and margins of 22%, 31% and 9% — ₹28.16 crore, ₹16.74 crore and ₹2.52 crore of a ₹47.42 crore total. Kidswear is 13.3% of revenue, 5.3% of contribution. Each general manager writes a defensible line-level narrative; the group version becomes an "and" list because nobody will write the sentence saying workwear is funded by ethnic wear and kidswear by neither. Mature groups do not solve this with one story: they write a portfolio memo whose only job is to state the funding direction between lines, and let each line keep its own.

Regulated markets change what an exclusion means. Oshadhi Care Networks, a Hyderabad teleconsultation and medicine-fulfilment platform, operates where the Drugs and Cosmetics framework, successive draft e-pharmacy rules and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 can each invalidate a "we will not build this" clause between planning cycles. The expert construction carries a named branch: the exclusion holds, here is the event that converts it into a commitment, here is who watches for it. Without the branch the organisation freezes or improvises.

Hardware-plus-software fails at the compensation seam — Falak's problem in its sharpest form. An open ingest running Falak's analytics on a competitor's meter is, in narrative terms, clean and defensible; in Imtiaz's quota it is a pay cut. Narratives fail not where they are disbelieved but where someone is paid against them, and the tell is an exclusion never argued with, merely not executed. AI-native firms face the opposite failure: Ojhal Intelligence Systems, a Bengaluru claims-extraction company, runs a narrative whose factual base moves quarterly. At 91% field-level extraction accuracy every claim still needs review, at about ₹96; at 97.5%, straight-through processing opens for the 62% of claims under ₹40,000 and blended cost falls to 0.62 × ₹9 + 0.38 × ₹96 = ₹42. A twelve-month memo with a fixed exclusion is dangerous when one model release crosses that threshold in six weeks; Ojhal writes six-month narratives with a capability tripwire and accepts rewriting more often.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The exclusion needs a reversal condition, not just conviction

A competent memo says what the company will not do. An expert memo says what would have to change that, who watches for it, and when it is reviewed. The tell is an organisation citing the "no" defensively rather than operationally — "we decided that already" — because an exclusion with no stated escape hatch reads as either permanent or arbitrary, and both readings suppress the information that should reopen it.

Name the number you are willing to make worse

Nandita's memo is only a strategy if it states that GMV will land ₹257 crore below the widened path. The obvious reading — lead with what improves — is wrong: a narrative that improves every metric offers no test of commitment and no defence when the sacrificed number misses. The tell: ask which line the CFO has been told to expect to disappoint, and watch whether anyone can answer.

Find the load-bearing assumption, not the loudest one

Fasal Kendra's room spent three weeks on buyer density, and the answer proved insensitive to it; the ranking flips on take rate. Experts run sensitivities before writing, to discover which assumption the story rests on, because that is the one the memo must name and instrument. The tell is a memo whose most-discussed and most decision-relevant variables coincide — usually a sign nobody tested the ranking.

Write for the person who must say no on your behalf

The intended reader is not the board or the all-hands. It is a district manager sitting opposite a customer asking for the excluded thing, with no slide and no escalation. Read the draft in that voice; if it supplies no sentence that person can say to a disappointed buyer, it is a board document in a memo's clothes.

Retelling decays asymmetrically

The "yes" survives retelling almost perfectly, the "no" drops out first, and numbers mutate by the third hop. This is not carelessness but a property of stories that flatter the teller. Experts instrument fidelity rather than assume it: ask five people in five locations for three sentences, count the versions, and note whether the exclusion appears at all.

Falsifiability must come with an owner and a date

"We will know by FY28" is not a tripwire. A tripwire is a named metric, a threshold, a named person and a review date already in a calendar. The obvious reading is that this is project hygiene; it is not. It is the only mechanism by which a narrative gets retired rather than quietly outlived, and its absence buys a story repeated correctly long after it stopped being true.

Drafting is the thinking; if it changed nothing, it is copy

A memo that took an afternoon and altered no one's view documented a decision rather than made one. The forcing function is prose: bullets let two incompatible clauses sit adjacent unnoticed; a sentence with a subject, a verb and a number does not. The tell is a draft with no deletions in its history.

The seam is where a narrative dies, and the seam is a pay line

Look for the person whose variable pay falls because of the choice: Falak's channel head, Odhani's kidswear GM. The expert move is to write that compensation change into the memo itself, because an exclusion that survives in the document and dies in the payroll is worse than none — it teaches the organisation that memos are decorative.

7. How the practice varies — and where it does not

Consumer products centre one archetype and one day; buyer and user coincide, so the narrative can be about experience. Business and enterprise products must centre the buyer's economics and, harder, the champion's story to their own boss — Fasal Kendra's memo must be repeatable by a procurement head justifying a 2.9% take rate to a mill owner. Marketplaces carry two protagonists and must say which side comes first; Nandita's memo is explicitly buyer-side, which costs her the supply organisation. Hardware adds irreversibility: Falak's Gen-2 tooling is an eighteen-month commitment with a bill of materials attached, so the memo must name the date after which reversal becomes expensive. AI products differ in cadence, not structure — Ojhal's memo is shorter-dated, not differently shaped.

Stage changes the job more than the text. At twenty people the strategy narrative and the fundraising story are nearly one document, read mostly by people who were in the room. At Fasal Kendra's scale its whole value is transmission to people who will never attend an offsite. At enterprise scale it becomes arbitration: what a general manager points at when refusing a peer. What does not change by stage is the need for the exclusion. Small companies are told they are too early to say no, large ones that they are too complex; both claims are a preference dressed as a constraint.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Falak Metering Systems. Per meter shipped, Sridhar's model reads: hardware margin of ₹22,000 less ₹14,800 of bill of materials, or ₹7,200; plus software, at a 38% attach rate, ₹1,247 of monthly contribution over a 22-month median life — 0.38 × ₹1,247 × 22 = ₹10,425. Total ₹17,625. Arunabha's Gen-2 plan cuts the bill of materials to ₹11,900, lifting hardware margin to ₹10,100 and volume to 3,000 units: 3,000 × ₹20,525 = ₹6.16 crore. The analytics plan leaves hardware at 2,300 units but lifts attach to 61% and median life to 34 months, worth ₹25,863 of software per meter, or ₹33,063 in all; plus 900 software-only subscriptions on rivals' meters at ₹42,398 each. Total: ₹1.66 + ₹7.60 + ₹3.82 = ₹11.42 crore — nearly double, and wholly dependent on the attach lift and the software-only pool, both running through Imtiaz.

Fasal Kendra. The Section 3 arithmetic is the second example, and its interest is the inversion: the recommended path reports a worse headline number for six quarters. Nandita's draft states the inversion before the recommendation.

Firdaus Hospitality Cloud, and the narrative that outlived its analysis. Firdaus, in Goa, sold property-management software to independent boutique hotels: 3,900 properties at ₹66,000 a year plus ₹5.3 crore of payments revenue, ₹31.0 crore of ARR in FY25. Its narrative — "the operating system for the independent hotel; we do not build chain-facing tooling" — was excellent by every test on this page: repeatable, exclusionary, dated, quoted accurately by joiners. It failed anyway. Over five quarters the share of the base taking a soft-brand affiliation with a national chain rose from 9% to 34%. Net revenue retention held at 104% in the unaffiliated cohort but fell to 61% in the affiliated one, because those properties adopted the chain's multi-property tooling and kept Firdaus only for the front desk. Blended: 0.66 × 104% + 0.34 × 61% = 89.4%, and ₹31.0 crore of base revenue decayed toward ₹27.7 crore before new sales. The excluded capability was the one that would have kept them.

The recovery is instructive because it was not a reversal. In Q3 FY27 the CEO, Harmeet Chadha, rewrote the memo around a narrower, more durable diagnosis: independents were not disappearing, they were being absorbed, and what they needed was a layer that kept them commercially distinct inside a chain's distribution. The exclusion moved rather than vanished — Firdaus still refused a chain-side revenue-management suite — and eleven months of multi-property and brand-compliance work lifted affiliated-cohort retention to 97% and ARR to ₹34.8 crore by FY28. Lateness cost six quarters of growth; the fix took under a year.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Exclusion dies at the pay lineNobody argues with the "no"; it is just not executedWhose variable pay falls if this is followed exactly?Two to three quarters spent on forbidden work
Narrative outlives its diagnosisQuoted accurately; feels increasingly abstractWhich metric would show this is now false, and who owns it?Firdaus: six quarters of growth
Numbers drift from the modelTwo teams quote the same figure differentlyWhen was the memo last reconciled to the live model?Credibility loss outlasting the correction
Written for delivery, not inheritanceFounder tells it well; joiners cannot a week laterHand a joiner the memo alone; time the cold retellingStrategy reopens every cycle at full cost
Conviction from thin analysisFine prose, one scenario, no sensitivityWhich assumption flips the ranking?A confidently wrong bet outrunning its correction

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Repeatability against precision. One camp holds that a narrative which cannot be retold has failed at its only job, citing the observable fact that field behaviour follows what people can say, not what they can look up. The other holds that a memo compressed for retelling loses the conditionality that makes strategy defensible, citing Amazon's practice of writing for silent reading precisely so nuance survives. The first camp is wrong if organisations reliably consult written strategy before acting; the second, if decisions are mostly made in rooms rather than customer conversations. The split correlates with span of control.

Ownership. Horowitz holds the narrative to be the chief executive's non-delegable work, since only the CEO can bind exclusions across functions. The product-leadership position is that a CEO-owned narrative becomes a fundraising story, unfalsifiable inside the company. The evidence is symmetrical: both camps point to firms that drifted.

Is narrative causal at all? The strongest sceptical position is that we read only the narratives of firms that won, and that crisp storytelling is a symptom of real advantage rather than a cause of it. Firdaus is the uncomfortable data point for enthusiasts: excellent narrative, correct retelling, wrong diagnosis. What would settle it is matched pairs — equally sharp narratives where one firm failed — and those are exactly the cases nobody writes up.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a good memo after the decision. Someone who has internalised it notices the memo will not write cleanly and takes that as a signal the decision is not yet made. They run sensitivities before drafting, not to defend the draft afterwards. They put the sacrificed number in the first paragraph, and the reversal condition and tripwire owner in the text rather than a follow-up email. They read the draft aloud as a district manager facing a disappointed customer. And they treat a stranger's clean retelling as necessary but not sufficient — Firdaus passed that test for five quarters while the world underneath it moved.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Nandita Karve chose to deepen. Her memo opens with the inversion: FY28 GMV will be roughly ₹257 crore lower than the alternative, on purpose, because the alternative buys volume the company cannot price. The exclusion is explicit — no new corridors before Q3 FY28 — with a reversal condition: if a competitor opens three or more Malwa-belt corridors with assay-backed grading, widening returns to the table. The tripwire is take rate, owned by Revathi Iyer, first three renegotiated contracts by 31 March. Balwinder Sahni appears in the memo as the executive whose plan was not chosen, with the reason stated in his own terms.

Sridhar Venkataraman chose the analytics path and wrote a shorter memo, his audience being three people. Its distinguishing feature is a paragraph most such documents omit: Imtiaz Qureshi's commission shifts from meter volume to subscribed meters under management in the same quarter the open ingest ships. Kalpana Rao's question is answered in one sentence Sridhar expects to be quoted back at him: Falak sells the measurement, not the meter.

Discussion questions. (1) Nandita asks a board to accept a worse headline number for six quarters on a take-rate assumption not yet tested with a single customer. Is that a strategy narrative or a bet dressed as one, and what would you require before signing it? (2) Firdaus's narrative passed every craft test here and still failed. Does that argue for shorter-dated narratives, for mandatory tripwires, or for less confidence in the genre? (3) Sridhar rewrote a compensation plan inside a strategy memo. Where does that paragraph belong, and what does the answer imply about who owns the narrative?

13. Going deeper

  • The product strategy document — the analysis the narrative compresses; without it the memo is confident prose over nothing.
  • Writing clearly — the mechanics that make prose a forcing function rather than decoration.
  • Selling the strategy internally — a narrative that survives retelling must still survive the quarter the numbers wobble.
  • What strategy is and isn't — separates strategy from goals and plans, which is what makes an exclusion possible.
  • Rumelt's kernel — diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action: the spine most good memos turn out to have.
  • Risks and assumptions in strategy — the discipline behind finding and instrumenting the load-bearing assumption.
  • Playing to Win: where to play, how to win — the cascade that makes "where we will not play" first-class.
  • Product-market fit — before fit, a narrative is a hypothesis; knowing which you have changes the memo's tense.
  • Wardley mapping — a complement for narratives whose diagnosis turns on how fast components are commoditising.

Kaarvaan Expense Cloud: Four Drafts of One Paragraph

A case for discussion. Figures in Indian rupees (₹ lakh = 100,000; ₹ crore = 10,000,000). Kaarvaan Expense Cloud, its channel, clients, rivals and investor are fictional; the institutions, regulations and brands around them are real.

1. Sunday night, 11 October 2026

The power flickered twice in Yamini Deshmukh's study in Arera Colony, Bhopal, before the inverter took over, and she read the same three sentences again. It was a little after eleven on Sunday, 11 October 2026. In fourteen hours she was due at a board offsite in Gurugram, and Friday's pre-read carried a section headed "Our strategy in one paragraph." She had written that paragraph four times since August. Draft one called Kaarvaan Expense Cloud "the travel and expense system built for how Indian enterprises actually approve money." Draft two called it "the compliance rail between every business trip and the GST return." Draft three, after Tarun Bhagat's Dubai trip, called it "the multi-country spend platform for emerging-market employers." Draft four, in the pre-read, said all three in ninety-one words, and Prateek Mundhra of Kanchan Growth Partners replied within the hour: "Yamini, I can't repeat this to my partners. Which one is it?"

Three clocks were running. The board wanted a direction on Monday. The exclusivity clause with Kinara Travel Management — the channel now carrying more than seventy per cent of enterprise revenue — renewed for three years unless Kaarvaan gave written notice by 31 October. And a letter of intent from Hadiqa Business Travel LLC in Dubai, for a white-labelled multi-country version, needed countersigning before Diwali week. Each clock implied a different paragraph. Yamini could not tell whether she had a writing problem, a strategy problem, or a company that had quietly become three companies while she was raising money.

2. How Kaarvaan was built, and the deal that still holds

Kaarvaan began in 2018 in two rented rooms near Bhopal's New Market, where Yamini, then thirty-one and four years out of a finance-shared-services job, had been reconciling travel claims for three manufacturers. She had watched a plant manager in Mandideep lose an ₹11,000 hotel bill and the input tax credit with it, because nobody had matched the invoice's GSTIN to the company's own. Her co-founder, Girish Talwar, a former payments engineer, built the core: a policy engine encoding an employer's own rules — grade-wise hotel caps, city tiers, who may approve a deviation — and a capture layer that read a bill, checked the GSTIN and pushed a clean line into the ERP.

The bet paid off in the middle market. By 2021 Kaarvaan had ninety-odd clients between ₹200 crore and ₹1,500 crore in turnover, sold by a small team on the phone from Bhopal. That was the year of the decision that still governs everything. A large deal — Himgiri Cement Works, 14,000 employees across nine plants — arrived through Kinara Travel Management, a TMC with desks in eleven cities and relationships Kaarvaan could not have bought. Kinara offered to carry Kaarvaan into every enterprise account it held. The price was exclusivity: for five years, any Indian employer above 5,000 employees would be sold Kaarvaan only through Kinara, at thirty-five per cent of contract value, with Kinara owning the relationship, the renewal, and — a clause nobody argued about — approval rights over any Kaarvaan-branded booking capability.

Yamini signed in a week; Kaarvaan had eleven months of cash and no enterprise brand. The agreement expires in March 2028 and renews for three years unless notice is given by 31 October 2026. A quieter decision followed: in 2022 the team built its own invoice-extraction stack rather than license one, arguing Indian hotel invoices were too messy for anything off the shelf. It took fourteen months and two of Girish's best engineers, and it worked. By 2025 rivals were doing comparable extraction with general-purpose models at a fraction of the cost.

3. The market Kaarvaan sits in

Corporate travel and expense in India is fought over by three kinds of firm, and Kaarvaan competes with all of them without looking like any of them. At the top sit global suites — SAP Concur above all — arriving bundled into ERP conversations and winning on the CFO's comfort rather than on Indian details. In the middle are Indian firms with distribution: Zoho's expense product inside a suite finance already runs, Happay's card-and-expense combination, a crowd of spend entrants. Alongside both are the TMCs and online agents — MakeMyTrip's corporate arm, EaseMyTrip, Cleartrip's business desks, houses like Kinara — who own the rate contracts and the employee's first click. Kaarvaan's differentiator has always been the boring middle: the approval hierarchy that matches how a conglomerate delegates authority, and the GST work that follows a trip.

Regulation has been the reliable tailwind: the phased lowering of the e-invoicing threshold, and the pressure to match input tax credit before filing, turned invoice hygiene from a finance preference into a board-level exposure. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act added a thread nobody planned for — itineraries are personal data, and since mid-2025 three large clients have asked in writing where employee travel data is processed. Air travel demand is strong, with IndiGo, Air India and Akasa Air expanding and hotel rates in Bengaluru and Mumbai up sharply in conference season, so travel budgets are visible enough that CFOs want control of them.

Kaarvaan's exposure abroad began as an accident. A Kalpvriksh Lifesciences executive who had used Kaarvaan in Hyderabad moved to a Gulf employer and asked whether it worked in the UAE. It did not: VAT is not GST, invoice formats differ, and approval chains in family-held Gulf groups do not resemble a listed Indian company's. Tarun Bhagat, who runs global accounts from New Jersey, followed the thread to Hadiqa Business Travel LLC, a Dubai TMC serving groups in the UAE, Oman and Saudi Arabia, which wants to white-label a policy-and-expense engine under its own brand. Its LOI values year one at AED 3.1 million, about ₹7.5 crore.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The last eighteen months read as a sequence of beliefs the company later found untrue.

In April 2025, Kaarvaan believed the Kinara channel would convert into direct relationships over time. Enterprise ARR rose from ₹24.0 crore to ₹41.8 crore in eighteen months (Exhibit 1). What turned out to be wrong: Kinara renewed fourteen of fifteen contracts in FY26, and in eleven Kaarvaan was not in the room. When Himgiri's group CIO asked for a roadmap conversation in June 2026, Kinara's account director attended and Kaarvaan's product director did not: Kinara is the customer of record.

In August 2025, as GST matching pressure intensified, Kaarvaan believed the mid-market would come to it: Ritwik Sahay's team shipped input-tax-credit reconciliation and sales raised list price eleven per cent. What turned out to be wrong: mid-market ARR has been flat for three half-years — ₹11.5 crore, ₹12.9, ₹13.4 — because finance heads did not buy a best-in-class module, they took whatever their accounting suite offered.

In January 2026, Kaarvaan believed its extraction accuracy was a moat, and Girish's benchmark still shows it ahead on messy Indian hotel invoices. What turned out weaker: in four losses this year the buyer never tested extraction. Hastakshar Spend Systems, a Chennai rival, and Hundi Expense Systems, which sells through chartered-accountancy firms, both demo a card-plus-app story in fifteen minutes.

In May 2026, after Tarun's first Dubai visit, Kaarvaan believed the Gulf was incremental revenue on an existing product. Multi-country work is not incremental: by the second quarter of FY27 it took forty-one per cent of sprint capacity for three per cent of revenue (Exhibit 6), and the VAT module promised for February is estimated at eleven to fourteen months.

And in July 2026, Yamini believed the confusion was external — a website problem. Then an onboarding survey asked seven joiners since April what Kaarvaan sells, in one line. Five answers differed materially. One salesperson wrote: "We are the Indian Concur, sold through Kinara." Another: "We are a GST compliance product that happens to do travel."

5. The people around the paragraph

Girish Talwar, co-founder and CTO, with a twenty-six-person pod in Bengaluru. Wants the Gulf fork stopped and eight months on reliability and the policy engine's rules language, which three clients find too rigid. Incentive: two senior engineers resigned in August. Not saying: he thinks the extraction advantage he built is gone.

Ritwik Sahay, Director of Product, Bhopal. Argues Kaarvaan should unbundle — sell the policy engine and GST layer to TMCs, ERP resellers, even rivals — but left it in a footnote because he expects Tarun to kill it. Incentive: his ITC module is the best thing he has shipped and is under-sold.

Bhavna Iyer, Head of Enterprise Sales, India, Bhopal, on the road three weeks a month. Position: Kinara must be renewed — without it there is no path into large employers, and her quota is channel pipeline. She sells what the CIO already believes Kaarvaan is: Kinara's software. Not saying: two Kinara account directors are steering clients to a rival for smaller sites, and she cannot prove it.

Tarun Bhagat, Head of Global Accounts, New Jersey. Position: the Gulf is what makes Kaarvaan fundable at a multiple India will not support. He has given Hadiqa a February date for the VAT module. Incentive: his variable pay is weighted to new-market bookings. Not saying: Hadiqa is also evaluating a global suite, and the LOI's value assumes a client count Hadiqa has not put in writing.

Lubna Qureshi, Customer Success Lead, Singapore, covering Indian accounts in her afternoon and Gulf accounts in her morning. Position: she needs one sentence she can say to a client without contradicting Kinara's desk. Not saying: she has begun writing her own description of Kaarvaan, because no official one survives a follow-up question.

Zoya Mirza, Data Scientist, Toronto, two years on contract. Built the telemetry behind Exhibit 4 and is uneasy about how it is quoted: usage says what customers do, not what they will pay for. Not saying: her contract ends in January and nobody has said whether it will be renewed.

Vivek Ranade, CFO, Bhopal, joined 2024 from a listed auto-components firm. Position: margin, not growth, is the story, and the board should see Exhibit 2 before Exhibit 1. Incentive: he owns the Series B and its ₹75 crore milestone. Not saying: on his own model, that milestone without Kinara needs either Tarun's Gulf revenue or a price rise the mid-market will refuse.

Prateek Mundhra, Partner, Kanchan Growth Partners, Delhi. Led the Series A, will lead or decline the B. Position: he does not care which story wins but will not underwrite three; he wants the paragraph and a list of what Kaarvaan will not build. Not saying: his firm has just written down a company that sold across three geographies on one engineering team.

6. Exhibits

The pre-read carried six exhibits. In Yamini's order they support the growth story; in Vivek's they do not.

7. Voices

"Every quarter we agree the policy engine is the crown jewel and every quarter it gets sixteen per cent of the sprint. I don't need a paragraph. I need to know which of the three roadmaps is real, so I can tell twenty-six people what they are doing in November."Girish Talwar, internal chat, 6 October 2026
"Hadiqa asked me a straight question: are you a platform company, or an India company with a Dubai project? I gave a long answer. They noticed it was long."Tarun Bhagat, email to Yamini and Vivek, 3 October 2026
"Your approval engine was better than the two others we looked at. We took the bundled option because in the meeting we still could not say what your company is for. That sounds unfair. It is what happened."Group CIO, Hariyali Agro Foods, in a loss debrief recorded by Lubna Qureshi, 22 August 2026
"Please don't put my usage chart next to Tarun's revenue chart without the footnote. One is measured and narrow. The other is an assumption with a decimal point."Zoya Mirza, message to Ritwik Sahay, 5 October 2026

8. The options as Yamini sees them on Sunday night

Option A — The compliance rail

Say Kaarvaan is the policy-and-compliance layer for large Indian employers: approval hierarchies, GST capture, audit. Renew Kinara, let the TMC own booking, kill the Gulf fork, spend FY28 on the rules language and reliability. Legible, and true to Exhibit 4. It also hands the customer relationship to Kinara for three more years and stakes the ₹75 crore milestone on a partner Bhavna already half-distrusts.

Option B — Own the whole trip

Give notice by 31 October, build direct enterprise sales, integrate airline and hotel rates, sell booking plus policy plus expense as one product. This is the story Bhavna's buyers half-believe and the one booking economics reward. It means competing with Kinara for Kinara's accounts, sixty hires, and a year of disruption inside a fourteen-month runway — with no model of what enterprise ARR does when the channel turns hostile.

Option C — The multi-country platform

Countersign Hadiqa, make the Gulf a second home market, tell the board Kaarvaan is an emerging-market spend platform. It is the largest number on any slide. It also rests on one unsigned counterparty, a module estimated at three times the promised timeline, and a roadmap that has stopped serving the Indian clients who pay the bills.

Yamini listed these three because they are the three ways money can arrive. Ritwik's footnote proposes a fourth: unbundle the policy and GST layer and sell it as embedded infrastructure to TMCs, ERP resellers and accounting-suite vendors — including, awkwardly, to Kinara. A fifth possibility nobody has written down is that the paragraph cannot be settled while all three revenue lines remain, and that the writing exercise has stood in for a choice about what to shut.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

  • The board offsite is Monday 12 October in Gurugram; Prateek wants the paragraph and a written list of what Kaarvaan will not build.
  • Notice of non-renewal must reach Kinara by 31 October 2026, or exclusivity extends to March 2031. Kinara's approval is also needed for any Kaarvaan-branded booking capability while it runs.
  • Hadiqa's LOI lapses unless countersigned before Diwali week, and commits Kaarvaan to a VAT module for February.
  • Cash: ₹31 crore, fourteen months at current burn. Kanchan's term sheet is conditioned on ₹75 crore ARR by 31 March 2027, which Vivek's model does not reach on India direct revenue.
  • People: hiring frozen since July but for two backfills; two senior engineers gone; Zoya's contract ends in January.
  • Regulation: three clients have DPDP questionnaires outstanding on itinerary data processed outside India, touching both the Toronto analytics work and any Gulf deployment.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Write, in no more than sixty words, the strategy statement Yamini should take to Gurugram, then have someone else repeat it back from memory.
  2. Which exhibit would you show the board first, and which would you refuse to show without its footnote read aloud? What does your ordering commit you to?
  3. The onboarding survey produced five different answers. Is that a writing failure, a strategy failure, or an incentive failure, and what would distinguish them?
  4. The 2021 Kinara agreement bought distribution and sold the customer relationship. What should Kaarvaan do about it by 31 October, and what does that do to each candidate narrative?
  5. Ritwik's unbundling idea sits in a footnote because he expects it to be killed. What does it say about Kaarvaan that the option nobody owns is the one nobody has costed?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Yamini do first, what does she say to the board, and what does she tell Girish, Bhavna and Tarun that afternoon, knowing each will repeat it to a different audience by Tuesday?

The rest of Sunday night

At a quarter to one, Yamini typed a heading in a new document — "What we will not build in FY28" — and sat looking at the empty space below it. She had written that list twice. The first time it had eleven items, four of which shipped by the quarter's end; the second time three, one of them the Gulf module now taking forty-one per cent of her engineering capacity. In the same folder sat the four drafts and the notice letter to Kinara, dated and unsent. Her phone showed Tarun: "Hadiqa asking if we can confirm Feb. Yes or no by Tuesday?" Below it, Girish: "Whatever you decide tomorrow, please decide it out loud."
